**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 1:**

(p-١)Surah al-An'am

Section on its revelation

Mujahid narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that al-An'am was among what was revealed in Makkah. This is also the view of al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Jabir ibn Zayd.

Yusuf ibn Mihran narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Surah [al-An'am] was revealed all at once at night in Makkah, and around it were seventy thousand angels.

Abu Salih narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: It is Makki, revealed all at once and revealed at night, and they wrote it down that same night, except for six verses, and they are: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden to you...﴾ to the end of the three verses, and His saying: ﴿They did not measure God with His due measure...﴾ the verse [6:151-153]. And His saying: "And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God," or he said: ﴿It has been revealed to me﴾ to the end of the two verses [6:93, 94]. Muqatil mentioned something similar and added two verses: His saying: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book know that it is sent down from your Lord in truth﴾ [6:114], and His saying: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognize it...﴾ [6:20].

(p-٢)It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah, who both said: It is Makki, except for two verses revealed in Madinah: His saying: ﴿They did not measure God with His due measure...﴾ the verse [6:91], and His saying: ﴿It is He who produced gardens, trellised and untrellised﴾ [6:141]. Abu al-Fath ibn Shaytha mentioned that it is Makki, except for two verses revealed in Madinah: ﴿Say: Come...﴾ and the one after it [6:151, 152].

﴿All praise is due to God, who created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light; then those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord.﴾

As for the interpretation, Ka'b said: The opening of al-Kahf is the opening of [al-An'am], and its conclusion is the conclusion of Hud. He mentioned the heavens and the earth only because they are among the greatest of created things.

By "made" (ja'ala) is meant "created." It has also been said that "ja'ala" here is redundant (silah), and the meaning is: and the darknesses. Regarding what is meant by the darknesses and the light, there are three views. The first: disbelief and faith, said by al-Hasan. The second: night and day, said by al-Suddi. The third: all darknesses and lights.

Qatadah said: God created the heavens before the earth, the darknesses before the light, and Paradise before Hellfire.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then those who disbelieve﴾, meaning: the polytheists, after this clarification, ﴿ascribe equals to their Lord﴾, i.e., they make for Him equals, so they worship dead stones, while acknowledging that He is the Creator of what He has described. It is said: "I equated this with that" when you made one equal to the other. Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is inverted (muqaddam wa mu'akhkhar), its meaning being: "they equate others with their Lord." Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: the particle "ba'" (bi) here means "'an" (about).

(p-٣) **Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verses 2–3:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is He who created you from clay﴾. This means Adam. This was because when the polytheists doubted the resurrection and said, "Who will bring these bones back to life?", He informed them that He created them from clay, so He is capable of recreating them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then He decreed a term, and a specified term is with Him﴾. Concerning this there are six opinions.

The first: the first term is the term of life until death, and the second is the term from death until resurrection. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibn al-Musayyab, Qatada, al-Dahhak, and Muqatil.

The second: the first term is sleep, in which the soul is taken, and then it returns in the state of wakefulness. The specified term with Him is the term of a person's death. This was transmitted by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: the first term is the term of the Hereafter, when it will come, and the second term is the term of this world. This was said by Mujahid in one narration.

The fourth: the first is the creation of things in six days, and the second is what comes after that until the Day of Resurrection. This was said by 'Ata' al-Khurasani.

The fifth: the first is when He decreed it at the time He took the covenant from His creation, and the second is life in this world. This was said by Ibn Zayd, as if he was pointing to the term of the offspring at the time He gave them life and addressed them.

The sixth: the first is the term of those who have already died, and the second is the term of those who will die afterward. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Yet you still doubt﴾, meaning: after this clarification, you still dispute (تمترون, tamtarun). Concerning this there are two opinions.

One: you doubt. This was said by Qatada and al-Suddi. Regarding what they doubted, there are two opinions: one is the oneness (of God), and the other is the resurrection.

The second: you dispute with one another. It is derived from al-mira' (disputation), and this was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

(p-٤) ﴿And He is God in the heavens and on the earth. He knows your secret and your open, and He knows what you earn﴾.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He is God in the heavens and on the earth﴾. Concerning this there are four opinions.

The first: He is the one worshipped in the heavens and on the earth. This was said by Ibn al-Anbari.

The second: He is the one who alone manages affairs in the heavens and on the earth. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The third: He is God in the heavens, and He knows your secret and your open in the earth. This was said by Ibn Jarir.

The fourth: it is inverted in order (muqaddam wa-mu'akhkhar). The meaning is: He is God who knows your secret and your open in the heavens and the earth. This was mentioned by some of the exegetes.

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verses 4–5:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿No sign comes to them from among the signs of their Lord﴾. It was revealed concerning the disbelievers of Quraysh.

There are two views on the meaning of "sign" in this verse. The first is that it is a verse from the Qur'an. The second is that it is a miracle, such as the splitting of the moon.

By "the truth" is meant the Qur'an. "The news" means the reports. The meaning is: they will come to know the consequence of their mockery.

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verses 4–5:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿No sign comes to them from among the signs of their Lord﴾. It was revealed concerning the disbelievers of Quraysh.

There are two views on the meaning of "sign" in this verse. The first is that it is a verse from the Qur'an. The second is that it is a miracle, such as the splitting of the moon.

By "the truth" is meant the Qur'an. "The news" means the reports. The meaning is: they will come to know the consequence of their mockery.

The phrase "How many generations (qurun) We destroyed before them" (﴿كَمْ أهْلَكْنا مِن قَبْلِهِمْ مِن قَرْنٍ﴾). The qarn (generation, a span of people living together in one era) is the name for the people of each age, and they were so called because of their coexistence (iqtiran) in existence. The exegetes differ on what qarn means here, and there are seven opinions.

The first is that it is forty years. Ibn Sirin mentioned this, citing the Prophet (ﷺ).

The second is eighty years. Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn Abbas.

The third is one hundred years. Abdullah ibn Bishr al-Mazini and Abu Salama ibn Abd al-Rahman said this.

The fourth is one hundred and twenty years. Zurara ibn Awfa and Iyas ibn Muawiya said this.

The fifth is twenty years. Al-Hasan al-Basri related it.

The sixth is seventy years. Al-Farra' mentioned it.

The seventh is that the qarn is the people of any period in which there was a prophet, or a class (tabaqa) of scholars. I say: whether the years are few or many, this is supported by his (ﷺ) saying: "The best of you is my qarn," meaning my Companions, "then those who follow them," meaning the Successors (tabi'un), "then those who follow them," meaning those who took from the Successors.

So qarn is the average measure of the lifespans of the people of an age. It therefore differs from one people to another according to their lifespans. As for the derivation of qarn from iqtiran (conjunction), there are two views on what that conjunction means.

One is that it was called qarn because it is the span in which the people of that age most often coexist in their survival. This is the preference of al-Zajjaj. The second is that it was called qarn because it joins one era to another and one community to another, as said by Ibn al-Anbari. Ibn Qutayba related from Abu Ubayda that he said: "They consider that the least distance between two qarns is thirty years."

The words ﴿مَكَّنّاهم في الأرْضِ﴾ (We had established them on the earth). Ibn Abbas said: "We gave them what We did not give you." One says makkantuhu and makkantu lahu when you empower him to do something by giving him what makes the action valid, namely the means (al-'udda). In this verse there is a shift from the report (third person) to direct address (second person).

As for "the sky" (al-sama'), what is meant by it is rain. The meaning of "arsalna" (We sent) is "anzalna" (We sent down). "Al-midrar" is on the pattern mif'al, from darra, yadirru, and the meaning is: We send it abundantly flowing.

Mif'al is among the forms of intensive emphasis, as in the saying of the Arabs: imra'a midhkar, when a woman bears many males. Likewise mi'nath.

If it is asked: the sky is feminine, so why is midrar masculine?

The answer is that the rule for adjectives that have departed from the pattern and form of the verb is that they must always take the masculine form, whether they describe a masculine or a feminine noun, as in the saying imra'a midhkar, and mi'tar (very fragrant). Also imra'a mudhakkar and mu'annath, and hiya kafur and shakur. If these adjectives were formed on the pattern of the verb, one would say kafira and shakira and mudhakkara. Since they departed from the verbal pattern, they took the path of words that do without a feminine marker because the sense of femininity is in them, as in the saying: "al-na'l labistuha" (I wore it, the sandal) and "al-fa's kasartuha" (I broke it, the axe). Their preference for the masculine was to distinguish between what is formed on the verb and what is derived from the pattern of the af'al (forms). The intended sense of midrar is intensive emphasis in the continuity and persistence of rain, meaning that it pours at the time of need, not that it lasts night and day so as to cause ruin. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

(p-7) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if We had sent down to you a book on parchment﴾. The occasion of its revelation: the polytheists of Mecca said, "O Muhammad, by God, we will never believe you until you bring us a book from God, and with it four angels, who will testify that it is from God and that you are His messenger." So this verse was revealed. This is related by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

Ibn Qutaybah said: al-qirtas (parchment) is the sheet (ṣaḥīfah), and it is said of an archer when he hits the sheet: qarTasa (he hit the target sheet). Our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi said: the word qirtas has been used by the Arabs in ancient times.

It is said that its origin is non-Arabic. The majority read its qaf with a kasra, while Abu Razin, Ikrimah, Talhah, and Yahya ibn Ya'mur read it with a damma.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and they touched it with their hands﴾, it is an emphasis on its descent. It is said that He linked it to touching with the hand only to distance it from magic, because magic produces illusions in visible things, not in things that can be touched. The meaning of the verse is that they would reject the sound (evidence).

The first view: the meaning is "they would have died, and would not have been delayed even for the blink of an eye for repentance." This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: "the Hour would have been established." This was said by ʿIkrimah and Mujahid.

The third: "He would have hastened the punishment for them." This was said by Qatadah.

The statement of His, the Exalted: ﴿And had We made it﴾, meaning: And had We made the Messenger to them an angel, We would have made him in the form of a man, because they would not be able to see the angel in his (true) form. ﴿And We would have confused for them﴾, meaning: We would have made it ambiguous for them. It is said: "albastu al-amr ʿala al-qawm" (I confused the matter for the people), "u× ulbisuhu," meaning: I made it ambiguous for them and made it unclear to them. The meaning: We would have mixed up for them what they mix up for themselves, until they doubt, so that they would not know whether he is an angel or a human. Thus We would have misguided them with that by which they had already been misguided, before the angel was sent. Al-Zajjaj said: They used to confuse their weak followers regarding the matter of the Prophet ﷺ, saying: "This is only a human being like you." So the Exalted said: If they saw the angel as a man, they would be subject to the same confusion (labs) that their weak followers were subject to regarding him. Al-Zuhri, Mu'adh al-Qari, and Abu Raja' read "wa-lalabasna," with shaddah (emphatic doubling), "ʿalayhim ma yalbisun" also with shaddah.

(p-9) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So there befell those who mocked [the messengers] what they had been mocking﴾, meaning: it encompassed them. Al-Zajjaj said: al-ḥayq (encompassing) in the language is what surrounds a person of the harm of his own deed. From it is: ﴿And the evil plotting does not encompass except its own people﴾ [Fatir 35:43], meaning: the consequence of its harm does not return except upon them. Al-Suddi said: the punishment they had mocked befell them.

(p-9) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So there befell those who mocked [the messengers] what they had been mocking﴾, meaning: it encompassed them. Al-Zajjaj said: al-ḥayq (encompassing) in the language is what surrounds a person of the harm of his own deed. From it is: ﴿And the evil plotting does not encompass except its own people﴾ [Fatir 35:43], meaning: the consequence of its harm does not return except upon them. Al-Suddi said: the punishment they had mocked befell them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 12:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: "To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?"﴾ The meaning: If they answer you, well and good; otherwise, say: "To Allah." ﴿He has prescribed for Himself mercy.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: He decreed for Himself that He is the Most Merciful of the merciful. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of "prescribed" (kataba) is: He made it obligatory with emphatic obligation. It is also permissible that it means He wrote it in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). The creation was addressed in terms they understand, for they understand that the emphatic securing of a deferred matter is by writing it down. Others said: His mercy is general, and among it is the deferral of punishment from one who deserves it, and the acceptance of the repentance of the disobedient.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He will surely gather you unto the Day of Resurrection﴾. The lam is the lam of oath, as if He said: "By Allah, He will surely gather you unto the Day that you denied." Some people went to the view that "ila" (unto) means "fi" (in), and then they differed. Some said: in the Day of Resurrection. Others said: in your graves until the Day of Resurrection.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who have lost their souls﴾, i.e., through polytheism. ﴿They do not believe﴾ because of the decree that preceded concerning them. Ibn Qutayba said: His saying ﴿Those who have lost their souls﴾ refers back to His saying ﴿how was the end of the deniers﴾, which refers back to ﴿those who have lost.﴾

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 6, verse 13:

Allah's words: ﴿And to Him belongs whatever rests in the night and the day.﴾ The occasion of its revelation (sabab al-nuzul) was that "the disbelievers of Mecca said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'We know that what drives you to what you call us to is only need. So we will give you a share of our wealth, so that you become one of the wealthiest among us, and you turn away from what you are upon.' Then this verse was revealed." This was related by Ibn 'Abbas.

Regarding the meaning of "sakana" (rested, dwelt), there are two views.

The first: it derives from al-sukna (dwelling, residing). Ibn al-A'rabi said: "sakana" means "halla" (dwelt, settled).

The second: it derives from al-sukun (stillness), which is the opposite of movement. Muqatil said: among created beings are those that become still by day and spread out by night, and among them are those that become still by night and spread out by day.

If it is asked: why was stillness singled out for mention rather than movement? There are three answers to this.

The first: stillness is more general in existence than movement.

The second: every moving thing may be made still, but not every still thing moves.

The third: the verse contains an ellipsis (idmar), and the meaning is: "and to Him belongs whatever is still and whatever moves," like His words ﴿who protects you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 82], meaning "and the cold," and it was abbreviated.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 14:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Shall I take other than Allah as a protector?﴾ Muqatil mentioned that the occasion of its revelation was: "The disbelievers of Quraysh said: O Muhammad, will you not return to the religion of your fathers? So this verse was revealed." This interrogative form means denial, i.e., "I will not take as a protector other than Allah, whom I would turn to, worship, and seek help from."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾. The majority read "fāṭir" with a kasra on the rā'. Ibn Abī ʿAbla read it with a ḍamma. Abu ʿUbayda said: "al-fāṭir" means "al-khāliq" (the Creator). Ibn Qutayba said: "al-mubtadi'" (the Originator). From it comes the saying: "Every child is born upon the fiṭrah" (ﷺ), meaning upon the beginning of creation, which is acknowledgment of Allah at the time He took the covenant from them in the loins of their fathers. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "I did not know what 'Fāṭir of the heavens and the earth' meant until two Bedouins came to me disputing over a well, and one of them said: 'I am the one who fataḥtuhā,' meaning: 'I am the one who originated it.'" Al-Zajjaj said: If it is asked, how can faṭr mean creation when infiṭār means splitting, as in His saying, ﴿When the sky splits open﴾? The answer is that both refer to one thing, because the meaning of "faṭarahumā" is creating them with a decisive creation. Infiṭār and fuṭūr are cutting apart and splitting.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He feeds but is not fed﴾. The majority read the second verb with a ḍamma on the yā', and its meaning is "and He provides but is not provided for," because some slaves provide for their masters. ʿIkrima and al-Aʿmash read "yaṭʿamu" with a fatḥa on the yā'. Al-Zajjaj said: This is the preferred reading according to the Basran grammarians, and its meaning is: "And He provides and feeds, but does not eat."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿I have been commanded to be the first to submit﴾, i.e., the first Muslim of this community, ﴿and do not be among the polytheists.﴾ Al-Akhfash said: Its meaning is: "And it was said to me: Do not be..." so "ummirtu" (I have been commanded) took the place of that, because when he said "ummirtu" he had already informed that it had been said to him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 15:

(p-12) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Indeed I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous day.﴾ Some exegetes (mufassirun) claimed that it was obligatory upon him to fear the consequences of sins, and then this was abrogated (naskh) by His saying: ﴿That Allah may forgive you your previous and later sins﴾ [al-Fath: 3]. The correct view is that the two verses are a statement (khabar), and a statement is not subject to abrogation; rather, it is conditional upon a condition. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿If you associate others with Allah, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾ [al-Zumar: 65].

The words of the Most High: ﴿Whoever is averted from it﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim read "man yusraf" (مَن يُصْرَفْ) with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the ra', meaning the punishment. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim read "yasrif" (يَصْرِفْ) with a fatha on the ya' and a kasra on the ra'; the pronoun refers to His saying: ﴿if I disobey my Lord﴾. What makes this reading preferable is His saying: ﴿then He has had mercy on him﴾, for the two pronouns are then both attributed to the name of Allah, the Most High. By His saying "yasrifu al-'adhab yawma'idhin" (يَصْرِفُ العَذابَ يَوْمَئِذٍ), He means: "on that Day," i.e., the Day of Resurrection, and that refers to the averting of the punishment.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 17:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if Allah touches you with harm﴾. Ad-durr (harm) is a comprehensive term for everything by which a person is harmed, such as poverty, sickness, and other things; and al-khayr (good) is a comprehensive term for everything by which a person benefits.

The exegetes have two views regarding ad-durr and al-khayr.

One of them: that ad-durr is illness, and al-khayr is well-being.

The second: that ad-durr is poverty, and al-khayr is wealth.

(p-13) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾. Al-Qahir: the Dominant. Al-Qahr: domination. The meaning is that He has subdued creation, turning them as He wills, willingly and unwillingly. So He is the one exalted over them, while they are under subjugation and humbling.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 19:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest in testimony?"﴾ The occasion of its revelation: "The chiefs of Makkah came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, we do not see anyone believing you in what you say. We have asked the Jews and the Christians about you, and they claimed that there is no mention of you among them, nor any description of you. So show us who will testify that you are the Messenger of Allah.' Then this verse was revealed." Related by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The meaning of the verse: Say to the Quraysh, "What thing is greater in testimony?" If they answer you, well and good; otherwise say, "Allah," and He is a Witness between me and you concerning what I say.

Al-Zajjaj said: Allah commanded that he argue against them by saying that Allah's testimony to his prophethood is the greatest testimony, and that the Qur'an which he brought testifies for him that he is the Messenger of Allah. This is His saying: ﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me that I may warn you thereby﴾. In the warning by it there is evidence of his prophethood, because no one has brought its like, nor will anyone bring it, and in it is the report of what has been and what will be, and it promised things, and they came to pass as it said. 'Ikrimah, Ibn as-Sumayfa' and al-Jahdari read "Uhiya ilayya" with a fatha on the hamza and the ha', and "al-Qur'an" in the accusative. As for "al-indhar" (warning), its meaning is intimidation. The meaning of "wa-man balagh" is: whoever the Qur'an has reached, I am a warner to him. Al-Qurazi said: whoever the Qur'an has reached, it is as if he saw the Prophet (ﷺ) and spoke with him.

"Anas ibn Malik said: When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote to Chosroes, Caesar, and every tyrant, calling them to Allah, mighty and majestic."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do you indeed testify that there are other gods with Allah?﴾ This is an interrogative whose meaning is denunciation of them. Al-Farra' said: He said "ukhra" (other, feminine) and did not say "akhar" (other, masculine) because "alihah" (gods) is a plural, and the plural takes the feminine form, as He said: ﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names﴾ [al-A'raf: 180] and He said: ﴿So what is the state of the former generations?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 51].

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 20:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those whom We gave the Scripture﴾, there are two opinions regarding "the Scripture."

One of them: it is the Torah and the Gospel, and this is the view of the majority.

The second: it is the Qur'an.

Regarding the pronoun in "they recognize it" (yaʻrifūnahu), there are three opinions.

The first: it refers to the Prophet ﷺ. This was said by al-Suddi. It is related from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab that he said to ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam: "God has sent down to His Prophet in Makkah, ﴿those whom We gave the Scripture recognize it as they recognize their sons﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:146; al-An'am 6:20]. So how is this recognition?" He said: "I recognized him when I saw him, as I recognize my son, and indeed I am more certain of Muhammad ﷺ than I am of my son." ʿUmar said: "And how is that?" He said: "I testify that he is truly the Messenger of God, and I do not know what women may do."

The second: it refers to the religion and the Prophet. The meaning is that they recognize Islam as the religion of God, the Mighty and Majestic, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God. This was said by Qatadah.

The third: it refers to the Qur'an.

The meaning is: they recognize the Book that testifies to its truthfulness. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Regarding ﴿those who have lost their souls﴾, there are two opinions.

One of them: they are the polytheists of Makkah.

The second: they are the disbelievers among the People of the Two Scriptures.

"His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents against Allah a lie﴾, meaning: who fabricates falsehood against Allah by claiming a partner with Him. Regarding "His signs" (āyātihi) there are two opinions.

The first: they are Muhammad and the Qur'an; this was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. The second: they are the Qur'an; this was said by Muqatil.

The injustice (ẓulm) mentioned in this verse is shirk (associating partners with Allah).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 22:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And [mention] the Day when We will gather them all together﴾. The word "al-yawm" (the day) is in the accusative case, governed by an implied verb whose estimated form is: "And mention the Day when We will gather them." Ibn Jarir said: the meaning is: "They will not prosper today, nor on the Day when We gather them." Ya'qub recited "yahshuruhum" and "thumma yaqulu" with the letter ya' (in the third person) in these two places.

Regarding "alladhina" (those) there are two opinions.

The first: they are the Muslims and the polytheists. The second: they are the worshippers and those who were worshipped.

His saying: ﴿Where are your partners﴾ is a question of reproach. By "their partners" is meant the idols, and He attributed them to them because they claimed that they were partners of God.

Regarding the meaning of "yazAAmuna" (they claim) there are two opinions. The first: they claim that they are partners with God. The second: they claim that they (the idols) will intercede for them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then their fitnah (trial, test, or temptation) will not be﴾. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read "lam takun" with the ta', and "fitnatuhum" in the nominative. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read "takun" with the ta' as well, and "fitnatuhum" in the accusative. It is also related from Ibn Kathir that he read it this way. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "yakun" with the ya', and "fitnatuhum" in the accusative.

There are four opinions regarding the fitnah.

The first: it means speech and utterance. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: "Their speech will not be."

The second: it means excuse. Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: "Their excuse will not be." Ibn al-Anbari said: The meaning is that they offered an excuse that was destructive to them and a cause of their disgrace.

The third: it means affliction. 'Ata' al-Khurasani said: "Their affliction will not be." Abu 'Ubayd said: "Their affliction will not be, the one that bound them to the proof and increased them in blame."

The fourth: it means being tested. The meaning is: the outcome of their fitnah will not be...

Al-Zajjaj said: Their being tested will not be through their polytheism and their persistence in it, except that they will disavow it. A similar usage in the language is that you see a person who loves a misguided one, and when that one falls into ruin, he disavows him, and says: "My love for so-and-so was nothing but that I have disowned him." He said: This is a subtle interpretation, which none knows except one who knows the meanings of speech and the ways the Arabs vary in that. (p-17)

Ibn al-Anbari said: The meaning is that they were tested by this saying of theirs, when they lied in it and denied of themselves what they had been known for in the world.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Except that they said: By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir read "wallahi rabbina" with a kasrah on the ba'. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read it with a fathah on the ba'.

Regarding these people whose description this is, there are two opinions.

One: they are the polytheists. The other: they are the hypocrites.

As for when they will swear, there are three opinions regarding it.

The first: when they see that none enters Paradise except one who was a Muslim, they say: "Come, let us deny our polytheism." So they swear. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: when they enter the Fire and see the people of tawhid (affirmation of Allah's oneness) coming out, they swear and make excuses. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid. (p-18)

The third: when they are asked: "Where are your partners?" they disavow them and swear: "We were not polytheists." This was said by Muqatil.

"His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Look how they lie against themselves﴾, that is: by their excuse with falsehood.

﴿And what they used to fabricate has vanished from them﴾, that is: gone is what they used to claim and invent, that the idols are partners of God and their intercessors in the Hereafter."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 25–26:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾. The occasion of its revelation: "A group of the polytheists, among them ʿUtba, Shayba, al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith, and Umayya and Ubayy, the two sons of Khalaf, sat down with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and listened to him. Then they said to al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith: 'What is Muhammad saying?' He said: 'By the One who made it a house (of worship), I do not know what he is saying, except that I see the movement of his lips. He says nothing but the fables of the ancients, just as I used to tell you about the past generations.' al-Naḍr used to narrate much about the earlier generations. So this verse was revealed." Narrated by Abu Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbas.

As for "al-akinna" (the coverings), al-Zajjaj said: they are the plural of kinān, which is a covering, like ʿanān and aʿinna.

As for "an yafqahūhu" (that they understand it), it is in the accusative as an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu). The meaning: "And We placed coverings upon their hearts out of aversion to their understanding it." When the lam (of purpose) was removed, the aversion (al-karāha) took the accusative, and when al-karāha was removed, its accusative shifted to "an" (that).

"Al-waqr" (the heaviness): heaviness of hearing. It is said: "in his ear is waqr," and "the ear has been made heavy (wuqirat al-udhun, tūqar)."

The poet said:

"And an evil speech has made my ear heavy regarding it, though there is no deafness in me."

Al-wiqr, with a kasra on the waw, is when a camel or other animal is loaded with what it can bear. It is said: "upon him is a wiqr," and "a palm laden (mūqir) and laden (mūqira)." This was done to them as a recompense for their persistence in disbelief. The meaning is not that they did not understand it or did not hear it; rather, when they turned away from it and diverted their thought from what awaits them of evil outcome, they became like one who neither knows nor hears. ﴿And if they see every sign﴾, i.e., every sign that indicates your message, ﴿they will not believe in it﴾.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed of the extent of their argumentation and dispute, and that they only use in argument that they say: "This" (i.e., this Qur'an) ﴿is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾. On this there are two views.

One: they are what was inscribed (suṭira) of their reports and narratives. Abu Ṣāliḥ narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "The fables of the ancients: their lies and their tales in their era." Abu al-Ḥasan al-Akhfash said: some claim that the singular of asāṭīr is ustūra, and others said asṭāra; I do not think it is anything but a plural without a singular, like ʿabādīd, madhākīr, and abābīl. Ibn Qutayba said: "The fables of the ancients: their reports and what was inscribed (suṭira) of them, i.e., what was written. From it is His saying: ﴿Nun. By the pen and what they inscribe﴾ [al-Qalam 68:1] i.e., what they write. Its singular is saṭr, then asṭār, then asāṭīr, a plural of a plural, like qawl, aqwāl, and aqāwīl."

The second view: the meaning of "asāṭīr al-awwalīn" is al-turrahāt (idle tales, nonsense). Abu ʿUbayda said: the singular of asāṭīr is ustūra and asṭāra, and its metaphorical sense is the metaphor of turrahāt. Ibn al-Anbari said: turrahāt, in the language of the Arabs, are obscure paths and confusing routes; one of them says: "We have taken to the turrahāt of the basābis," meaning: we have deviated from the clear road to the confusing one, and from what is known to what is not known. "Al-basābis" are the wide deserts, and "turrahāt" are paths branching off from the main road, becoming numerous and confusing, so they were made a metaphor for what is not sound and does not become clear.

If it is said: Why did they fault the Qur'an as "fables of the ancients," when the ancients wrote what contains knowledge and wisdom, and there is no fault in its author? There are two answers.

One: they attributed it to not being a revelation from Allah.

The second: they faulted it for being confusing and obscure, seeking rest in slander and falsehood. On the first answer, "asāṭīr" is from tasṭīr (writing); on the second, it has the meaning of turrahāt, and we have already explained the meaning of turrahāt.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they forbid it and keep away from it﴾. Regarding its occasion of revelation there are two views.

One: Abu Ṭālib used to forbid the polytheists from harming the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and kept away from what he brought, so this verse was revealed concerning him. Narrated by Saʿid ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbas, and this is the view of ʿAmr ibn Dinar, ʿAṭāʾ ibn Dinar, and al-Qasim ibn Mukhayma. Muqatil said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was with Abu Ṭālib, calling him to Islam. The Quraysh gathered to Abu Ṭālib, intending evil against the Prophet (ﷺ), and they asked Abu Ṭālib to hand him over to them so they could kill him. He said: 'I have no patience regarding him.' They said: 'We will give you from our youth whomever you wish in place of your nephew.' Abu Ṭālib said: 'When the camels return at evening, if a she-camel longs for other than her young, I will hand him over to you.' And he said:

"By Allah, they will never reach you with their gathering, until I am placed under the dust, buried.
So proclaim your matter, there is no shame upon you, and rejoice, and let your eyes be cooled by it.
And you have presented a religion that is undoubtedly among the best religions of mankind.
Were it not for blame, or my fear of a disgrace, you would find me generous in it, clear."

So this verse was revealed concerning him."

The second: the disbelievers of Makkah used to forbid people from following the Prophet (ﷺ) and kept themselves away from him. Narrated by al-Walibi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and this is the view of Ibn al-Hanafiyya, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and al-Suddi. On the first view, "wa-hum" refers to one person; on the second, to a group.

Regarding the pronoun in "ʿanhu" there are two views.

One: it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ). Then there are two views on it: one, they forbid (people) from harming him; the second, from following him.

The second view: it refers to the Qur'an, said by Mujahid, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd.

"Yanʾawna" means "they keep far away." Regarding the pronoun in "ʿanhu" there are two views: one, that it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ); the second, to the Qur'an.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they destroy only themselves﴾, i.e., they destroy none but themselves, by keeping away from him, ﴿and they perceive it not﴾ that they are destroying themselves.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 27:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if only you could see when they are made to stand before the Fire﴾. Regarding the meaning of "wuqifu" (they were made to stand) there are six opinions.

The first: they were detained over it (the Fire). This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. The second: they were presented to it. This was said by Muqatil.

The third: they witnessed it (ʿayanuha). The fourth: they were made to stand over it while it was beneath them.

The fifth: they entered it and then the magnitude of its punishment was lifted from them. You say, "I stood over what so-and-so has" (waqaftu ʿala ma ʿinda fulan), meaning: I understood it and clarified it. Al-Zajjaj mentioned these three opinions, and he preferred the last one. Ibn Jarir said: "ʿala" here carries the meaning of "fi" (in).

The sixth: they made it (the Fire) a perpetual endowment (waqf) upon them, like the endowments that are made permanent for their paths (sububuha). This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. The address in this verse is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the warning is for the disbelievers. The answer to "law" (if/if only) is omitted, and its meaning is: if you saw them in that state, you would see a wonder.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that we would not deny the signs of our Lord﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, recited the "ba'" of "nukadhdhibu" with a damma (raising it), and the "nun" of "nakunu" (with a damma as well).

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that they wished for a return, and they guaranteed that they would not deny. The meaning is: "Would that we were returned, and we would not deny the signs of our Lord, whether we are returned or not, and that we would be among the believers, for we have witnessed what, with it, we will never deny again."

He said: The raising may also be permitted in another way, in the sense of "Would that we were returned," (meaning) "would that we did not deny," as though they wished for the return and for the success to believe.

Al-Akhfash said: When you raise it, you make it like an oath, as if they said: "And we do not deny, by God, the signs of our Lord, and we will be, by God, among the believers."

Hamza, except al-ʿIjli, Hafs from ʿAsim, and Yaʿqub recited the "ba'" of "nukadhdhiba" with a fatha (putting it in the subjunctive), and the "nun" of "nakuna" likewise.

Makki ibn Abi Talib said: This accusative form is as an answer to the wish (tamanni), and that is by the implied "an" (that), taking as the basis the verbal noun of "nuraddu," so you imply "an" so that it, with the verb, becomes a verbal noun, and then you join a verbal noun to a verbal noun with the "wa" (and).

Its meaning: "Would that we had a return and an absence of denial, and being among the believers." Ibn ʿAmir recited the "ba'" of "nukadhdhiba" with a damma and the "nun" of "nakuna" with a fatha. As for the raising, we have already explained its reason, and the fatha is as an answer to the wish.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 28–29:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Nay, but there has become apparent to them what they used to conceal before﴾. "Bal" (nay, but) here is a rebuttal of their speech, meaning: the matter is not as they said, that if they were returned they would believe.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Bal" is a corrective and affirmative statement after a negation; you say, "Zayd did not come, but ʿAmr [did]." Regarding the meaning of the verse there are four opinions.

The first: what some of them used to hide from others became apparent. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: what they used to conceal with their tongues became apparent through the speech of their limbs. This was said by Muqatil.

The third: there became apparent to them the recompense of what they used to conceal. This was said by al-Mubarrad.

(p-24) The fourth: there became apparent to the followers what the leaders used to conceal. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if they were returned, they would certainly return to that which they were forbidden﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they would return to what they were forbidden of, namely shirk, and indeed they are liars in their saying: ﴿And we would not deny the signs of our Lord and we would be among the believers﴾.

Ibn al-Anbari said: Allah called them liars in their report about themselves, that if they were returned they would believe and not deny; and He did not call them liars in the wish (tamanni).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they say, "There is not but our worldly life"﴾. This is a report about those who deny the Resurrection. Muqatil said: when the Prophet (ﷺ) informed the disbelievers of Makkah about the Resurrection, they said this. And ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam used to say: this is a narration of their statement, that if they were returned they would say it.
