Ibn al-Anbari said: Allah called them liars in their report about themselves, that if they were returned they would believe and not deny; and He did not call them liars in the wish (tamanni).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they say, "There is not but our worldly life"﴾. This is a report about those who deny the Resurrection. Muqatil said: when the Prophet (ﷺ) informed the disbelievers of Makkah about the Resurrection, they said this. And ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam used to say: this is a narration of their statement, that if they were returned they would say it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 30:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord﴾. Muqatil said: they are presented to their Lord. ﴿He will say: Is this not the truth?﴾ meaning the punishment. Others said: "Is this not the Resurrection the truth?" According to Muqatil's view, ﴿because you used to disbelieve﴾ refers to the punishment, and according to the view of the others, you used to disbelieve in the Resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 31:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They have certainly lost who denied the meeting with Allah﴾. They were described as losers only because they sold faith for disbelief, so their loss was great.

What is meant by "the meeting with Allah" is the resurrection (al-ba'th) and the recompense (al-jaza'), and "as-sa'ah" is the Resurrection (al-qiyamah), and "al-baghtah" is the sudden arrival (al-faj'ah). Al-Zajjaj said: Whatever comes suddenly has come "baghta," one says: "baghathahu al-amr yabghathuhu baghtan and baghtatan," when it comes upon him suddenly. The poet said:

"But they departed and I did not fear a sudden blow, and the most dreadful thing is when the sudden blow (al-bagh't) overtakes you."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Alas for our regret (ya hasratana)﴾. Al-hasrah is the anguish (al-talahhuf) over a thing that has passed, and the people of tafsir say: "ya nadamatana" (O our remorse).

If it is said: What is the meaning of calling upon regret, when it does not understand?

The answer: When the Arabs strive to emphasize the magnitude of something that befalls them, they make it a vocative, so they prefix "ya" for alerting (al-tanbih), and the intended meaning is alerting the people, not alerting the one calling. A similar example is their saying: "La uriyannaka huna" (I will certainly not let you see yourself here); its wording is that of one forbidding himself, while the meaning is for the one being forbidden. From this is their saying: "Ya khayla Allah urkabi" (O horses of Allah, mount up), meaning: O horsemen of the horses of Allah. Sibawayh said: When you say "ya 'ajaba-hu" (O wonder!), it is as if you said: "Be present and come, O wonder, for this is your time." As for al-tafrit, it is neglect (al-tadyi').

Al-Zajjaj said: Tafrit in the language is: incapacity precedes him. Regarding what is referred to by his saying "fiha" (in it), there are three views.

One: It refers to the world, so the meaning is: over what we neglected in the world of the deeds of the Hereafter. This was said by Muqatil.

Second: It refers to the transaction (al-saf'ah), because loss occurs only in a transaction, and its mention was omitted being satisfied with the mention of the loss. This was said by Ibn Jarir.

Third: It refers to obedience (al-ta'ah), mentioned by some of the exegetes.

As for al-awzar, Ibn Qutaybah said: they are sins (al-athám), and the origin of al-wizr is carrying on the back. Ibn Faris said: al-wizr is weight. Is this carrying literal? There are two views on it.

One: It is on its literal meaning. Umayr ibn Hani said: With every disbeliever his deed will be brought forth in the form of an ugly man; whenever there is a terror he magnifies it upon him and increases his fear, so he says: "What a wretched companion you are! What is between me and you?" He says: "I am your deed, which you mounted me in the world for so long, so I will mount you today until I disgrace you before the heads of the people." He mounts him, and people step aside from him, until he stands before his Lord. This is his saying: ﴿while they carry their burdens upon their backs﴾. This is the view of al-Suddi, Amr ibn Qays al-Mala'i, and Muqatil.

Second: It is a parable, and the meaning is: they carry the weight of their sins. This was said by al-Zajjaj, who said: He made what reaches them of punishment like the heaviest thing that is borne. And the meaning of ﴿Unquestionably, evil is what they bear﴾ is: wretched is the thing they carry, that is, what they bear.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 32:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the worldly life is nothing but play and amusement﴾, has three opinions.

(p-27) One: The worldly life, in its swift passing away and the brevity of its lifespan, is nothing but like a thing one plays with.

The second: The affair of this world and working for it is nothing but play and amusement. As for doing good, it is from the deeds of the Hereafter, not of this world.

The third: The people of the worldly life are nothing but people of play and amusement, because of their preoccupation with what they were commanded to do. And play (la'ib) is that which yields no benefit.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the Hereafter abode is better﴾. The lam is the lam of oath (lam al-qasam). The Hereafter abode is Paradise. ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ so that they would act for it. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "ya'qilun" (they reason) with the yaʾ in al-An'am, al-A'raf, Yusuf and Ya-Sin, and they read it with the ta' in al-Qasas. Nafi' read all of these with the yaʾ. Hafs related from 'Asim all of these with the ta', except in Ya-Sin, in ﴿Will they not then reason?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 67], with the yaʾ. Ibn 'Amir read the one in [Ya-Sin] with the yaʾ, and the rest with the ta'.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 33:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We know indeed that what they say grieves you﴾.

Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are four reports.

The first: "A man from Quraysh called al-Harith ibn 'Amir said: 'By God, O Muhammad, you have never lied to us, so we would accuse you today; rather, if we follow you, we will be snatched away from our land.' So this verse was revealed." Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas. Muqatil said: al-Harith ibn 'Amir used to deny the Prophet openly, but when he was alone with his family he would say: "Muhammad is not one of the people of lying," and this verse was revealed concerning him. (p-28) The second: when the polytheists saw the Prophet (ﷺ), they would say among themselves: "He is indeed a prophet," and so this verse was revealed; Abu Salih said this.

The third: "Abu Jahl said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'We do not deny you, but we deny what you have brought,' and so this verse was revealed." Najiyah ibn Ka'b said this.

Abu Yazid al-Madani said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) met Abu Jahl, and Abu Jahl shook his hand. It was said to him: "Do you shake hands with this Sabian?" He said: "By God, I know that he is a prophet, but when have we been followers of the Banu 'Abd Manaf?" So God revealed this verse.

The fourth: al-Akhnas ibn Shariq met Abu Jahl, and al-Akhnas said: "O Abu al-Hakam, tell me about Muhammad: is he truthful or a liar? There is no one here who hears your words except me." Abu Jahl said: "By God, Muhammad is truthful, and he has never lied; but if the Banu Qusayy take the banner, the water-supply, the custody of the Ka'bah, and the prophethood, what will remain for the rest of Quraysh?" So this verse was revealed; al-Suddi said this.

As for "what they say," it is the denial of the Prophet (ﷺ) and disbelief in God. In the verse there is consolation and solace for the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding what they confront him with.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So they do not deny you﴾. Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read "yukadhdhibunaka" with lightness (takhfif) and a sukun on the kaf. Regarding its meaning there are two views. (p-29) One: they do not find you a liar; this was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: they do not deny what you have brought; rather they reject the signs of God and expose themselves to His punishments. Ibn al-Anbari said: al-Kisa'i used to argue for this reading by saying that the Arabs say "kadhabtu al-rajul" when one attributes to him lying and the fabrication of falsehoods in speech, and "akdhabtuhu" when one reports that what he narrates is a lie, though he is not the one who fabricated it. He said: Other than al-Kisa'i said: one says "akdhdhabta al-rajul" when one places him among the liars and attributes to him their description, as one says "abkhalta al-rajul" when one attributes stinginess to him, and "ajbantuhu" when one finds him a coward. The poet said:

"A group has declared me an unbeliever for loving you, and another group said: he is a wrongdoer and a sinner."

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamzah and Ibn 'Amir read "yukadhdhibunaka" with doubling (tashdid) and a fatha on the kaf. Regarding its meaning there are five views.

One: they do not deny you with proof; it is only denial out of obstinacy and bluster; this was said by Qatadah and al-Suddi.

The second: they do not say to you that you are a liar, knowing your truthfulness, but they deny what you have brought; this was said by Najiyah ibn Ka'b.

The third: they do not deny you in private, but they deny you openly out of enmity toward you; this was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil.

The fourth: they are not able to say to you, regarding what you report of what is in their books: "You have lied."

The fifth: they do not deny you in their hearts, because they know that you are truthful; al-Zajjaj mentioned the two views.

(p-30) Abu 'Ali said: It is possible that the meaning of the two readings is one, even though the wording differs, except that "fa''ala" is used when they wish to attribute to him a matter greater than "af'ala." He confirms that the two readings have the same meaning by what Sibawayh related, that they said "qallalta" and "aqlalta," and "kaththarta" and "akthartа" with the same meaning.

Abu 'Ali said: The meaning of "la yukadhdhibunaka" is: they are not able to attribute to you lying regarding what you report of what is in their books. It is also possible that the literal meaning is: they do not find you lying, just as one says "ahmadtu al-rajul" when one finds him praiseworthy, because they know you for truthfulness and trustworthiness. ﴿But the wrongdoers deny the signs of God﴾ with their tongues what they know with certainty, out of their obstinacy.

Regarding "the signs of God" here there are three views.

One: they are Muhammad (ﷺ); said by al-Suddi.

The second: Muhammad and the Qur'an; said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The third: the Qur'an; said by Muqatil.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 34:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And messengers were denied before you﴾. This is a consolation to him for what he suffers from them. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿So they were patient over what they were denied﴾, seeking My reward, and they were harmed until they were sawn apart with saws and burned with fire, ﴿until Our help came to them﴾ with the punishment of their denial. (p-31) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And none can alter the words of Allah﴾. Concerning it there are five opinions.

The first: there is no breaking of His promises. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: none can alter what He has informed of or what He has commanded. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The third: none can alter His judgments and His decrees that are executed upon His servants. The "words" here express this meaning, as in His saying: ﴿But the word of punishment has been justified against the disbelievers﴾ [az-Zumar: 71], meaning: what was decreed against them became binding. According to this view and the one before it, the meaning is: none can alter the ruling of Allah's words, nor can anyone annul what He has judged. He has judged the victory of His prophets in His saying: ﴿Surely I and My messengers will prevail﴾ [al-Mujadila: 21].

The fourth: the meaning of the statement is that of a prohibition, although its apparent form is informative. The meaning is: let no one alter the words of Allah. It is like His saying: ﴿There is no doubt in it﴾ [al-Baqara: 2].

The fifth: the meaning is that no one is able to alter the speech of Allah, however much he embellishes and strives, because Allah, Exalted is He, has protected it with precise wording and upright judgment from being mixed with the words of people of deviation. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned these three opinions.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And there has certainly come to you some of the news of the messengers﴾. That is: concerning what they were patient over of harm, and so they were helped. It was said that "min" (some of) is redundant (silah).

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 6, verse 35:**

One of them: from hearing the Qur'an. The second: from following the Prophet (ﷺ).

As for "*al-nafaq*" (a tunnel or passage), Ibn Qutaybah said: "*al-nafaq* in the earth is the entrance, which is the *sirb* (burrow). And *al-sullam* (a ladder) in the sky is the means of ascent." Al-Zajjaj said: "*al-nafaq* is the passage that goes through the earth. And *al-nafiqa'*, with a long vowel, is one of the two holes of the jerboa (*al-yarbu'*). It bores through from the inside of the earth up to the thin skin of the surface. When it reaches the skin and finds it very thin, then if it senses any danger, it pushes out with its head at that spot and escapes. From this, the hypocrite (*al-munafiq*) is so named, because he conceals something other than what he shows, like the *nafiqa'*, whose outer surface is not clearly visible while its inside is dug out in the earth."

"*Al-sullam*" (the ladder) is derived from *al-salama* (safety), and it is the thing that brings you safely to your place of ascent. The meaning is: "If you are able to do this, then do it." The response "then do it" (*fa-if'al*) has been omitted, because the context indicates it.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: "*al-sullam* means a means and a rung. You say, 'She made me a ladder for her need,' meaning a means."

Regarding His words, ﴿Then bring them a sign﴾, there are two views:

One: a sign that they have asked you for. That is because they asked for an angel to descend, and for signs like those of the prophets, such as the staff of Musa and the she-camel of Salih.

The second: a sign that is better than your sign.

His words, the Exalted: ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance﴾. Regarding this there are three views:

One: If He had willed to seal their hearts upon guidance, He would have sealed them.

The second: If He had willed, He would have sent down angels to compel them to belief. Al-Zajjaj mentioned both of these.

The third: If He had willed, they would all have believed. He informs us that they abandoned faith only by His will and His all-binding decree.

His words, the Exalted: ﴿So do not be among the ignorant﴾. Regarding this there are three views:

One: Do not be ignorant that He, if He had willed, would have gathered them upon guidance.

The second: Do not be ignorant that some of them will believe in you and some of them will disbelieve.

The third: Do not be among those who have no patience, because lack of patience is among the traits of the ignorant.

(p-33)

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 36:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Only those who listen will respond﴾ means: only the one who listens will answer you, and what is meant is the hearing of acceptance (sama' qabul).

Regarding who is meant by "the dead," there are two opinions.

The first: they are the disbelievers. This was said by al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatadah. The meaning then is: only the believers respond. As for the disbelievers, they do not respond until Allah resurrects them, then gathers them as disbelievers, and they respond out of compulsion. (p-34)

The second: they are the dead in the literal sense, whom Allah has made into a parable. The meaning is: the dead do not respond until Allah resurrects them, and likewise those who do not hear.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then to Him they will be returned﴾ means: the believers and the disbelievers, so He will recompense all of them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 37:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "Why was not a sign sent down to him from his Lord?"﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: It was revealed concerning the leaders of Quraysh. "Lawla" here carries the meaning of "halla" (why not), and we have explained it in surah (al-Nisa'). Muqatil said: They meant by the sign something like the signs of the prophets. Others said: They meant the descent of an angel who would bear witness to his prophethood.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾, there are three opinions.

The first: they do not know that God is able to send down a sign.

The second: they do not know the harm upon them in its descent, for if they do not believe in it, their punishment will increase.

The third: they do not know the benefit (maslaha) in the descent of the sign.

**Ibn al-Jawzi, *Zad al-Masir*, on Surah 6, verse 38:**

His statement, may He be exalted, ﴿Nor any creature (*dabbah*) on the earth﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: He means everything that crawls upon the earth. Al-Zajjaj (a grammarian and exegete) said: The mention of "two wings" is for emphasis, and everything He created either crawls or flies. [p-35] His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿but they are communities like you﴾. Mujahid said: they are classes, each one classified. Abu 'Ubayda said: they are kinds that know Allah and worship Him.

Regarding the meaning of "like you" (*amthalukum*), there are four opinions:

The first: they are like you in that some of them understand one another. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: they are like you in knowing Allah. This was said by 'Ata'.

The third: they are like you in creation, death, and resurrection. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The fourth: they are like you in seeking food, pursuing sustenance, and avoiding destruction. This was said by Ibn Qutayba. Ibn al-Anbari said: The point of argument in this verse is that Allah, may He be exalted, placed in the polytheists intellects and gave them understanding, by which He obligates them to reflect upon the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ) and to adhere to his obedience. Just as He gave birds understanding by which some of them recognize the signals of others, and guided the male of them to mate with the female, and in all of that there is evidence of the penetrating power of the One who composed that in them.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾. Regarding "the Book," there are two opinions.

The first: it is the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*). Ibn Abi Talha narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: We have left nothing out but that We have recorded it in the Mother of the Book (*Umm al-Kitab*). Qatada and Ibn Zayd also held this meaning.

The second: it is the Qur'an. 'Ata' narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: We have left nothing out but that We have explained it to you. According to this view, it is of the general (*al-'amm*, an expression of general scope) that is intended in a specific sense (*al-khass*, particular), so the meaning becomes: We have neglected nothing that you need but that We have explained it in the Book, either explicitly, or in summary (*mujmal*, unspecified), or by indication, as in His statement: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾ [An-Nahl 16:89], meaning: of everything that they need in matters of religion.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Then to their Lord they will be gathered﴾. There are two opinions regarding this.

The first: it is the gathering on the Day of Resurrection. Abu Dharr narrated: Two sheep butted each other in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), so he said: "O Abu Dharr, do you know why they butted each other?" I said: "No." He said: "But Allah knows, and He will judge between them." Abu Hurayra said: Allah will gather the creation on the Day of Resurrection, the beasts, the animals, the birds, and everything else. His justice will be such that He will take retribution for the hornless (*al-jamma'*) from the horned (*al-qarna'*). Then He will say: "Be dust!" And the disbeliever will say: ﴿Would that I were dust!﴾ [An-Naba' 78:40].

The second: the meaning of their gathering is their death. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 39:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who denied Our signs﴾, meaning what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. ﴿Deaf﴾ to the Qur'an, not hearing it, and ﴿dumb﴾ concerning it, not speaking it. ﴿In darknesses﴾, that is, in polytheism (shirk) and misguidance (ḍalāla). ﴿Whomever Allah wills, He leaves astray﴾, so he dies in disbelief. ﴿And whomever He wills, He places on a straight path﴾, which is Islam.

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 40:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Tell me⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and Hamza read "أرَأيْتُمْ" (ara'aytum), "وَأرَأيْتَكُمْ" (wa-ara'aytakum) and "أرَأيْتَ" (ara'ayta) with a hamza and an alif throughout the Qur'an. Nafi' softened the hamza in all of them. Al-Kisa'i read them without a hamza or an alif. Al-Farra' said: the Arabs say "أرَأيْتَكَ" (ara'aytaka), and they mean "أخْبَرَنِي" (akhbarani, "tell me").

As for "the punishment of Allah" (ʿadhab Allah), there are two views on what is meant here.

The first: it is death. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it is the punishment that used to come upon the earlier nations. This was said by Muqatil.

As for "the Hour" (al-sa'a), it is the Resurrection. Al-Zajjaj said: it is also the name for the time in which the servants will be struck unconscious, and for the time in which they will be resurrected.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Would you call upon other than Allah?﴾ That is: would you call upon an idol or a stone to remove what afflicts you? He thus argued against them with something they cannot deny, for they used to call upon Allah when harm touched them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If you are truthful﴾ is the response to His saying "أرَأيْتَكُمْ" (ara'aytakum), because it has the meaning of "أخْبَرُوا" (akhbiru, "inform me"). It is as if it was said to them: "If you are truthful, then inform [us] whom you call upon when the calamity comes upon you?"

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 41:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Rather, it is Him you call upon﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: He informed them that they do not call upon anyone in times of hardship except Him. In this lies the greatest of proofs against them, because they worshipped idols.

﴿So He removes what you call upon Him for, if He wills﴾. The meaning: He removes the harm for which you called upon Him. This is, given the breadth of speech (ittisa' al-kalam), like His saying: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], meaning: the people of the town.

﴿And you forget﴾ may mean "you abandon"; and it may also mean: in your abandoning of calling upon them, you are in the position of one who has forgotten them.

(p-38) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly sent [messengers] to communities before you﴾. In the verse there is an omitted element; its estimated meaning is: "And We certainly sent to communities before you messengers, and they opposed them, so We seized them with al-ba'sa'" (distress). And regarding it there are three opinions.

The first: that it is the affliction and fear. This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that it is misery, which is poverty. This was said by Ibn Qutayba.

The third: that it is hunger. This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

Regarding al-darra' (adversity) there are three opinions.

The first: calamity and hunger. This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: loss of wealth and of lives. This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

The third: sicknesses and diseases. This was said by Abu Sulayman.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so that they might humble themselves﴾, meaning: in order that they would humble themselves. And al-tada arru' (humbling oneself) is submissiveness and lowliness. In the speech there is an omitted element; its estimated meaning is: "but they did not humble themselves."

Ibn al-Jawzi, Zad al-Masir, on surah 6, verse 43:

"His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Why then﴾ (fa-law-la) means "fa-hallā" (why did they not...). And al-ba's (the severity) means al-'adhab (the punishment).

The purport of the verse is that Allah the Exalted informed His Prophet (ﷺ) that He had sent messengers to peoples before him who reached such hardness that they were seized with calamities, yet they did not humble themselves, persisted in their disbelief, and Satan made their misguidance appear attractive to them, so they insisted upon it."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 44:

(p. 39) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: They abandoned what they had been admonished with. ﴿We opened for them the gates of all things﴾: he means the ease and pleasures of this world. Abu Ja'far and Ibn 'Amir read *fatahna* with the intensive form (*tashdid*, doubling of the middle consonant) here, and in [surah al-A'raf], and in [surah al-Anbiya'] *fatahat*, and in [surah al-Qamar] *fatahna*. The majority read these forms with the light form (*takhfif*). Al-Zajjaj said: "The gates of all things" means every good that had been closed to them. Until, when they thought that what had befallen them was not a punishment, and that what had been opened for them was because they deserved it, ﴿We seized them suddenly﴾, that is, Our punishment came upon them unexpectedly.

Ibn al-Anbari said: By His saying ﴿all things﴾ He intended emphasis, like the saying of one who says: "We ate at so-and-so's place everything [of food], and we were with him in every kind of joy." By this generality he intends to magnify what is described and to elaborate upon it, like His saying ﴿and she was given of every thing﴾ [surah al-Naml 27:23].

Al-Hasan said: Whoever is given abundance and does not see that he is not being deceived by it, has no sound judgment; and whoever is restricted and does not see that he is being given time, has no sound judgment. Then he recited this verse and said: "The people were deceived, by the Lord of the Ka'ba! They were given what they wanted, and then they were seized."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then they were suddenly in despair﴾. There are five sayings concerning *al-mublis*:

The first: that it is one who despairs of the mercy of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. In another narration he said: one who despairs of every good. Al-Farra' said: *al-mublis* is the despairing one whose hope has been cut off. For this reason, one who falls silent when his argument fails, so that he has no answer, is said to have been struck dumb (*ablasa*). Al-'Ajjaj said:

*O companion, do you know a faded trace of an abandoned camp?*
*He said: "Yes, I know it, and I am struck dumb."*

That is, he could not produce an answer. It is also said: *al-mukarras* is the place in which camels have left their dung and urine, so that some of it lies upon other parts.

The second: that it is one who is disgraced. Mujahid said: *al-iblas* is disgrace.

The third: that it is one who is destroyed. This was said by al-Suddi.

The fourth: that it is one who is exhausted and distressed, upon whom has come down from evil what he cannot bear. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The fifth: that it is one who is grieved and regretful. This was said by Abu 'Ubayda, who recited Ru'ba's line:

*On the day of al-Khamis, of the Akhmas [a battle], and upon the faces was yellowness and dejection.*

That is, depression, dimness, and sorrow.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is one who is extremely remorseful, grieved, and despairing. In another place he said: *al-mublis* is the silent, bewildered one.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 45:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off﴾. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: "Dabiruhum" (their last remnant) is the one who remains behind at their rear. The meaning is that they were uprooted entirely. Abu 'Ubayda said: "Dabiruhum" is their last one, the one who manages their affairs. Ibn Qutayba said: it is like the saying "ijtutta asluhum" (their root was torn out).

The exegetes said: He praised Himself for cutting off their remnant because that is a blessing upon their messengers, whom they had denied, and He taught the praise for His sufficiency against the evil of the wrongdoers.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 46:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Have you considered, if Allah were to take away your hearing and your sight"﴾, meaning, remove them, ﴿and seal over your hearts﴾ so that you do not recognize anything, ﴿what god other than Allah could bring them back to you?﴾ Concerning the pronoun in "bihi" (with it/him) there are three opinions.

The first: it refers to the act (al-fi'l), and the meaning is: "brings you back what Allah took from you." This is the view of al-Zajjaj. Al-Farra' said: when you refer back to actions, even if they are many, you use the singular pronoun, as in saying to a man: "Your coming and your going bother me."

The second: it refers to guidance (al-huda), as mentioned by al-Farra'. On this view the pronoun refers to something unmentioned, but the meaning includes it, because whoever has his hearing and sight taken away and a seal placed over his heart does not become guided.

The third: it refers to hearing (al-sam'), and what is conjoined to it is included with it in the account, because it is conjoined to it. This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj. The majority recite: ﴿bihi unzur﴾ (ﷺ... ) with the kasra on the ha' of "bihi," but Ruways narrated from Nafi': "bihi unzur" with a damma. Abu 'Ali said: whoever uses the kasra drops the yā' which joins the ha' in forms such as "bihi 'ayb," and whoever uses the damma follows the view of one who said: "fakhasafna bihu wa bi-daarihu al-ard," dropping the wāw.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Look how We vary the signs﴾. Muqatil said: meaning the signs come in various matters, so He frightens them with the taking away of hearing, sight and hearts, and with what He did to the past nations. ﴿Yet they turn away﴾, meaning they turn aside and so do not take heed.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 47:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Tell me, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you suddenly or openly﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "Al-baghta (suddenness) is the surprise; and al-jahra (openly) is that it comes upon them while they are seeing it." ﴿Will anyone be destroyed except the wrongdoing people?﴾ That is: will anyone be destroyed except you and those like you, because you disbelieved stubbornly, and you know that you are wrongdoers.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 48–49:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We send the messengers only as bearers of good news and warners﴾ — meaning, of reward, and warners of punishment. Their being sent is not so that they would bring whatever signs are demanded of them. Then He mentioned the reward of the one who believes and the punishment of the one who denies, in the rest of this verse and the one that follows. And Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿yafsuqun﴾ means ﴿yakfurun﴾ (they disbelieve).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 48–49:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We send the messengers only as bearers of good news and warners﴾ — meaning, of reward, and warners of punishment. Their being sent is not so that they would bring whatever signs are demanded of them. Then He mentioned the reward of the one who believes and the punishment of the one who denies, in the rest of this verse and the one that follows. And Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿yafsuqun﴾ means ﴿yakfurun﴾ (they disbelieve).

Al-Zajjaj said: This verse is connected to His saying: "Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" So He informed them that he does not possess the treasuries of Allah from which He provides and gives, nor does he know the unseen so as to inform them of it except through revelation, and he does not claim to be an angel, because an angel witnesses of the affairs of Allah the Exalted what a human being does not witness. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Jubayr, Ikrimah, and al-Jahdari read: "Inni malik" (I am a king), with a kasra on the lam.

Regarding "the blind and the seeing," there are two opinions.

The first: the blind is the disbeliever, and the seeing is the believer. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Qatadah.

The second: the blind is the one who is astray, and the seeing is the one who is guided. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid.

Regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Will you not then reflect?﴾ there are two opinions.

The first: concerning what He has made clear to you of the signs that indicate His oneness and the truthfulness of His Messenger.

The second: concerning the example He has struck for you of the blind and the seeing, and that the two are not equal.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 51:

Allah's words: ﴿And warn thereby﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: He means by the Qur'an. He mentioned those who fear being gathered (al-hashr) to the exclusion of others, although he is a warner to all creation, because the proof against those who fear the gathering is more evident, since they acknowledge the return (al-ma'ad). They are one of two men: either a Muslim, so that he may warn him to fulfil Allah's right over him in his Islam, or a People of the Book (kitabi), and the People of the Book are agreed upon the resurrection (al-ba'th).

He also mentioned the protector (wali) and the intercessor (shafi'), because the Jews and the Christians claimed that they are the sons of Allah and His beloved ones. So the Mighty and Majestic informed them that the people of disbelief have no protector or intercessor apart from Him. Another said: "They have no protector apart from Him," meaning: they have no protector other than Allah, nor any intercessor, because the intercession of the intercessors is by His command.

Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: This verse is connected to His words: ﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me so that I may warn you thereby﴾ [al-An'am 6:19].

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 52:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord﴾. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) narrated: "This verse was revealed concerning six people: me, Ibn Mas'ud, Suhayb, ʿAmmar, al-Miqdad, and Bilal. The Quraysh said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'We will not be content to be followers of these people, so drive them away from you.' So there came upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of that what Allah willed to come upon him, and then this verse was revealed."

And Khabbab ibn al-Aratt said: "It was revealed concerning us. We were weak people with the Prophet (ﷺ), and he would teach us in the morning and the evening what would benefit us. Then al-Aqraʿ ibn Habis and ʿUyayna ibn Hisn came and said: 'We are from the nobles of our people, and we dislike that they see us with them, so drive them away when we sit with you.' He said: 'Yes.'"

(p-45) They said: "We will not be content until you write a document between us." So he brought a piece of leather and an inkwell, and called ʿAli to write. When he was about to do that, and we were sitting in a corner, Jibril descended with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord﴾, up to His saying: ﴿We have tried some of them through others﴾. So he threw down the sheet and called us, and we came to him while he was saying: ﴿Peace be upon you. Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾. So we drew close to him that day until we placed our knees upon his knee."

Ibn Mas'ud said: "The chiefs of the Quraysh passed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while Khabbab, Suhayb, Bilal, and ʿAmmar were with him, and they said: 'O Muhammad, are you pleased with these people? Do you want us to be followers of them?' Then this was revealed: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord﴾."

ʿIkrima said: "ʿUtba and Shayba, the two sons of Rabiʿa, Mutʿim ibn ʿAdi, and al-Harith ibn Nawfal, along with the nobles of the Banu ʿAbd Manaf, came to Abu Talib and said: 'If your nephew were to drive away from himself our clients and our slaves, it would be greater in our breasts and closer to our following him.' Abu Talib came to him and told him of that. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said: 'If you did that, so that we may see what they want...' Then these verses were revealed, and ʿUmar came apologizing for his statement."

Abu Salih narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that these verses were revealed concerning the clients (mawali), among them Bilal, Suhayb, Khabbab, ʿAmmar, Mihja', Salman, ʿAmir ibn Fuhayra, and Salim, the client of Abu Hudhayfa. And that His saying: ﴿And warn thereby those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord﴾ was also revealed concerning them.

Al-ʿAwfi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: "Some people of (p-46) the nobles said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'We will believe in you, but when we pray, delay these who are with you, so that they pray behind us.'" Based on this, they only asked him to delay them from the row; and according to the sayings before it, they asked him to drive them away from his gathering.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿who call upon their Lord﴾. Regarding this calling there are five sayings.

The first: it is the prayer, the obligatory prayer. This is said by Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbas. Mujahid said: it is the five prayers; in a narration from Mujahid and Qatada, they said: it means the dawn prayer and the afternoon prayer. Muqatil claimed that the prayer at that time was two rak'as in the morning and two rak'as in the evening; then the five prayers were made obligatory after that.

The second: it is the remembrance of Allah, exalted is He. This is said by Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, and from him, similar to the first saying.

The third: it is the worship of Allah. This is said by al-Dahhak.

The fourth: it is learning the Qur'an morning and evening. This is said by Abu Jaʿfar.

The fifth: it is calling upon Allah with monotheism, sincerity toward Him, and worship of Him. This is said by al-Zajjaj. The majority read: "bil-ghadah" (in the morning). Ibn ʿAmir read here and also in [al-Kahf]: "bil-ghadwah," with a damma on the ghayn, sukun on the dal, and a waw after it.

Al-Farra' said: The Arabs do not put the definite article (alif and lam) on "al-ghadwah," because it is definite without alif and lam, and the Arabs do not make it an idafa. They say: "I came to you at the morning (ghadāt) of Thursday," and they do not say "ghadwat al-Khamis." So this is evidence that it is definite.

Abu ʿAli said: The preferred reading is "al-ghadāh," because it is used as indefinite and becomes definite with the article; whereas "ghadwatan" is definite.

Al-Khalil said: It is permissible to say: "I came to you today in the morning (ghadwatan) and in the early day (bakratan)," treating it as equivalent to ḍaḥwatan. This is the reading of Ibn ʿAmir.

(p-47) If it is said: the calling of the people was continuous by night and day, so why did He specify the morning and the evening? The answer: by mentioning the morning He drew attention to the whole day, and by the evening to the night, because when the work of the day is purely for Him, the work of the night is purer.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿they desire His face﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, they desire Allah, so Allah testifies for them to the soundness of their intentions, and that they are sincere in that.

As for the reckoning mentioned in the verse, there are three sayings.

The first: it is the reckoning of deeds. This is said by al-Hasan.

The second: the reckoning of provisions. The third: it means sufficiency; the meaning being: you are not responsible for their sustenance, nor are they responsible for yours.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so you would be among the wrongdoers﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: This matter weighed heavily upon the Prophet (ﷺ), and he was warned of entering the category of wrongdoers, because he had intended to give precedence to the chiefs over the weak.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 53:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And thus We have tried some of them through others﴾. The meaning: Just as We tested before you the wealthy through the poor, We also test some of them through others. "And We tried" means: We tested and examined. "So that they say," meaning the great ones (al-kubara'), "Is it these whom Allah has favoured (manna Allahu 'alayhim) ﴿among us?﴾" They mean the poor and the weak, "﴿...Allah has favoured among us?﴾" with guidance? This is a question whose meaning is denial (al-inkar), as if they denied that these people could have preceded them in virtue.

Ibn al-Sa'ib said: Allah tested the leaders (al-ru'asa') through the clients (al-mawali). When the noble man looks at the lowly one who has believed before him, he is too proud (anifa) to accept Islam and says: "Has this one preceded me?" (p. 48)

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is not Allah most knowing of those who are grateful?﴾ That is: of those who give thanks for His blessing when He favours them with guidance. The meaning: Allah guides only the one whom He knows will be grateful. The interrogative in "Is not" (alaysa) carries the sense of affirmation (al-taqrir), i.e., it is indeed so.

The Qur'anic verse: ﴿And when those who believe in Our signs come to you﴾. Its interpreters disagree about who it was revealed concerning, and there are five opinions.

The first: it was revealed concerning men who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said, "We have committed great sins." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) remained silent toward them, and then this verse was revealed. This was said by Anas ibn Malik.

The second: it was revealed concerning those whom he (ﷺ) was forbidden to drive away. Whenever the Prophet (ﷺ) saw them, he would begin by greeting them with peace and say, "Praise be to Allah, who has placed in my community one whom He commanded me to begin with peace." This was said by al-Hasan and 'Ikrimah.

The third: it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman, 'Ali, Hamzah, Ja'far, 'Uthman ibn Maz'un, Abu 'Ubaydah, Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, Salim, Abu Salamah, al-Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam, 'Ammar, and Bilal. This was said by 'Ata'.

The fourth: "'Umar ibn al-Khattab had advised the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to delay the poor, in order to win over the chiefs to Islam. When the verse was revealed, ﴿and do not drive away those who call upon their Lord﴾, 'Umar came apologizing for his statement and seeking forgiveness for it, and so this verse was revealed concerning him." This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The fifth: it was revealed as good news of the Islam of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. When he came and embraced Islam, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited it to him. This was related by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

As for the verse ﴿who believe in Our signs﴾, its meaning is: they affirm Our proofs and evidences.

The verse ﴿So say: Peace be upon you﴾ has two opinions.

The first: he was commanded to give them the greeting of peace as an honour to them. We have already mentioned this from al-Hasan and 'Ikrimah.

The second: he was commanded to convey the greeting of peace to them from Allah, the Exalted. This was said by Ibn Zayd. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of peace (salam) is a supplication for a person that he be safe from calamities.

Regarding ﴿evil﴾ (su') there are two opinions.

The first: it is polytheism (shirk). The second: it is acts of disobedience.

We have already discussed the meaning of "ignorance" (jahalah) in Surah an-Nisa'.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "أنَّهُ مَن عَمِلَ مِنكم سُوءًا فَإنَّهُ غَفُورٌ" with a kasrah on the alif in both places (إنّه and فإنّه). 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read with a fathah on the alif in both places. Nafi' read with a fathah on the alif of "أنَّهُ" and a kasrah on the alif of "فَإنَّهُ غَفُورٌ".

Abu 'Ali said: whoever reads the alif of "إنّه" with a kasrah makes it an explanation of the mercy. Whoever reads the alif of "فإنّه" with a kasrah does so because what follows the fa' is the place of the sense of inception (hikmat al-ibtida', meaning that the clause begins a new independent statement). Whoever reads the alif of "أنّه مَن عَمِلَ" with a fathah makes "أنْ" a substitute (badal) for the mercy, and the meaning is: "Your Lord has prescribed that whoever among you does evil..." Whoever reads it with a fathah after the fa' supposes a predicate (khabar) omitted, its estimated form being: "then for him is that He is forgiving and merciful," and the meaning is: "then for him is His forgiveness." Similarly the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿indeed for him is the fire of Hell﴾ [at-Tawbah: 63], meaning: "for him is that for him is the fire of Hell." As for the reading of Nafi', he made it a substitute for the mercy and began anew with what follows the fa'.

(p-50) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And thus We detail the signs﴾, meaning: just as We have detailed for you in this sura Our proofs and signs against the polytheists, so too We make clear to you Our argument concerning every truth that the people of falsehood deny. Ibn Qutayba said: The meaning of "detailing" them is bringing them in separate pieces, one after another.

His saying, may He be exalted: "and that the way of the wicked may become clear" (wa-li-tastabīna). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "wa-li-tastabīna" with the ta', and "sabīlu" in the nominative. Nafi' and Zayd on the authority of Ya'qub also read with the ta', except that they both put "al-sabīla" in the accusative. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim read "wa-li-yastabīna" with the ya', and "sabīlu" in the nominative. As for whoever reads "wa-li-tastabīna" with the ya' or the ta', this is because "sabīl" may be masculine or feminine, as we explained in (Al 'Imran). As for whoever puts the lam in the accusative, the meaning is: and that you, O Muhammad, may make clear the way of the criminals. Regarding "their way" that was made clear to him, there are two views.

One: it is their path in polytheism and their destination to disgrace, related from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it is their aim in driving away the poor from him, and that is only envy, not a preference for his company and following him, related by Abu Sulayman.

If it is asked: how is the lam of purpose (lam kay) isolated in His saying "wa-li-tastabīna", when its rule is that it be tied to a verb preceding it or coming after it? Ibn al-Anbari has answered this with two answers.

One: it is tied to a hidden verb, intended as: and We do that so that you may make clear.

The second: it is conjoined to a hidden lam, its interpretation being: We detail the signs so that their affair may be exposed, and so that their way may become clear.

"Second: 'you worship'; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. 'Their desires' means: their religion. Al-Zajjaj said: he intended, 'I would only have worshipped them by way of desire, not by way of clear proof and evidence.' The meaning of 'idha' (then) is the meaning of a condition; the sense is: 'I would have gone astray if I worshipped them.' Talha and Ibn Abi Layla read: 'qad dalilt' with a kasra on the lam."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 57:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Say: Indeed, I am upon clear evidence from my Lord⦈. The occasion of its revelation: "An-Nadr ibn al-Harith and the rest of the Quraysh said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'O Muhammad, bring us the punishment you threaten us with,' mockingly; and an-Nadr stood beside the Ka'bah and said, 'O Allah, if what he says is true, then bring us the punishment,' so this verse was revealed." This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. As for al-Bayyinah (clear evidence), it is the proof that separates truth from falsehood. Al-Zajjaj said: "I am upon a clear matter, not following desire."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿But you have denied it⦈. Regarding the pronoun (ha al-kinayah) in "bihi" there are three opinions.

The first: it refers to the Lord. The second: it refers to the clear evidence. The third: it refers to the punishment they had sought mockingly.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿What you are asking to be hastened is not with me⦈, meaning: it is not in my hand. Regarding what they sought to hasten there are two opinions.

The first: it is the punishment; this was said by Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan.

The second: it is the signs which they were proposing; this was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿The decision is only for Allah﴾. Regarding it there are two opinions.

The first: it is the judgment by which He distinguishes between the disputing parties through the bestowal of reward and punishment.

The second: it is the decree of sending down punishment upon the opponent.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿He relates the truth⦈. Ibn Kathir, Asim and Nafi' read "yaqussu al-haqq" with a doubled sad, from al-qasas (relating); the meaning being that everything He informs of is true. Abu Amr, Ibn Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "yaqdi al-haqq," from al-qada' (judgment); the meaning being that He issues the true judgment.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 58:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: If I had that for which you are impatient [i.e., the punishment] within my power, the matter would have been decided between me and you.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: He means, "I would not have given you a respite for an hour, and I would have destroyed you."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah is most knowing of the wrongdoers.﴾ Regarding this there are two opinions.

The first: the meaning is, if He wills, He hastens it for them, and if He wills, He delays their punishment.

The second: He knows best what their affair will end in, and that some of them will be guided while others will not be guided; therefore He delays it for them.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وَعِنْدَهُ مَفاتِحُ الغَيْبِ﴾ قالَ ابْنُ جَرِيرٍ: المَفاتِحُ: جَمْعُ مِفْتَحٌ؛ (p-٥٣) يُقالُ مِفْتَحٌ ومِفْتاحٌ، فَمَن قالَ مِفْتَحٌ، جَمَعَهُ: مَفاتِحُ. ومَن قالَ: مِفْتاحٌ، جَمَعَهُ: مَفاتِيحُ. وفي "مَفاتِحِ الغَيْبِ" سَبْعَةُ أقْوالٍ.

أحَدُها: أنَّها خَمْسٌ لا يَعْلَمُها إلّا اللَّهُ عَزَّ وجَلَّ. رَوى البُخارِيُّ في أفْرادِهِ مِن حَدِيثِ ابْنِ عُمَرَ قالَ: قالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ: « "مَفاتِحُ الغَيْبِ خَمْسٌ لا يَعْلَمُهُنَّ إلّا اللَّهُ، لا يَعْلَمُ مَتى تَقُومُ السّاعَةُ إلّا اللَّهُ، ولا يَعْلَمُ ما تَغِيضُ الأرْحامُ إلّا اللَّهُ، ولا يَعْلَمُ ما في غَدٍ إلّا اللَّهُ، ولا تَعْلَمُ نَفْسٌ بِأيِّ أرْضٍ تَمُوتُ إلّا اللَّهُ، ولا يَعْلَمُ مَتى يَنْزِلُ الغَيْثُ إلّا اللَّهُ" » قالَ ابْنُ مَسْعُودٍ: أُوتِيَ نَبِيُّكم عِلْمَ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ إلّا مَفاتِيحَ الغَيْبِ.

والثّانِي: أنَّها خَزائِنُ غَيْبِ السَّماواتِ مِنَ الأقْدارِ والأرْزاقِ، قالَهُ ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ.

والثّالِثُ: ما غابَ عَنِ الخَلْقِ مِنَ الثَّوابِ والعِقابِ، وما تَصِيرُ إلَيْهِ الأُمُورُ، قالَهُ عَطاءٌ.

والرّابِعُ: خَزائِنُ غَيْبِ العَذابِ، مَتى يَنْزِلُ، قالَهُ مُقاتِلٌ. (p-٥٤) والخامِسُ: الوَصْلَةُ إلى عِلْمِ الغَيْبِ إذا اسْتَعْلَمَ، قالَهُ الزَّجّاجُ.

والسّادِسُ: عَواقِبُ الأعْمارِ وخَواتِيمُ الأعْمالِ.

والسّابِعُ: ما لَمْ يَكُنْ، هَلْ يَكُونُ أمْ لا يَكُونُ؟ وما يَكُونُ كَيْفَ يَكُونُ؟ وما لا يَكُونُ، إنْ كانَ كَيْفَ يَكُونُ؟ فَأمّا البَرُّ، فَهو القَفْرُ. وفي البَحْرِ قَوْلانِ. أحَدُهُما: أنَّهُ الماءُ، قالَهُ الجُمْهُورُ. والثّانِي: أنَّهُ القُرى، قالَهُ مُجاهِدٌ.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وَما تَسْقُطُ مِن ورَقَةٍ إلا يَعْلَمُها﴾ قالَ الزَّجّاجُ: المَعْنى: أنَّهُ يَعْلَمُها ساقِطَةً وثابِتَةً، كَما تَقُولُ: ما يَجِيئُكَ أحَدٌ إلّا وأنا أعْرِفُهُ، لَيْسَ تَأْوِيلُهُ: اعْرِفْهُ في حالِ مَجِيئِهِ فَقَطْ. فَأمّا ظُلُماتُ الأرْضِ، فالمُرادُ بِها بَطْنُ الأرْضِ.

وفي الرَّطْبِ واليابِسِ خَمْسَةُ أقْوالٍ.

أحَدُها: أنَّ الرَّطْبَ: الماءُ، واليابِسَ: البادِيَةُ. والثّانِي: الرَّطْبُ: ما يَنْبُتُ، واليابِسُ: ما لا يَنْبُتُ. والثّالِثُ: الرَّطْبُ: الحَيُّ، واليابِسُ: المَيِّتُ. والرّابِعُ: الرَّطْبُ: لِسانُ المُؤْمِنِ يَذْكُرُ اللَّهَ، واليابِسُ: لِسانُ الكافِرِ لا يَتَحَرَّكُ بِذِكْرِ اللَّهِ. والخامِسُ: أنَّهُما الشَّيْءُ يَنْتَقِلُ مِن إحْدى الحالَتَيْنِ إلى الأُخْرى، فَهو يَعْلَمُهُ رَطْبًا، ويَعْلَمُهُ يابِسًا. وفي الكِتابِ المُبِينِ قَوْلانِ.

أحَدُهُما: أنَّهُ اللَّوْحُ المَحْفُوظُ (the Preserved Tablet)؛ قالَهُ مُقاتِلٌ. والثّانِي: أنَّهُ عِلْمُ اللَّهِ المُتْقَنُ؛ ذَكَرَهُ الزَّجّاجُ. فَإنْ قِيلَ: ما الفائِدَةُ في إحْصاءِ هَذِهِ الأشْياءِ في كِتابٍ؟ فَعَنْهُ ثَلاثَةُ أجْوِبَةٍ، ذَكَرَهُنَّ ابْنُ الأنْبارِيِّ.

أحَدُها: أنَّهُ أحْصاها في كِتابٍ، لِتَقِفَ المَلائِكَةُ عَلى نَفاذِ عِلْمِهِ.

والثّانِي: أنَّهُ نَبَّهَ بِذَلِكَ عِبادَهُ عَلى تَعْظِيمِ الحِسابِ، وأعْلَمَهم أنَّهُ لا يَفُوتُهُ ما يَصْنَعُونَ، لِأنَّ مَن يُثْبِتُ ما لا ثَوابَ فِيهِ ولا عِقابَ، فَهو إلى إثْباتِ ما فِيهِ ثَوابٌ وعِقابٌ أسْرَعُ. (p-٥٥) والثّالِثُ: أنَّ المُرادَ بِالكِتابِ: العِلْمُ؛ فالمَعْنى: أنَّها مُثْبَتَةٌ في عِلْمِهِ.

It is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it is He who takes you back [to Himself] at night﴾. He means by it sleep, because it seizes the souls from acting freely through sleep, just as it seizes them through death. Ibn Abbas said: He seizes your souls during your sleep. "And you have wounded [yourselves]" means: you have earned (kasabtum). "Then He raises you up" means: He wakes you in it, that is, in the daytime. ﴿So that a specified term may be fulfilled﴾ means: so that you may reach the specified term, the cutting off of your lives. Thus the waking after sleep points to the resurrection after death.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 6, verse 61:**

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And He sends over you guardians (ḥafaẓah)﴾. The *ḥafaẓah* are the angels. The singular is *ḥāfiẓ*, and the plural is *ḥafaẓah*, like *kātib* and *kataba* (scribe and scribes), and *fāʿil* and *faʿala* (doer and doers). There are two views about what they guard.

The first is that they guard the deeds of the children of Adam. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second is that they guard their deeds and their bodies. This was said by al-Suddi.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Our messengers (rusuluna) take him in death﴾. Ḥamzah read *tuwaffāhu rusluna* (تُوَفّاهُ رُسْلُنا), with the verb in the feminine form and *rusl* without the extra vowel. His argument is that the verb is attached to a feminine noun that is not a real feminine, since the feminine marking is for the plural. It is therefore like ﴿And women said﴾ [Yusuf: 30]. There are three views about who is meant by "the messengers."

The first is that they are the helpers of the Angel of Death (malak al-mawt). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. al-Nakhaʿi said: his helpers take the souls, and he takes them from them.

The second is that "the messengers" means the Angel of Death alone. This was said by Muqatil.

The third is that they are the guardians. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and they do not fail (yufarriṭūna)﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they do not neglect.

If it is asked: how is His saying ﴿Our messengers take him in death﴾ reconciled with His saying ﴿Say: the Angel of Death who has been entrusted with you takes you﴾ [al-Sajdah: 11]? There are two answers.

The first is that it is permissible to mean by "the messengers" the Angel of Death alone, since the plural may be used for the singular. The second is that the helpers of the Angel of Death act by his command, so the whole action is attributed to his act.

It has also been said: the helpers of the Angel of Death cause death by extraction, the Angel of Death causes it by commanding the spirits and they respond, and he calls them and they come out, and God, Exalted is He, causes it by creating death in the dead person.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 62:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then they are returned to Allah﴾, meaning the servants. Concerning the one who carries out the returning, there are two opinions.

One of them: they are the angels, who return them by death to Allah, the Exalted.

The second: it is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, who returns them by resurrection in the Hereafter. Concerning the meaning of their being returned to Allah, the Exalted, there are two opinions.

One of them: they are returned to the place in which none holds judgment except Allah alone.

The second: they are returned to Allah's management alone; because when He brought them into being, He was solely in charge of their management, then when He empowered them to act, they came to be in charge of their own affairs, then He restrained them from that by death, so they became returned [to His management].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Surely, to Him belongs the judgment﴾, meaning the decision. And the explanation of the swiftness of the reckoning is in [al-Baqarah] (the Surah of the Cow).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verses 63–64:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Who delivers you from the darknesses of the land and the sea?"﴾ Ᾱṣim, Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī and Abū Ja'far read: "Qul man yunajjīkum, qul Allāhu yunajjīkum" with the letter nūn doubled (tashdīd). Yaʿqūb and al-Qazzāz, from ʿAbd al-Wārith, read it with a sukūn on the nūn and a light jīm (takhfīf). Al-Zajjāj said: the doubled form is better because it is the more common usage (li-l-kathrah). "The darknesses of the land and the sea" means their hardships (shadāʾiduhā). The Arabs say of a day on which one encounters hardship, "a dark day" (yawm muẓlim), to the extent that they say "a day with stars" (yawm dhū kawākib), meaning its darkness has grown intense until it becomes like night. The poet said:

"I ransom for the Banū Dhuhl ibn Shaybān my she-camel, on a day that is 'with stars' and grievous."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿calling upon Him humbly﴾, meaning openly displaying humility (ḍarāʿah), which is the intense need for and dependence upon a thing.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and secretly﴾. ʿĀṣim, except Ḥafṣ, read "wa-khifyatan" with a kasrah on the khāʾ, and likewise in [al-Aʿrāf]. The rest read it with a ḍammah on the khāʾ, and both are dialects (lughatān). Al-Farrāʾ said: there is another dialect with a waw, khifwatan and khafwatan, but it is not suitable for recitation. The meaning of the speech is that you call upon Him within yourselves as you call upon Him openly: ﴿"If You deliver us from this, we will surely be among the thankful."﴾ Thus Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū ʿAmr read "la-in anjaytanā"; but ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read "la-in anjānā" with an alif, because of the third-person form in His saying "tadʿūnahu." Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī and Khalaf used imālah on the jīm.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿from this﴾, meaning: whatever hardship you fall into, you say, "If You deliver us from this..." Ibn ʿAbbās said: "the thankful" here means the believers. Quraysh used to travel by land and sea, and when they lost their way and feared destruction, they called upon Allah sincerely, and He delivered them. As for "al-karb," it is the grief that seizes the soul, and from it the word "al-kurbah" is derived.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 65:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: He is the One able to send upon you a punishment from above you or from beneath your feet.﴾ Concerning this there are two opinions.

(p-59) One: that "from above you" is the punishment descending from the sky, as the people of Lot were pelted and the companions of the Elephant (Ashab al-Fil). And "from beneath your feet" is like the sinking into the earth that befell Qarun. This was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi, and Muqatil. Others said that it includes the Flood, the wind, the Cry (al-Sayhah), and the earthquake (al-Rajfah).

The second opinion: that "from above you" is from your rulers, and "from beneath your feet" is from your common people (sifalatihim). This was narrated by Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas. In another narration he said: "from above you" refers to the wicked leaders (a'immat al-su'), and "from beneath your feet" refers to the wicked subjects (abid al-su').

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or to confuse you with division into sects (shiya')﴾. Ibn Abbas said: He spreads among you divergent desires, so that you become factions. Ibn Qutaybah said: "yalbisakum" comes from confusion (al-iltibas) upon them, and the meaning is: until you become sects (shiya'), that is, divided factions. Then He makes some of you taste the violence of others, through fighting and war. Al-Zajjaj said: "yalbisakum" means He mixes your affair with a mixture of turmoil, not a mixture of agreement. It is said: "labistu 'alayhimu al-amr, ulbisuhu," when I have not made it clear. The meaning of "shiya'" is that He makes you into factions; so when you are divided, some of you fight others.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and make some of you taste the violence of others﴾, that is, some of you kill others by the hands of others. Concerning those intended by this verse, there are three opinions.

The first: that it refers to the Muslims who pray. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Abu al-Aliyah, and Qatadah. Ubayy ibn Ka'b said concerning this verse: "They are four traits, and all of them are punishments, and all of them will occur before the Day of Resurrection. Two of them had already passed before the death of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by twenty-five years: they were confused into sects and some of them were made to taste the violence of others. Two are certain to occur without doubt: the sinking into the earth and the stoning."

(p-60) The second: that the punishment is for the polytheists, and the rest of the verse is for the Muslims. This was said by al-Hasan. It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "I asked my Lord for three things; He granted me two and denied me one. I asked Him not to afflict you with a punishment by which He afflicted those before you, and He granted it to me. I asked Him not to give power over you to an enemy who would devastate your community (baydatakum), and He granted it to me. I asked Him not to confuse you into sects and to make some of you taste the violence of others, and He denied me this."

The third: that it is a threat to the polytheists. This was said by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And your people denied it﴾. There are three opinions concerning the pronoun in "bihi" (by it/him).

The first: it refers to the Qur'an. The second: it refers to the variation of the signs (taṣrīf al-āyāt). The third: it refers to the punishment (al-ʿadhāb).

(p-61) Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: I am not a guardian over you﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions.

The first: "I am not a guardian (ḥafīẓ) over your deeds so as to recompense you for them; I am only a warner." This was said by al-Ḥasan.

The second: "I am not a guardian over you to compel you to faith; I only call you to Allah." This was said by al-Zajjāj.

Section

Concerning this portion of the verse there are two opinions.

The first: it required limiting their case to warning alone, without anything further; then this was abrogated (nasakh) by the verse of the sword.

The second: its meaning is: "I am not a guardian over you; I only hold you to the outward (ẓawāhir) of affirmation and action, not to what is concealed (al-isrār). According to this, the verse is muḥkam (definitive, not abrogated)."

For the Qur'anic verse: ﴿For every news there is a fixed time⦆... Let me translate properly.

"His saying, the Exalted: ﴿For every tidings there is a fixed time⦈ — meaning: for every report that Allah informs of, there is a time at which it will occur, without any failure or delay. Al-Suddi (Isma'il ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Suddi, d. 127 AH, a major early Qur'an commentator) said: 'So the tidings of the Qur'an were established by what He had been promising them of punishment on the day of Badr.' Muqatil (Muqatil ibn Sulayman, d. 150 AH, an early tafsir scholar) said: 'Part of it is in this world on the day of Badr, and in the Hereafter it is Jahannam.'"

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 68:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our verses﴾ — there are three opinions regarding who is meant by this verse. The first: the polytheists (al-mushrikun). The second: the Jews. The third: the people of desires (ahl al-ahwa'). The "verses" are the Qur'an. The "engaging" (khawd) of the polytheists in it is their denying it and mocking it, and close to it is the engaging of the Jews, and the engaging of the people of desires is through disputation (mira') and quarrels.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿then turn away from them﴾ — that is, leave off sitting with them, until their talk is about something other than the Qur'an. ﴿And if Satan causes you to forget﴾ — Ibn 'Amir recited "yunsiyannaka" with a fatha on the nun, a shadda on the sin, and a second nun. Similar to this is "gharramtuhu" and "aghramtuhu" (I made him pay a fine). In the revelation: ﴿So give respite to the disbelievers; give them a little respite﴾. The meaning is: if Satan makes you forget, and you sit with them forgetting, Our prohibition to you (applies), so do not sit after the reminder. The "dhikr" and the "dhikra" are one and the same. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Stand up as soon as you remember it." And "the wrongdoers" (al-zalimun) are the polytheists.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 69:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who guard against (evil) are not accountable for them in anything﴾. Concerning the occasion of its revelation there are three opinions.

The first: the Muslims said, "If whenever the polytheists mock the Qur'an and engage in it (in disputation), we forbid them, we will not be able to sit in the Sacred Mosque or circumambulate the House." So this verse was revealed.

The second: the Muslims said, "We fear sin if we do not forbid them from engaging (in such talk)." So this verse was revealed.

The third: the Muslims said, "If we rise from them when they engage (in such talk), we fear sin in sitting with them." So this verse was revealed. This is from Muqatil, while the first two are from Ibn 'Abbas.

(p-63) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who guard against (evil)﴾ has two interpretations.

One: they guard against shirk. The other: they guard against engaging (in such talk).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿from their accountability﴾ means: the accountability of those who engage (in such talk). Regarding "their accountability" there are two interpretations.

One: it is their disbelief and their sins. The other: it is the punishment for their engaging (in such talk).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿but (it is) a reminder﴾, meaning: but it is incumbent upon you to remind them. Regarding what you remind them with, there are two interpretations.

One: admonitions. The other: your rising from them. Muqatil said: when you rise from them, their shame before you and their desire to sit with you will prevent them from engaging (in such talk).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿so that they may guard against (evil)﴾ has two interpretations.

One: they guard against mockery. The other: they guard against the threat (of punishment).

Section

Some people held that this verse is abrogated, because it permitted sitting with those who engage (in such talk) and limiting oneself to reminding them, and then it was abrogated by His saying: ﴿And He has already sent down to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of Allah being disbelieved in and mocked, do not sit with them﴾ [al-Nisa': 140]. The correct view is that it is muhkam (not abrogated), because it is a report, and it only indicates that each servant is responsible for his own accountability and is not obligated to bear the accountability of another.

﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as amusement and play﴾. Regarding this, there are two opinions.

One is that they are the disbelievers. The other is that they are the Jews and the Christians.

Concerning their taking their religion as amusement and play, there are three opinions. The first is that it is their mockery of God's signs when they hear them.

The second is that they adhered to whatever they desired, just as one plays with what one desires.

The third is that they observe their religion when they desire to, just as they play when they desire to. Al-Farra' said: It is said that there is no people except that they have a festival, and they play during their festivals, except the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), for their festivals are prayer, glorification of God (takbir), righteousness and good.

**Section**

Scholars of *naskh* (abrogation) hold two opinions regarding this portion of the verse.

One is that it came as a threat, like His saying: ﴿Leave Me with the one whom I created alone﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:11]. According to this view, the verse is *muhkam* (not abrogated), and Mujahid held this meaning.

The second is that it required leniency toward them and turning away from them, and then it was abrogated by the verse of the sword. Qatadah and al-Suddi held this view.

His saying: ﴿And remind with it﴾, i.e., admonish with the Qur'an. Regarding His saying: ﴿lest a soul be delivered to destruction (an tubsala)﴾ there are two opinions.

One is: lest a soul be delivered up, like His saying: ﴿lest you go astray﴾ [an-Nisa' 4:176].

The second is: remind them of the delivering up of those who are delivered up for their offenses, perhaps they will fear.

Regarding the meaning of *tubsala*, there are seven opinions.

The first: it will be handed over (taslam). This was narrated by Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Hasan, Mujahid and al-Suddi also said so. Ibn Qutaybah said: it will be handed over to ruin. The poet said:

*And my handing over my sons, without any crime, (their) offense we did not commit, nor (for) blood shed*

That is: without a crime that we committed. *Al-ba'w* is the offense. Al-Zajjaj said: it will be handed over, by its deed, unable to escape. *Al-mustabsil* is one who surrenders, who does not know that he is able to escape.

The second: it will be disgraced (tufda'), narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: it will be repelled (tudfa'), narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: it will be destroyed (tuhlak), also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fifth: it will be detained and seized (tuhbas wa tu'khadh), said by Qatadah and Ibn Zayd.

The sixth: it will be recompensed (tujza), said by Ibn al-Sa'ib and al-Kisa'i.

The seventh: it will be held in pledge (turtahan), said by al-Farra'. Abu 'Ubaydah said: it will be held in pledge and handed over; and he recited:

*There, I do not hope for a life that gladdens me, a companion of the nights (forever), delivered up for offenses*

(p-66) *Samir al-layali* (companion of the nights) means *abad al-layali* (the eternity of the nights). As for *al-waliyy*, it is the helper who protects it from the punishment of God. *Al-'adl* is ransom. Ibn Zayd said: and if it should offer every ransom, it will not be accepted from it. As for *al-hamim*, it is hot water. Ibn Qutaybah said: from it the bathhouse (hammam) was named.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 71–72:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say, "Shall we call upon, instead of Allah, that which can neither benefit us nor harm us, and be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us?"﴾ That is: shall we worship what neither harms us if we do not worship it, nor benefits us if we do worship it, namely the idols? ﴿And be turned back on our heels﴾ means: return to disbelief ﴿after Allah has guided us﴾ to Islam, so that we would be ﴿like one whom the devils have enticed, bewildered, on the earth﴾. Hamzah recited "istahwahu al-shayatin" (اسْتَهْواهُ الشَّياطِينُ) in analogy with his recitation "tawaffahu rusuluna" (تُوَفّاهُ رُسُلُنا). There are two opinions concerning the meaning of "istihwa'uha" (اسْتِهْوائِها).

The first: they made him fall and go away with him; this is the view of Ibn Qutaybah. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the devils make him appear to him (in a false form), so he follows them until they cast him down into the earth and lead him astray.

The second: they made his desire appealing to him; this is the view of al-Zajjaj. He said: "ḥayrān" (حَيْرانَ) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, meaning: they enticed him while he was in bewilderment. As-Suddi said: the polytheists said to the Muslims, "Follow our way and leave the religion of Muhammad." So He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Say, "Shall we call upon, instead of Allah, that which neither benefits us nor harms us, and be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us?"﴾ Then we would be like a man who was with a people on a road, who was lost, and the devils confused him, while his companions on the road were calling him: "O so-and-so, come to us, for we are on the road," but he refused. Ibn 'Abbas said: this verse was revealed concerning 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr al-Siddiq, whom his father and mother invited to Islam, but he refused. Muqatil said: by his companions is meant his parents.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say, "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the (true) guidance."﴾ This is a rebuttal of those who invited to the worship of idols, and a warning against responding to them, as if it were said to him: do not do that, for the guidance of Allah is the guidance, not the guidance of anyone else.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And we have been commanded, "that we submit to the Lord of the worlds"﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the Arabs say "amartuka an taf'al" (أمَرْتُكَ أنْ تَفْعَلَ), "amartuka li-taf'al" (أمَرْتُكَ لَتَفْعَلَ), and "amartuka bi-an taf'al" (أمَرْتُكَ بِأنْ تَفْعَلَ). Whoever says "bi-an" has the particle "bi" for attachment, meaning the command was issued for this act. Whoever says "an taf'al" does so with the particle "bi" omitted. Whoever says "li-taf'al" has stated the reason for which the command was issued. He said: regarding His saying ﴿and that we establish prayer﴾ there are two possibilities.

The first: "We were commanded so that we submit, and so that we establish prayer."

The second: that it is understood according to meaning, since the meaning is: "We were commanded to submit (to Islam) and to establish prayer."
