Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 73:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in truth﴾. Concerning this there are four opinions.

The first: He created them for the truth (lil-haqq). The second: He created them truly (haqqan). The third: He created them by His word, and His word is the truth. The fourth: He created them with wisdom (al-hikmah).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the day He says, "Be," and it is, [His word is the truth]﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The better view is that it is in the accusative on the basis of an implied meaning: "Mention the day He says, 'Be,' and it is," because what follows is ﴿And when Ibrahim said﴾. So the meaning is: "Mention this and this." Concerning the one of whom He says "Be" and it is, there are three opinions.

The first: that it is the Day of Resurrection, as reported by Muqatil. The second: that it is what occurs at the Resurrection. The third: that it is the Trumpet (al-Sur), and what is mentioned concerning the Trumpet indicates this; this is what al-Zajjaj said, both of them. He said: That day is singled out for the swiftness of bringing a thing into being, so as to indicate the swiftness of the matter of the Resurrection.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿His word is the truth﴾, i.e., the true statement that will certainly come to pass. ﴿And to Him belongs the dominion on the day the Trumpet is blown﴾. Ishaq ibn Yusuf al-Azraq narrated from Abu 'Amr: "nanfukh" with two nuns. The meaning of the statement is that on that day kings will have no kingship; He alone will be the sole possessor of dominion, as He said: ﴿And the command that day belongs to Allah﴾ [al-Infitar: 19]. Concerning "al-Sur" there are two opinions.

One of them: that it is a horn which is blown into. Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As narrated that he asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the Sur, and he said: "It is a horn that is blown into." Mujahid said: The Sur is like the shape of a trumpet (buq). Ibn Qutaybah related that al-Sur means the horn in the dialect of a people of Yemen, and he recited:

"We struck them on the morning of the two hosts with the galloping steeds amid the dust of the two clouds of dust,
a fierce striking, not like the striking of the two horns (al-sawrayn)."

And al-Farra' recited:

"Had it not been for Ibn Ja'dah, they would not have conquered your Quhundudh,
nor Khurasan, until the Sur is blown."

This is the view chosen by the majority.

The second: that al-Sur is the plural of surah (form); it is said: surah and suwar, like surah (a section/wall) and suwar, as in the surah of a building; and the intended meaning is the blowing of spirits into the forms of people. This was said by Qatadah and Abu 'Ubaydah. Likewise al-Hasan, Mu'adh al-Qari', Abu Mijlaz, and Abu al-Mutawakkil recited "fi al-Sur" with a fatha on the waw. Tha'lab said: The better view is that al-Sur is the horn, because He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will fall unconscious﴾; then He said: ﴿It will be blown into again﴾; and if it were al-Sur, it would have said: "then He blew into them" or "into them (all)"; and this indicates that it is one; and the apparent meaning of the Qur'an bears witness that it is blown into twice. The people of tafsir have related from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: "The Sur is a horn into which three blasts will be blown: the first is the blast of terror, the second is the blast of swooning, and the third is the blast of rising for the Lord of the worlds." Ibn 'Abbas said: This blast mentioned in this verse is the first, meaning the blast of swooning.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Knower of the unseen﴾, which is what is hidden from the servants, of what they have not witnessed, "and the witnessed," which is what they have seen and observed. Al-Hasan said: By this is meant the secret and the open.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 74:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar﴾. Regarding Azar there are four opinions.

The first: it is the name of his father. This is related from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Suddi, and Ibn Ishaq.

The second: it is the name of an idol. As for the name of Abraham's father, it is Tarih (Tarikh), as said by Mujahid. The meaning then is: "Do you take Azar as idols?" It is as though he made "idols" a substitute for "Azar," and the interrogative carries the sense of denunciation.

The third: it is not a name at all, but rather an insult by way of a defect. Regarding its meaning there are two sayings. One is that it means "the crooked one," as though he was reproached for his turning and his deviation from the truth; this was mentioned by al-Farra'. The other is that it means "the mistaken one," as though he said: "O mistaken one, do you take idols?" This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

The fourth: it is a title (laqab) for his father, not his name, as said by Muqatil ibn Hayyan. Ibn al-Anbari said: "A person's title may come to predominate over his given name, until he becomes better known by it than by his name."

The majority read "Azara" with a fatha (accusative). Al-Hasan and Ya'qub read it with a damma (nominative). Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads it in the accusative, the position of "Azara" is genitive as an apposition (badal) to "abihi" (his father); and whoever reads it in the nominative, it is in the vocative (nida').

Ibn al-Jawzi, *Zad al-Masir*, on Surah 6, verse 75:

God's words: ﴿And thus We showed Abraham﴾, meaning: just as We granted him insight into his religion and the truth in opposition to his people, We showed him ﴿the malakut (dominion) of the heavens and the earth﴾. It has been said that "nuri" (We show) has the sense of "arayna" (We showed). Al-Zajjaj said: "The malakut is equivalent to the malik (sovereignty), except that malakut is more intensive in the language, because the waw and the ta' are added for emphasis. Similar to malakut are al-raghabut and al-rahabut." Mujahid said: "The malakut of the heavens and the earth means its signs. The seven heavens were opened for him, up to the Throne, and he looked into them. The seven earths were opened for him, and he looked into them." Qatadah said: "The malakut of the heavens is the sun, the moon and the stars, and the malakut of the earth is the mountains, the trees and the seas." Al-Suddi said: "He was made to stand upon a rock, and the heavens and the earth were opened for him, so he looked upon the dominion of God, the Mighty and Majestic, until he looked upon the Throne and upon his abode in Paradise. The seven earths were opened for him, until he looked upon the rock upon which the earths rest."

God's words: ﴿and that he might be among the certain﴾. This is a conjunction with the meaning, because the sense of the verse is: We showed him the malakut of the heavens and the earth so that he might reason by it, and that he might be among the certain. There are three opinions on what he became certain of:

First: the oneness of God and His power. Second: His prophethood and His messengership. Third: that he would be certain of the knowledge of everything through direct perception (ḥissan), not through report (khabaran).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When the night covered him﴾. Al-Zajjaj (the grammarian) said: It is said *jamma 'alayhi al-layl* and *ajannahu al-layl*, meaning the night became dark until he was concealed by its darkness. It is also said of anything that is concealed: *jinn* and *ajanna*. The preferred form is to say *jamma 'alayhi al-layl* and *ajannahu al-layl*.

**The indication of the beginning of the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him**

Abu Salih narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Ibrahim was born in the time of Namrud. Namrud had soothsayers, and they said to him: "In this year a boy will be born who will corrupt the gods of the people of the earth and call them to other than their religion, and the destruction of your household will be at his hands." So he separated the women from the men, and Azar entered his wife's home and had intercourse with her, and she conceived. The soothsayers then told Namrud: "The boy has been conceived tonight." He said: "Kill every boy that is born." When the pains of labour seized Ibrahim's mother, she went out fleeing and gave birth to him in a dry riverbed. She wrapped him in a cloth and placed him among reeds, and she informed his father of him. The father came, dug a tunnel for him, and sealed its entrance with a rock. His mother used to visit him and nurse him until he grew up and could speak. He said to his mother: "Who is my Lord?" She said: "I am." He said: "Then who is your lord?" She said: "Your father." He said: "Then who is the lord of my father?" She said: "Be silent." So he was silent. She returned to her husband and said: "The boy about whom we used to talk, that he would change the religion of the people of the earth, is your son." So the father came to him and said to him the same as that. When the night covered him, he approached the entrance of the tunnel, looked, and saw a star.

Ibn Kathir, Hafs (from 'Asim) read *ra'a* with a fatha on the *ra'* and the hamza. Abu 'Amr read *ra'a* with a fatha on the *ra'* and a kasra on the hamza. Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr (from 'Asim) read *ra'a* with a kasra on the *ra'* and the hamza. They differed about these forms when they are followed by a letter with sukun (a silent letter). This occurs in six places: ﴿ra'a al-qamar﴾ (the moon), ﴿falamma ra'a al-shams﴾ (when he saw the sun), in al-Nahl ﴿wa-idha ra'a alladhina zalamu﴾ (And when those who did wrong see) [16:85], ﴿wa-idha ra'a alladhina ashraku﴾ (And when those who associated partners see) [16:86], in al-Kahf ﴿wa-ra'a al-mujrimuna al-nar﴾ (And the criminals will see the Fire) [18:53], and in al-Ahzab ﴿wa-lamma ra'a al-mu'minun﴾ (And when the believers saw) [33:22].

Abu Bakr (from 'Asim), Hamza except al-'Absi, and Khalaf in his own choice read with a kasra on the *ra'* and a fatha on the hamza in all cases. Al-'Absi also narrated a kasra on the hamza. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read with a fatha on the *ra'* and the hamza.

If this is attached to a pronoun, as in *ra'aka*, *ra'ahu* and *ra'aha*, then Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf, al-Walid (from Ibn 'Amir), al-Mufaddal, Aban and al-Qazzaz (from 'Abd al-Warith), and al-Kisa'i (from Abu Bakr) read with a kasra on the *ra'* and incline the hamza (*imala*, pronouncing the vowel toward i).

Regarding the star that he saw, there are two opinions. One is that it was Venus, said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. The second is that it was Jupiter, said by Mujahid and al-Suddi.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said: "This is my lord."﴾ There are three opinions about it.

One: it is on its apparent meaning. 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "This is my lord," and he worshipped it until it set, then worshipped the moon until it set, then worshipped the sun until it set. Those who held this view argued with his saying: ﴿Unless my Lord guides me, I shall surely be among the people who go astray﴾ [6:77], and this indicates a kind of bewilderment. They said: He said this in his childhood, as it occurred to his mind before a proof had become established for him.

This opinion is not acceptable, since those qualified for prophethood are protected from such things in every case.

As for his saying: ﴿Unless my Lord guides me﴾, the prophets continued to ask for guidance and to humbly plead for protection from error, like His saying: ﴿And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ [14:35]. Also, He had already given him his right guidance before, and showed him the dominion of the heavens and the earth so that he would be certain. How then would He not protect him from such confusion?

The second: he said this as *istidraj* (leading step by step) for the argument, so that he might reproach their gods and show them his hatred of them when they set. He must have intended, in his own mind, either "according to your claim" or "in what you suppose," so it is like His saying: "Where are My partners?" Or he intended "they say," so it is like His saying: ﴿Our Lord, accept from us﴾ [2:127], meaning: they say that. Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari mentioned something similar. His aim was to lead them step by step to the proof against them, as was related about a certain wise man who came to a people who worshipped an idol. He showed reverence for it, so they honoured him and deferred to his opinion. Then an enemy attacked them, and their king consulted them. He said: "Let us call on our god so that he may remove what afflicts us." They gathered and called upon it, but it did not benefit them. He then said: "Here is a god whom we should call upon, and he will respond." So they called upon God, and He turned away from them what they feared, and they embraced Islam.

The third: he said it as a question. Its implied form is: "Is this my lord?" The interrogative particle was omitted, like His saying: ﴿Then if you die, will they be immortal?﴾ [21:34], meaning: "Will they be immortal?" The poet said:

*Your eye deceived you, or did you see in Wasit*
*a shadow of a phantom from al-Rabab in the dark of night?*

He meant: "Did it deceive you?" Ibn al-Anbari said: This opinion is anomalous, because the interrogative particle is not omitted when it distinguishes between a statement and a question.

The apparent meaning of his saying: ﴿This is my lord﴾ is that it refers to the Creator. Al-Zajjaj said: They were astrologers, so he said: "This is my lord," meaning: "This is the one who manages me." He then argued against them that what you claim to be a manager, we see in it only the trace of something managed. *Afala* means to set: it is said *afala al-najm yaʼfilu* and *yafulu ufulan* (the star set).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿I do not love those that set﴾. That is, the love of a Lord who is worshipped, because what appears and sets is created and managed.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 77–78:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When he saw the moon﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: The moon (qamar) was so named for its whiteness; al-aqmar means the white one, and a night described as qamra'  means bright, i.e., luminous. As for al-bazigh (the rising one), it means the one that rises. The meaning of ﴿Unless my Lord guides me﴾ is: unless my Lord keeps me firm upon guidance. If it is asked: why did He say "this" about the sun and not "this one"? There are four answers to this.

The first: he saw the light of the sun, not the sun itself. This was said by Muhammad ibn Muqatil. The second: (p-76) he meant: "This rising one is my Lord." This was said by al-Akhfash. The third: the sun is in the sense of light and radiance, so he treated the word according to its meaning. The fourth: the word "sun" (shams) has no sign of the feminine in its form, and its form resembles that of the masculine, so its masculine reference is permitted. This was mentioned by him and by the one before him, Ibn al-Anbari.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verses 79–80:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, I have turned my face﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: I have made my intention in my worship and my monotheism directed to Allah, the Lord of the worlds, the Mighty and Majestic. The rest of the verse has already been discussed.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And his people argued with him﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: They disputed with him about their gods and threatened him with them, so he said, denouncing them: ﴿Do you argue with me﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "Atuhaajjoonni" [أتُحاجُّونِّي] and "ta'murunni" [تَأْمُرُونِّي] (Az-Zumar 39:64) with a doubled nun (shaddah). Nafi' and Ibn ʿAmir read them with a single nun, deleting the second nun because two nuns came together (idghaam/elision of the repeated nun). The meaning of ﴿Do you argue with me about Allah﴾ is: about His oneness (tawhid). ﴿And He has already guided me﴾, that is, He has made clear to me that by which I was guided. Al-Kisa'i read "hadani" [هَدانِي] with imalah of the dal. Imalah (vowel-raising, a pronunciation in which the alif is inclined toward the i-sound) is good in cases where the original root has a ya', and this is from hada, yahdi (to guide).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And I do not fear what you associate with Him﴾, that is: I do not dread your gods. That is because they said: "We fear that your gods will afflict you with harm," and he said: "I do not fear them, because they neither harm nor benefit," ﴿except that my Lord wills something﴾, so of that I am afraid. ﴿My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge﴾, that is, He has known everything with complete knowledge.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, I have turned my face﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: I have made my intention in my worship and my monotheism directed to Allah, the Lord of the worlds, the Mighty and Majestic. The rest of the verse has already been discussed.

Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "Atuhaajjoonni" [أتُحاجُّونِّي] and "ta'murunni" [تَأْمُرُونِّي] (Az-Zumar 39:64) with a doubled nun (shaddah). Nafi' and Ibn ʿAmir read them with a single nun, deleting the second nun because two nuns came together (idghaam/elision of the repeated nun). The meaning of ﴿Do you argue with me about Allah﴾ is: about His oneness (tawhid). ﴿And He has already guided me﴾, that is, He has made clear to me that by which I was guided. Al-Kisa'i read "hadani" [هَدانِي] with imalah of the dal. Imalah (vowel-raising, a pronunciation in which the alif is inclined toward the i-sound) is good in cases where the original root has a ya', and this is from hada, yahdi (to guide).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And I do not fear what you associate with Him﴾, that is: I do not dread your gods. That is because they said: "We fear that your gods will afflict you with harm," and he said: "I do not fear them, because they neither harm nor benefit," ﴿except that my Lord wills something﴾, so of that I am afraid. ﴿My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge﴾, that is, He has known everything with complete knowledge.

(p-77) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And how should I fear what you associate with Him?﴾ That is, of these idols that neither harm nor benefit. ﴿And you do not fear that you have associated with Allah, who created you and provided for you, and who is able to harm you and benefit you, that for which He has not sent down to you any authority﴾, that is, any proof. ﴿So which of the two parties is more deserving of security﴾, that is, more deserving of being safe from punishment: the monotheist who worships the One in whose hand is harm and benefit, or the polytheist who worships what neither harms nor benefits? Then He clarified who is more deserving by His saying: ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾, that is, do not mix it with association (shirk). Al-Bukhari and Muslim in their two Sahihs (the two authentic collections of hadith) narrated from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "When this verse was revealed, it weighed heavily on the Muslims. They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, which of us does not do wrong?' He said: 'It is only association (shirk). Have you not heard what Luqman said to his son: ﴿Indeed, association is great injustice﴾ [Luqman: 13]?'"

Regarding who is meant by this verse, there are three opinions.

The first: it refers to Ibrahim and his companions, and it does not apply to this Ummah. This was said by Ali ibn Abi Talib. In another narration he said: this verse is specific to Ibrahim, and this Ummah has no share in it.

The second: it refers to whoever emigrated to Madinah. This was said by Ikrimah.

The third: it is general. This was mentioned by some of the exegetes. Is it part of Ibrahim's statement to his people, or a response from Allah, may He be exalted? On this there are two views.

(p-78) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that was Our argument﴾, meaning what passed between him and his people of the reasoning about the creation of the star, the moon and the sun, his criticism of them when they equated the small with the great and worshipped what does not speak, and his imposing the proof upon them. ﴿We bestowed it upon Abraham﴾: We guided him to it by inspiration.

Mujahid said: The argument is Abraham's saying, ﴿So which of the two groups has more right to security?﴾

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will.﴾ Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Ibn 'Amr recited "darajat man nasha'" (darajāt man nashāʾ) with an annexed construction. 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i (the recitations) recited "darajatin" with tanwin, and they recited likewise in "Yusuf" [Yusuf: 76]. Then there are two opinions regarding the meaning.

One of them: the raising is by knowledge, understanding and recognition. The second: by choosing him for the message.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed your Lord is All-Wise.﴾ Ibn Jarir said: He is All-Wise in governing His creation and in teaching His prophets the proof against their disbelieving nations, [He is] "All-Knowing" of what the affair of all will come to.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 84–87:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We gave him Isaac﴾, as a son of his loins, "and Jacob" as a son of Isaac, "each" of these mentioned, "We guided" – i.e., We directed.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And of his descendants﴾ – regarding the "pronoun of reference" (ha' al-kinayah) there are two opinions.

One of them: that it refers to Noah. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and it was chosen by al-Farra', Muqatil, and Ibn Jarir al-Tabari.

The second: that it refers to Abraham. This was said by 'Ata'. Al-Zajjaj said: Both opinions are permissible, because both of them have been mentioned. Ibn Jarir argued for the first opinion by saying that Allah, may He be exalted, mentioned Lot in the context of the verses, and Lot is not a descendant of Abraham. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi answered him by saying that it is possible that He meant: "And We gave him Lot" in support and assistance. Then His saying: ﴿And thus do We reward the good-doers﴾ is among the clearest evidence that it is Abraham, because the opening of the discourse is only with the mention of what Abraham was rewarded with. As for "Yusuf," it is a non-Arabic name. Al-Farra' said: "Yusuf," with a damma on the sin without a hamza, is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz; some of Banu Asad say "Yu'suf" with a hamza; some of the Arabs say "Yusif" with a kasra on the sin; and some of Banu 'Uqayl say "Yusaf" with a fatha on the sin.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And thus do We reward the good-doers﴾ – i.e., just as We rewarded Abraham for his monotheism and his steadfastness upon his religion, by raising his rank and granting him children who were prophets and pious, thus do We reward the good-doers. As for 'Isa, Ilyas, al-Yasa', and Lut, they are non-Arabic names. The majority of reciters read "al-Yasa'" with a single lam, lightened, among them Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Amir. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it here and in "Sad" as "al-Layasa'" with two lams and with shaddah. Al-Farra' said: It is more correct and more similar to the names of the prophets of the Children of Israel, and because the Arabs do not add the definite article "al-" to "yaf'alu" when it has the meaning of a proper name; they say: "Hadha Yasa'u qad ja'a," "Hadha Ya'muru," "Hadha Yazidu," and so the eloquent speech is like this.

Some of them recited to me:

"We found al-Walid ibn Yazid blessed, strong, with the bends of the caliphate on his shoulders."

When he mentioned "al-Walid" with the definite article, he followed it with "Yazid" with the definite article, and both are correct. Makki said: Whoever reads it with a single lam, the original form in his view is "Yasa'," and whoever reads it with two lams, the original form in his view is "Layasa'," then they added the article to it. The clarification of the rest of the names of the prophets has already preceded, and what is meant by "the worlds" is the people of their times.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And of their forefathers and their descendants and their brothers﴾ – "min" here is for partition. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: We guided these, and We guided some of their forefathers, descendants, and brothers. ﴿And We chose them﴾ is like "We selected them" and "We preferred them," and it is derived from "jabaytu al-shay'" when you purify it for yourself, and "jabaytu al-ma' fi al-hawd" when you gather water in the basin. As for ﴿the straight path﴾, it is monotheism.

He said, may Allah be exalted: ﴿That is the guidance of Allah; He guides whom He wills of His servants.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: "That" is the religion of Allah that they follow. ﴿He guides whom He wills of His servants.﴾

"Had they associated [others with Allah]" means the prophets mentioned. "Their deeds would have been nullified" means their deeds would have been invalidated and gone void, because the deed of a polytheist is not accepted.

(p-81) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are the ones to whom We gave the Book﴾, meaning the scriptures that He sent down to them.

And "al-hukm" means understanding (fiqh) and knowledge. ﴿But if they disbelieve in it﴾, meaning in Our signs.

Regarding those referred to by "these" (hā'ulā'), there are three opinions.

The first: they are the people of Makkah. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, and Qatadah.

The second: they are the Quraysh. This was said by al-Suddi. The third: they are the Ummah of the Prophet (ﷺ). This was said by al-Hasan.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We have entrusted it to a people﴾. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Then We have provided it for a people." Al-Zajjaj said: "We have entrusted the belief in it to a people." Regarding these people there are four opinions.

The first: they are the people of Madinah from the Ansar. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Musayyib, Qatadah, and al-Suddi.

The second: they are the prophets and the righteous. This was said by al-Hasan. Qatadah said: they are the eighteen prophets mentioned in this place, and this is the view preferred by al-Zajjaj and Ibn Jarir.

The third: they are the angels. This was said by Abu Raja'. The fourth: they are the Muhajirun and the Ansar.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 90:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided﴾ means the prophets mentioned.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So follow their guidance﴾, there are two opinions.

The first: follow their legislations and their sunan (ways), a view related from Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The second: follow them in their patience, a view stated by al-Zajjaj. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and 'Asim used to affirm the ha' in His saying "iqtadih" ( اقْتَدِهِ) as a sakin (silent vowel) when connected. Hamzah, Khalaf, Ya'qub, al-Kisa'i (from Abu Bakr), and al-Yazidi in his own choice, used to drop the ha' when connected. There is no disagreement about affirming it when pausing, and about its being sakin (vowelled with sukun) in pause.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: I do not ask you for any wage for it﴾ means for the Qur'an. And al-Dhikra (the reminder) means the admonition. And al-'Alamin (the worlds) here means the jinn and mankind.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 91:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾. Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are seven reports.

The first: "Malik ibn al-Sayf, the head of the Jews, came to the Messenger of God ﷺ one day, and the Messenger of God ﷺ said to him: 'I adjure you by He who sent down the Torah to Moses: do you find in it that God hates the fat rabbi?' He said: Yes. He said: 'You are the fat rabbi.' He became angry and said: ﴿God did not send down anything upon any human being﴾, and then this verse was revealed." This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. Likewise Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ikrimah said: it was revealed concerning Malik ibn al-Sayf.

The second: "The Jews said: O Muhammad, has God sent down a Book to you? He said: 'Yes.' They said: By God, God did not send down any Book from the heaven. Then this verse was revealed." This was related by al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: "The Jews said: O Muhammad, Moses brought tablets carrying them from God; bring us a sign as Moses brought. Then it was revealed: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a Book from the heaven﴾ up to His words: ﴿a great [injustice]﴾ [al-Nisa': 153-156]. When he informed them of their evil deeds, they said: By God, God did not send down anything upon you, nor upon Moses and Jesus, nor upon any human being. Then this verse was revealed." This was stated by Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

The fourth: it was revealed concerning the Jews and the Christians, to whom God gave knowledge, but they did not benefit from it. This was stated by Qatadah.

The fifth: it was revealed concerning Phinehas the Jew, who is the one who said: ﴿God did not send down anything upon any human being﴾. This was stated by al-Suddi.

The sixth: it was revealed concerning the polytheists of Quraysh, who said: By God, God did not send down anything upon any human being. This was related by Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid.

The seventh: its beginning, up to His words ﴿anything﴾, concerns the polytheists of Quraysh, and His words ﴿who sent down the Book that Moses brought﴾ concern the Jews. This was related by Ibn Kathir from Mujahid. Regarding the meaning of ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾ there are three views.

The first: they did not magnify God with His true magnificence. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Farra', Tha'lab and al-Zajjaj.

The second: they did not describe Him with His true description. This was said by Abu al-'Aliyah, and chosen by al-Khalil.

The third: they did not know Him with His true knowing. This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah.

(p-84) His words, exalted is He: (﴿yaj'alunahu qarativs﴾) its meaning is that they write it on sheets (qarativs). It is said that He said "qarativs" because they used to write it on separated sheets, so that it would not be gathered, and so that they could conceal from it whatever they wished.

His words, exalted is He: (﴿yubdunaha﴾). Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited "yaj'alunahu qarativs yubdunaha" and "yukhfuna" with the ya' in them. Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited with the ta' in them. As for whoever recited with the ya', it is because the people are absent (third person), as evidenced by His words ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾. As for whoever recited with the ta', it is in address; and the meaning is: you show from it what you like, and you conceal much, such as the description of Muhammad ﷺ and the verse of stoning, and similar things that they concealed.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And you were taught what you did not know, neither you nor your fathers﴾. Regarding who is addressed by this there are two views.

One: they are the Jews. This was said by the majority.

The second: it is an address to the Muslims. This was said by Mujahid. According to the first, they knew what is in the Torah; according to the second, they knew through the tongue of Muhammad ﷺ.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Say: God﴾. This is the answer to His words ﴿Who sent down the Book﴾, and its implied sense is: if they answer you, well; otherwise say: God sent it down.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then leave them﴾ is a threat. Their "plunging" is their falsehood. It was said: this is a command to turn away from them, then it was abrogated by the verse of the sword.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down﴾ means the Qur'an. Al-Zajjaj said: "blessed" (al-mubarak) is one from whom much good comes. The meaning is: We sent it down for blessing and warning.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 92:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that you may warn the Mother of the Cities﴾. ʿĀṣim (in the reading of Ḥafṣ excepted) recited "wa-liyundhira" with the yāʾ (ي), so that the Book (al-Kitāb) is the one who warns. The rest recited it with the tāʾ (ت), in the form of address to the Prophet ﷺ. As for Umm al-Qurā (the Mother of the Cities), it is Makkah. Al-Zajjāj said: the meaning is: that you may warn the people of Umm al-Qurā.

Regarding its being named Umm al-Qurā, there are four opinions.

The first: it was so named because the earth was spread out (duḥiya) from beneath it. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās.

The second: because it is the oldest of them (the cities), said by Ibn Qutaybah. The third: because it is the qiblah of all people, whom they face (yaʾummūnahā). The fourth: because it was the greatest of the cities in standing. Al-Zajjāj mentioned both of these.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and those around it﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: he means the whole earth.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who believe in the Hereafter believe in it﴾. Regarding the pronoun of reference (hāʾ al-kināyah) there are two views. The first: it refers to the Qur'an. The second: it refers to the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ. The meaning: whoever believes in the Hereafter believes in it; and whoever does not believe in it, his belief in the Hereafter is not genuine and is not counted. Do you not see His saying: ﴿and they are attentive to their prayers﴾? This indicates that He meant the believers who are attentive to the prayers.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 93:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah or says, "It has been revealed to me"﴾ — the scholars (mufassirun) differed concerning whom it was revealed, in three opinions.

One of them: that its beginning, up to His saying ﴿and nothing has been revealed to him﴾, was revealed concerning Musaylima al-Kadhdhab (the liar).

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or one who says, "I will reveal like what Allah has revealed"﴾ was revealed concerning "Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh. He had professed Islam and used to write for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at times. When it was dictated to him, "Mighty, Wise," he would write, "Forgiving, Merciful." He would say to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "This and that are the same." Then when ﴿And We certainly created man from an extract of clay﴾ was revealed, he dictated it to him, and when he reached His saying ﴿another creation﴾, 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'd was amazed and said: "So blessed is Allah, the best of creators" [al-Mu'minun: 12-14]. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "It was revealed to me thus, so write it." Then he doubted at that point and said: "If Muhammad is truthful, then it has been revealed to me as it was revealed to him, and if he is lying, then I have said as he said." This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. 'Ikrimah said: Then he returned to Islam before the conquest of Makkah.

The second opinion: that the whole verse was concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'd; this was said by al-Suddi.

The third: that it was revealed concerning Musaylima and al-Aswad al-'Ansi; this was said by Qatada. If it is said: How did He single out His saying ﴿or says, "It has been revealed to me"﴾ from His saying ﴿who invents﴾, when that one is also an inventor? There are two answers to this.

One of them: the two descriptions are for one man, describing him with one matter after another to show his audacity.

The second: He specified with His saying ﴿or says, "It has been revealed to me"﴾ after He had generalized with His saying ﴿invents a lie against Allah﴾, because not every inventor of lies against Allah claims that revelation came to him. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned both answers.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I will reveal like what Allah has revealed﴾ means: "I will say." Ibn 'Abbas said: they meant poetry, and they were the mocking ones. It was also said: it is the saying of 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh. Al-Zajjaj said: this is a reply to their saying, "If we willed, we would say the like of this."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you could see when the wrongdoers﴾ — there are three opinions concerning them.

One of them: they were people who had been Muslims in Makkah, whom the disbelievers took with them to fight at Badr. When they saw the small number of the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), they turned back from faith, and this was revealed concerning them. This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: they are those who said, "Allah has not revealed anything to a human being." This was said by Abu Sulayman.

The third: they are those described in this verse, namely the inventors and those who claim revelation came to them and who equal Allah's speech. Al-Zajjaj said: the answer to "law" (law) is omitted, and the meaning is: if you saw them in the agonies of death, you would see a great torment. It is said of anyone who is overwhelmed by a great matter: "that has overwhelmed so-and-so." Ibn 'Abbas said: the agonies of death (ghamarat al-mawt) are its pangs. Ibn al-Anbari said, the linguists said: they were named ghamarat because their terrors overwhelm whoever they befall.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the angels are extending their hands﴾ — there are three opinions concerning it.

One of them: with beating, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: with torment, said by al-Hasan and al-Dahhak. The third: extending them to seize the souls from the bodies, said by al-Farra'. Concerning the time when this occurs, there are three opinions.

One of them: at death. Ibn 'Abbas said: this is at death; the angels strike their faces and their backs, and the Angel of Death takes them.

The second: the Day of Resurrection; narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: in the Fire; said by al-Hasan.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Bring forth your souls﴾ — there is an implied "they will say" in it, and concerning its meaning there are two opinions.

One of them: submit to the bringing forth of your souls.

The second: bring forth your souls from the torment, if you are able.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You will be recompensed with the torment of humiliation (al-hawn)﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: al-Hawn with a damma is humiliation (al-hawan); and when they open its first letter, it means gentleness and ease. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: you will be recompensed with the torment in which severe humiliation settles.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 94:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾. The occasion of its revelation: al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said, "Al-Lat and al-Uzza will intercede for me." So this verse was revealed. This is related by Ikrimah. The meaning of "furada" (alone, individually) is "wuhdanan" (singly). This is a report from Allah, exalted is He, of that with which He will rebuke the polytheists on the Day of Resurrection. Abu 'Ubayda said: "furada" means fard fard (one by one). Ibn Qutayba said: "furada" is the plural of fard (single).

The exegetes have five sayings on the meaning of "furada," which are close in meaning.

The first: "furada" means free of family, wealth and children; this is related from Ibn Abbas. The second: each one on his own; this is related from al-Hasan. The third: nothing of the world is with you; this is related from Muqatil. The fourth: each one is separated from his partner in error and from his companion; this is related from al-Zajjaj. The fifth: "furada" means free of those worshipped; this is related from Ibn Kaysan.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿as We created you the first time﴾. Regarding this there are three sayings.

The first: no wealth, no family, no children. The second: barefoot, naked, uncircumcised (ghurl); "ghurl" means "qalf" (uncircumcised). The third: living beings. "Khawwalnakum" means "mallaknakum" (We gave you possession). ﴿Behind your backs﴾ means: (p-89) in the world. The meaning is that what you strove to acquire in the world has perished, and regret over the bad choice remains. Regarding "their intercessors" there are two sayings.

One: they are the idols. Ibn Abbas said: "your intercessors" means your gods whom you claimed would intercede for you. And "you claimed that they are among you" means partners with you. Ibn Qutayba said: "you claimed that they were partners to Me in your creation."

The second: they are the angels; they used to believe in their intercession. This is related by Muqatil.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Now your connections have been severed among you﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read it with a raised (ar-raf') "baynakum" (as a nominative). Al-Kisa'i and Hafs from 'Asim read it with a fatha on the nun, as an adverb of place (zarf). Al-Zajjaj said: the raf' is better, and its meaning is: "your connection has been severed." The nasb is permissible, and its meaning is: "what you had in partnership among you has been severed." Ibn al-Anbari said: the implied reading is: "what was between you has been severed," so "ma" was omitted because its meaning is clear. Abu 'Ali said: those who read it with raf' made it a noun, and attributed the verb "taqatta'a" to it; the meaning: "your connection has been severed." Those who read it with nasb supplied an agent noun within the verb, and the implied term is "the connection"; so the estimate is: "your connection has been severed among you." Regarding "that which they used to claim" there are two sayings.

One: the intercession of their gods. The second: the absence of resurrection and recompense.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 95:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the splitter of the grain and the date-stone﴾. Regarding the meaning of "falq" (splitting, cleaving) there are two views.

The first: it means "khalq" (creation), so the meaning is: the Creator of the grain and the date-stone. This was narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Dahhak and Muqatil also said it.

The second: "falq" means "shaqq" (splitting). Then, regarding the meaning of the statement, there are two views.

The first: that He split the grain from the ear of grain, and the date-stone from the date palm. This meaning was related by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Hasan, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd also said it.

The second: that it refers to the two halves that are in the grain and the date-stone. This was said by Mujahid and Abu Malik. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: "Habb" (grain) is that which has no stone, such as wheat and barley; and "nawa" (date-stone) is like the stone of the date.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He brings the living out of the dead, and brings the dead out of the living﴾. Its explanation has already preceded in [Al 'Imran].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then how are you turned away?﴾ That is: how are you turned away from the truth after this clear proof?

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 96:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Splitter of the daybreak﴾. Regarding the meaning of al-falaq (splitting) there are two opinions, which have already been mentioned. As for al-Isbah (the daybreak), al-Akhfash said it is a verbal noun (masdar) from asbaha, and al-Zajjaj said: al-Isbah and al-Subh (morning) are one and the same.

Regarding al-Isbah, the exegetes have three opinions.

The first: that it is the light of the sun by day and the light of the moon by night. Ibn Abi Talha related it from Ibn Abbas.

The second: that it is the brightening of dawn (al-fajr). This was said by Mujahid. Ibn Zayd said: the splitting of the daybreak from the night.

The third: that it is the light of day. This was said by al-Dahhak. Anas ibn Malik, al-Hasan, Abu Mijlaz, Ayyub and al-Jahdari recited it as "Faliq al-Asbah" with a fatha on the hamza. Abu Ubayd said: its meaning is the plural of subh (morning).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He made the night a repose﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu Amr and Ibn Amir read "jaail" with an alif (as the active participle). Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "wa-ja'ala" without an alif, with "al-layla" in the accusative. Abu Ali said: whoever reads "jaail" does so because of "faliq", since they observe harmony (al-mushakala). Whoever reads "ja'ala" does so because the form "fa'il" here carries the meaning of "fi'l" (verb/act), as evidenced by His saying: ﴿And the sun and the moon as a reckoning﴾. As for al-Sakan (repose), it is that to which you turn for rest; the meaning is that people rest in it with the rest of comfort. Regarding al-Husban (reckoning), there are two opinions.

One of them: that it is the calculation (al-hisab), said by the majority. Ibn Qutayba said: it is said, "Take from everything according to its husban," i.e., according to its calculation. Regarding the intended meaning of this calculation, there are three opinions. The first: that they both run until a term appointed for them, related by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas. The second: that they run in their stations according to calculation, and return to increase and decrease, said by al-Suddi. The third: that their running is the means of knowing the reckoning of months and years, said by Muqatil.

The second opinion: that the meaning of al-husban is the light, said by Qatada. Al-Mawardi said: it seems he took it from His saying: ﴿and He sends upon it a husban from the sky﴾, i.e., fire. Ibn Jarir said: this has nothing to do with that.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 97:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it is He who has made for you the stars﴾. "Made" (ja'ala) here means "created" (khalaqa). He bestowed favor upon them with the stars because those who traverse the deserts (al-qifa') and those who ride the seas only find their way at night toward their destinations by means of them.

One view: "a settled place" refers to the wombs, and "a place of deposit" refers to the loins. This is narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Ata', al-Dahhak, al-Nakha'i, Qatada, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd said the same.

The second: "a settled place" is the wombs, and "a place of deposit" is the grave. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud.

The third: "a settled place" is the earth, and "a place of deposit" is the loins. Ibn Jubayr narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: both "a settled place" and "a place of deposit" are the womb. Qabus narrated it from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fifth: "a settled place" is where one dwells, and "a place of deposit" is where one dies. Muqsim narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas.

The sixth: "a settled place" is in this world, and "a place of deposit" is in the grave.

The seventh: "a settled place" is in the grave, and "a place of deposit" is in this world. This is the reverse of the one before it, and it was reported from al-Hasan.

The eighth: "a settled place" is in this world, and "a place of deposit" is with God, Exalted is He. Mujahid said this.

The ninth: "a settled place" is in the loins, and "a place of deposit" is in the wombs. Ibn Bahr said this, and it is the reverse of the first view.

(p-93) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it is He who sends down water from the sky﴾ — meaning rain — ﴿and We bring forth by it﴾ — that is, by the rain — ﴿the growth of every thing﴾. There are two opinions regarding His saying ﴿the growth of every thing﴾.

One: it is the growth of every thing of fruits, because everything that grows, its growth is by water.

The second: it is the provision of every thing, its nourishment. Regarding His saying ﴿So We bring forth from it﴾ there are two opinions. One: from the water, that is, by it.

The second: from the vegetation. Al-Zajjaj said: "Khadir" means "akhdar" (green). It is said: "ikhdarra," so he is "akhdar" and "khadir," like "a'war" and "fa-huwa a'war" and "a'wir."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We bring forth from it﴾ — that is, from the green — ﴿grain piled up (mutarakiban)﴾, such as spikes of grain and barley.

Al-mutarakib is that of which some is upon others.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And from the palm trees, from their spathes, are clusters hanging low (qinwanun daniyah)﴾. Al-Khaffaf related from Abu 'Amr: "qinwanun" with a dammah on the qaf; Harun related from him with a fathah on it. Al-Farra' said: its meaning is: "And from the palm trees are those whose clusters are hanging low." The people of the Hijaz say "qinwani" with a kasrah on the qaf; Qays pronounce it with a dammah; and Dabbah and Tamim say "qinyani." Al-Mufaddal recited to me from them:

"So its tops became thick and its roots became strong, and it inclined with clusters of unripe dates, reddish."

(p-94) And they all come together and say "qinw" and "qunw," and they do not say "qiny" or "quny." And Kalb say: "wa-mala bi-qinyanin." The author said: The verse is by Imru' al-Qays; Abu Sa'id al-Sukkari related it as "wa-mala biqinwanin" with the qaf kasrah and the waw, so there are four dialects: qinwan, qunwan, qinyan, qunyan. "Athdat" means: became abundant; from it comes "sha'r athith" (thick hair). "Adat" means: became strong.

Ibn Qutaybah said: al-qinwan are the clusters of the palm tree; its singular is qinw, pluralized in the form of a dual; similarly, sinw and sinwan in the dual, and sinwan in the plural. Al-Zajjaj said: qinwan is the plural of qinw, and when you make it dual it is qinwani, with a kasrah on the nun.

"Daniyah" means: near to reach. He did not say "wa-minha qinwanun ba'idah" (and from them are distant clusters), because the context indicates that the distant, far-off ones were not far off; so mention of the near was sufficient in place of mention of the distant, as in His saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81]. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-qinwan al-daniyah are the short palm trees whose clusters stick to the ground.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And gardens of grapes﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is a coordination with His saying "green," and ﴿the olive and the pomegranate﴾ — the meaning being: "and We brought forth from it trees of olive and pomegranate." Abu Zayd related from al-Mufaddal: "jannatun" with a raf'.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿similar and dissimilar﴾ — regarding this there are three opinions.

One: similar in appearance and dissimilar in taste; narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: similar in its leaves, differing in its fruit; said by Qatadah, and it is in the meaning of the first.

The third: some of it resembles other parts, and some of it differs. Al-Zajjaj said: Allah paired the olive with the pomegranate only because they are two trees which the Arabs know have leaves that cover the branch from its beginning to its end. The poet said: (p-95)

"Blessed is the strange dead, as blessing is upon the sprinkling of pomegranate and olive."

Its meaning: the blessing in its leaves is that they cover the whole of its stem.

His saying, Exalted is He: (Look at its fruit when it bears fruit). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim recited: "unzuru ila thamarihi," "wa-kulu min thamarihi" [al-An'am: 141], and "liya'kulu min thamarihi" [Ya-Sin: 35], with a fathah in these. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf recited them with a dammah in all of these. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said thamarah, thamar, thimar, and thumur; whoever recites "ila thamarihi" with a dammah intends the plural of the plural. Abu 'Ali said: it has two possibilities: one is this, that thamar is the plural of thimar; the second is that thamar is the plural of thamarah, as in akamah and ukum, and khashabah and khushub. Al-Farra' said: it means: look at it when it first sets fruit, and look at its yan', which is its ripening and maturity. The people of the Hijaz say yanaa with a fathah on the ya', and some of the people of Najd pronounce it with a dammah. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is said yana'at al-thamarah and ayna'at, when it ripens, and it is al-yun' and al-yan'. Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-A'mash and Ibn Muhaysin recited "wa-yan'ihi" with a dammah on the ya'. Al-Zajjaj said: al-yan' is ripeness. The poet said:

"In domes around a monastery, around which the olives have ripened."

And Allah, Exalted, made clear to them, through the transformation of what He created and His moving it from one state to another, which creation cannot do, that He will in the same way raise them.

(p-96) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: those who affirm that He who brought forth this vegetation is able to give life to the dead. Muqatil said: those who affirm monotheism.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 100:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they made the jinn partners with Allah﴾. "Jaʿalū" (they made) here means "waṣafū" (they attributed/described). Al-Zajjaj said: "al-Jinn" is in the accusative case for two reasons.

The first: that it is an object (maf'ul), so the meaning is: "and they made the jinn partners for Allah," and "al-jinn" is the second object, like His saying: ﴿And they made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 19].

The second: that "al-jinn" is an apposition (badal) for "shuraka'" (partners), explaining the partners. Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu ʿImran, Abu Haywah, and al-Jahdari read "shuraka'a al-jinnu" with a nominative "n" (al-jinnu). Ibn Abi ʿAblah and Muʿadh al-Qari read "al-jinni" with a genitive "n" (al-jinni).

As for the meaning of "the jinn made them partners," there are three opinions.

The first: that they obeyed the devils in worshipping idols, so they made them partners with Allah. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj.

The second: they said the angels are the daughters of Allah, so they are His partners, like His saying: ﴿And they made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ [al-Saffat: 158]. He called the angels "jinn" because they are hidden (ijtinan). This was said by Qatadah, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd.

The third: the heretics (zanadiqah) said: Allah created light, water, beasts and livestock, and Iblis created darkness, predators, snakes and scorpions. This verse was revealed concerning them. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He created them﴾. Regarding the pronoun there are two opinions.

The first: it refers to those who make partners for Him, so the meaning is: "they made partners for the One who created them, who create nothing."

The second: it refers to the jinn, so the meaning is: "Allah created the jinn, so how can a partner of Allah be created?" Al-Zajjaj mentioned both.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they invented for Him sons and daughters﴾. Nafi' read "wa kharraqu" with shaddah, for emphasis and intensification, because the polytheists claimed the angels were the daughters of Allah, the Christians claimed the Messiah, and the Jews claimed ʿUzayr. Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Raja', and Abu al-Jawza' read "wa harrafu" with an unpointed ḥāʾ, a doubled rāʾ, and a fāʾ. Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ and al-Jahdari read "kharaqu" with an alif and a pointed khāʾ. Al-Suddi said: As for "sons," it is the saying of the Jews: "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah," and the saying of the Christians: "the Messiah is the son of Allah"; and as for "daughters," it is the saying of the Arab polytheists: "the angels are the daughters of Allah." Al-Farra' said: kharaqu, ikhtaraqu, khalaqu, and ikhtalaqu all mean iftaraw (fabricated). Abu ʿUbaydah said: kharaqu means "jaʿalu" (made/invented). Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of "without knowledge" is that they did not mention it from knowledge; they mentioned it only as falsehood.

"His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿How can He have a child when He has no companion?﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: That is, from where could He have a child, when a child can only come from a consort?! He argued against them concerning the negation of a child by His saying: ﴿And He created all things﴾. So the Creator of things is not like anything created, so how could a child belong to one who has no like? If a child is attributed to Him, then a likeness has been made for Him."

"His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿How can He have a child when He has no companion?﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: That is, from where could He have a child, when a child can only come from a consort?! He argued against them concerning the negation of a child by His saying: ﴿And He created all things﴾. So the Creator of things is not like anything created, so how could a child belong to one who has no like? If a child is attributed to Him, then a likeness has been made for Him."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 103:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾. Regarding the word *idrak* (perceiving), there are two views.

The first is that it means encompassing (*al-ihatah*). The second is that it means seeing (*al-ru'yah*). Regarding "the visions" (*al-absar*), there are two views. The first is that it means the eyes, which is the view of the majority (*al-jumhur*). The second is that it means the intellects, as narrated by 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi from Abu Husayn al-Qari'. So there are three views on the meaning of the verse.

The first: no visions encompass Him. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and 'Ata' also said it. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of the verse is encompassing His reality, and it does not negate seeing, because what is authentically related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning seeing [Allah] is established. This is the position of the People of the Sunnah (*Ahl al-Sunnah*), of the scholars of knowledge, and of the people of hadith.

The second: no visions perceive Him when He manifests Himself with His light, which is His light. This was narrated by 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: no visions perceive Him in this world. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Hasan and Muqatil also said it. What indicates that the verse is restricted to this world is His saying: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant, looking at their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22–23] (p-99). He restricted looking at Him to the Day of Resurrection and left it unrestricted in this verse, and the unrestricted is interpreted in light of the restricted.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He perceives the visions﴾, the two views apply to it as well. Al-Zajjaj said: in this information there is evidence that His creation do not perceive the visions, meaning they do not know the reality of sight, or what it is that enables a person to see through his two eyes and not through other limbs. Allah has informed that none of His creation can perceive the reality of His essence or encompass His knowledge, so how then can He, Mighty and Majestic, be perceived?

As for "the Subtle" (*al-Latif*), Abu Sulayman al-Khattabi said: He is the Benevolent toward His servants, who is gentle with them from where they do not know, and who arranges their interests for them from where they do not expect. Ibn al-A'rabi said: *al-Latif* is the One who brings you your need gently; from this is their saying, "Allah was gentle with you" (*lataf Allah bika*). It is also said: He is the One who is too subtle to be perceived by way of modality (*al-kayfiyyah*). Subtlety may also mean fineness and obscurity, and it may mean smallness in the description of bodies, and that is not suitable to the attributes of the Creator, glorified is He. Al-Azhari said: *al-Latif* is one of Allah's names, its meaning being: the Gentle toward His servants. As for *al-Khabir*, it means the One who knows the reality of a thing and is acquainted with its true nature.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 104:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Clear proofs (basa'ir) have certainly come to you from your Lord.﴾ Al-basa'ir is the plural of basira, which is the indication that brings about sight (insight) into a thing and knowledge of it. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: the Qur'an has certainly come to you, in which there is clarification and clear proofs. ﴿So whoever sees [clearly], it is for his own benefit;﴾ the benefit of that returns to him. ﴿And whoever is blind, it is to his own harm;﴾ the harm of that falls upon him, because God, Mighty and Majestic, is free of need from His creation. ﴿And I am not a guardian over you.﴾ That is: I do not take you to faith in the manner of a guardian or a trustee, and this was before the command to fight.(p-100)

Section

The exegetes mentioned that this verse was abrogated (naskh) by the verse of the sword. Some of them said: its meaning is: I am not a watcher over you who counts your deeds; according to this, there is no basis for abrogation.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 105:

His saying, Most High: ﴿And thus We variously explain the verses﴾. Al-Akhfash said: "Thus" (wa-kadhalika) means "in this manner" (wa-hakadha). Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: "Just as We have made clear what is recited to you, We make the verses clear." Ibn Abbas said: "We variously explain the verses," that is, We make them clear in every way: We call them to faith with them once, and We warn them with them another time. ﴿And that they may say﴾, meaning the people of Makkah, when the Qur'an is recited to them: "You have studied (darasta)."

Ibn al-Anbari said: The meaning of the verse is: "And thus We variously explain the verses, so that We may establish the proof against them, and that they may say, 'You have studied.'" He varied the verses so that one people would be made happy by understanding them and acting upon them, while others would be made wretched by turning away from them. Whoever acts upon them is made happy, and whoever says "You have studied" is made wretched. Al-Zajjaj said: This lam in "li-yaqulu" is called by the grammarians lam al-sayrura (the lam of outcome). The meaning is that the cause which led them to say "You have studied" is the recitation of the verses. This is like His saying: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a sorrow﴾ [al-Qasas 28:8]. They did not take him up with the aim that he would become their enemy, but the outcome of the matter was that he became for them an enemy and a sorrow. Similarly, you might say: "So-and-so wrote the book for his own destruction," where he did not intend to ruin himself by the book, but the outcome was destruction.

As for "darasta" (you have studied): Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read "darasat" with an alif, a sukun on the sin and a fatha on the ta'; its meaning is: you discussed with the People of the Book. Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "darasta" (ﷺ-less, with no alif), with a sukun on the sin and a fatha on the ta', meaning: you read the books of the People of the Book. The commentators said: its meaning is: you learned from Jabr and Yasar. We will explain this in His saying: ﴿Only a human being teaches him﴾ [al-Nahl 16:103], if God wills. Ibn Amir and Ya'qub read "darasta" with a fatha on the ra' and the sin and a sukun on the ta', with no alif. The meaning: these reports which you recite to us are ancient, and have been effaced (duris), that is, they have passed away and been obliterated. All of those we have mentioned put a fatha on the dal in their reading. It is narrated from Nafi' that he said: "durista" with a damma on the dal, a kasra on the ra' and a light ta', and this is the reading of Ibn Ya'mur; its meaning: it was recited. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "darusat" with a fatha on the dal and the sin, a damma on the ra' and a sukun on the ta'. Al-Zajjaj said: it has the same meaning as "darasat," that is, it was effaced; except that the one with the damma on the ra' is more intensive. Mu'adh al-Qari, Abu al-Aliyah and Mu'awwiq read "durrista" with a damma on the dal, a kasra on the ra' and a shadda on it, with the sin sakin. Ibn Mas'ud and Talhah ibn Musarrif read "darasa" with a fatha on the ra' and the sin, without an alif or a ta'. Ismah narrated from al-A'mash: "darasa" with an alif.

His saying, Most High: ﴿And that We may make it clear﴾, meaning the variation, ﴿to a people who know﴾, that is, those who, when the truth became clear to them, accepted it.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And turn away from the polytheists.﴾ The exegetes said: it was abrogated by the verse of the sword.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Had Allah willed, they would not have associated others with Him.﴾ Regarding this there are three opinions, related by al-Zajjaj.

(p-102) The first: Had He willed, He would have made them believers. The second: Had He willed, He would have sent down a sign that compels them to faith. The third: Had He willed, He would have uprooted them entirely, cutting off the cause of their polytheism. Ibn Abbas said: the rest of the verse was abrogated by the verse of the sword.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And turn away from the polytheists.﴾ The exegetes said: it was abrogated by the verse of the sword.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Had Allah willed, they would not have associated others with Him.﴾ Regarding this there are three opinions, related by al-Zajjaj.

(p-102) The first: Had He willed, He would have made them believers. The second: Had He willed, He would have sent down a sign that compels them to faith. The third: Had He willed, He would have uprooted them entirely, cutting off the cause of their polytheism. Ibn Abbas said: the rest of the verse was abrogated by the verse of the sword.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 108:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not revile those who call upon other than Allah﴾. Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are two views.

The first: when He said to the polytheists, ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship other than Allah are fuel for Hell﴾, they said: "O Muhammad, you will either stop reviling our gods and disparaging them, or we will certainly revile your God whom you worship." So this verse was revealed. Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn Abbas.

The second: the Muslims used to revile the idols of the disbelievers, and the disbelievers would retaliate in kind. So Allah, exalted is He, forbade them to revile, in return, the Lord of the believers before a people who were ignorant and had no knowledge of Allah. This was said by Qatadah. The meaning of "call upon" (yad'una) is "worship" (ya'budun), and they are the idols. ﴿Lest they revile Allah﴾, i.e., lest they revile, out of enmity, the One you command them to worship, so that this reverts to Allah, exalted is He. It does not mean that they openly reviled Allah, exalted is He, because they acknowledged that He is their Creator, even though they associated others with Him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Out of enmity, without knowledge﴾, i.e., wrongfully, out of ignorance. Ya'qub recited (p-103) "ʿaduwwan" with a damma on the ʿayn and the dal and a shaddah on the waw. The Arabs say, regarding wrongdoing: ʿada Fulan ʿadwan, ʿudwan, and ʿudwanan. And ʿada means: he wronged.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus We have made attractive to every community their deeds﴾, i.e., just as We made the worship of idols and obedience to Satan attractive to these polytheists, so We make attractive to every group that has united upon truth or falsehood its deeds, whether good or evil. The commentators said: this verse was abrogated by the implied address in the verse of the sword.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 109:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they swore by Allah with their most solemn oaths﴾. Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are two accounts.

The first: When the verse ﴿If We willed, We would send down upon them a sign from the heaven﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 4] was revealed, the polytheists said: "Let Him send it down upon us, and by Allah we will believe in it." The Muslims said: "O Messenger of Allah, He would send it down upon them so that they may believe." So this verse was revealed. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: "The Quraysh said: 'O Muhammad, you tell us that Musa had a staff with which he struck the rock, and twelve springs gushed forth from it, and that 'Isa used to revive the dead, and that Thamud had a she-camel. So bring us signs like these, so that we may believe you.' He said: 'What is it that you wish?' They said: 'That you make Safa into gold for us.' He said: 'If I do so, will you believe me?' They said: 'Yes, by Allah, if you do it we will follow you all.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood up and supplicated, and Jibril came to him and said: 'If you wish, Safa will become gold, but I do not send a sign which they then do not believe in, except that the punishment is sent down. Or if you wish, leave them until their repentant one repents.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'I will leave them until their repentant one repents.' So this verse was revealed up to His saying: '...they are ignorant.'" This is the view of Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi.

We have already mentioned the meaning of ﴿jahda aymanihim﴾ in [al-Ma'idah]. They swore concerning the signs they had proposed, like their saying: ﴿We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth﴾ [al-Isra' 90].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Indeed the signs are with Allah﴾, meaning: He is the One able to bring them, not I, nor anyone of His creation. ﴿And what will make you aware that they [will not believe]﴾, meaning: what will inform you that they [will believe]? Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, and Khalaf in his choice read it with a kasra on the alif (ʾinnaha, "innahā" with kasra). According to this reading, the address in ﴿yush'irukum﴾ is to the polytheists, and the sentence is complete at ﴿wa-ma yush'irukum﴾, and the meaning is: What will make you aware that you will believe when it comes? And "innaha" is kasra as a resumption and an informing about their state. Abu 'Ali said: the estimate is: "wa-ma yush'irukum iman-hum?" (What will make you aware of their faith?), so the object was omitted. The meaning is: even if the sign they proposed came, they would not believe. According to this, the address is to the believers. Sibawayh said: I asked al-Khalil about His saying ﴿And what will make you aware that they [will not believe]﴾, and I said: what prevents it from being like your saying: "What will make you aware that He does not act?" He said: that is not well-used in this place; He only said ﴿And what will make you aware﴾, then He began and affirmed, saying ﴿that when they come they will not believe﴾. Had He said: ﴿And what will make you aware that when they come they will not believe?﴾, that would have been an excuse for them. Nafi', Hafs from 'Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "annaha" with a fatha on the alif. According to this, the one addressed by ﴿wa-ma yush'irukum﴾ is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions. Then there are two views regarding the meaning of the speech.

The first: "And what will make you aware? Perhaps when they come they will not believe." In the reading of Ubayy: "Perhaps when they come they will not believe" (la'allaha idha ja'at la yu'minun). The Arabs use "an" with the meaning of "la'alla" (perhaps). They say: "Go to the market, that you may buy something for us," meaning: perhaps you will buy.

'Adi ibn Zayd said:

"O blamer, what will make you aware that my death is at an hour in the day, or at the forenoon of tomorrow?"

Meaning: perhaps my death. Al-Khalil, Sibawayh, and al-Farra' in explaining this reading adopted this meaning.

The second: the meaning is: "And what will make you aware that when they come they will believe?" and "la" is then extra (silah), as in His saying: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?﴾ [al-A'raf 12], and His saying: ﴿And it is forbidden for a town which We destroyed that they will not return﴾ [al-Anbiya' 95]. This was mentioned by al-Farra' and rejected by al-Zajjaj, who chose the first view. Most readers read "yu'minun" with the ya': among them Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim. Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah read with the ta', as address to the polytheists. Abu 'Ali said: whoever reads with the ya', it is because those who swore are absent (third person); whoever reads with the ta', it is a turning from absence to address.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 110:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We will turn their hearts and their sight away﴾. At-taqlib (turning over) is turning a thing away from its direction. Regarding the meaning of the statement, there are four opinions.

The first: If We had brought them a sign as they asked, We would have turned their hearts and their sight away from believing in it, and We would have placed a barrier between them and guidance, so they would not believe, just as they did not believe in what they had seen before it, as a punishment for them for that. This meaning was held by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Ibn Zayd.

The second: that it is a reply to their request, in the Hereafter, to return to the world. The meaning is: If they were returned, We would place a barrier between them and guidance just as We placed a barrier between them and it the first time, when they were in the world. This meaning was narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: "And We turn their hearts and their sight away from believing in the signs, just as their predecessors from the earlier nations did not believe in the signs they saw." This was said by Muqatil.

The fourth: that this turning in the Fire is a punishment for them. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. Regarding the pronoun in "bihi" (in it/by it), there are four opinions: the first is that it refers to the Qur'an; the second, to the Prophet ﷺ; the third, to the signs that appeared; and the fourth, to the turning. Regarding what is meant by "the first time" (awwala marrah), there are three opinions. The first is that the first time is the abode of the world. The second is that it refers to the miracles of the prophets before Muhammad, peace and blessings of Allah be upon them. The third is that it refers to the turning of their hearts away from belief before the signs were sent down, even if they had been sent down; and transgression (tughyan) and bewilderment (ʿamah) are mentioned in [Surat al-Baqarah].

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 6, verse 111:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels﴾. The occasion of its revelation: "The mockers came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with a group of the people of Makkah and said to him: 'Raise for us some of our dead so that we may ask them whether what you say is true or false. Or show us the angels bearing witness for you that you are the Messenger of Allah. Or bring us Allah and the angels as a tribe (qabilan).' Then this verse was revealed." Narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

The meaning of the verse: "Even if We had sent down to them the angels as they asked, and the dead had spoken to them and borne witness to your prophethood, and We had gathered (wa-hasharna) against them, that is, assembled, ﴿every thing before them face to face (qubulan)﴾ in this world, ﴿they would not have believed unless Allah willed﴾." He informs that the occurrence of faith depends on His will, not as they supposed, that they could believe whenever they wished and refrain whenever they wished.

As for His saying qubulan: Ibn Amir and Nafi' read it with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the ba' (قِبَلًا). Ibn Qutayba said: its meaning is "direct witnessing" (mu'ayanah). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it "qubulan" (قُبُلًا) with a damma on the qaf and the ba'. Regarding its meaning there are three opinions.

The first: it is the plural of qabil (قَبِيل), meaning "kind" or "category" (al-sinf). The meaning then is: "And We gathered against them every thing, kind by kind." This was said by Mujahid, and it was preferred by Abu 'Ubayda and Ibn Qutayba.

The second: it is also the plural of qabil, but with the meaning of "surety" (al-kafil). The meaning then is: "And We gathered against them every thing, and it vouched for the truth of what you say." This was preferred by al-Farra', and an objection is raised against it: it may be said that if they did not believe when the angels were sent down and the dead spoke, then they would be even less likely to believe through a surety, which is merely a statement. The answer: if the gathered things stood surety and spoke what they had not spoken, that would be a clear sign.

The third: it means "opposite" (al-muqabil), so the meaning is: "And We gathered against them every thing, and it confronted them." This was said by Ibn Zayd. Abu Zayd said: it is said, "I met so-and-so qabalan, qiblan, qubulan, qabilan, qabaliyyan, and muqabalah," and all of these are one, meaning "face to face." Abu 'Ali said: the meaning in the Qur'an, according to what Abu Zayd said, is one, even though the wordings differ.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But most of them are ignorant﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions.

One: they are ignorant that things do not come about except by the will of Allah, may He be exalted.

The second: they are ignorant that, even if every sign were given to them, they would not believe.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 112:

(p. 108) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy﴾. That is: just as We appointed for you and your community enemies from the devils of mankind and the jinn, so We appointed for those before you among the prophets and their peoples. The meaning is: just as We tested you with enemies, those before you were tested, so that the reward for patience in the face of harm might be greater. Al-Zajjaj (a grammarian and Qur'an scholar) said: "ʿAduwwan" (an enemy), in the sense of "aʿdāʾ" (enemies), and "shayāṭīna al-insi wa al-jinn" (the devils of mankind and the jinn) is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for "ʿaduwwan" and an explanation of it. It is also permissible for "ʿaduwwan" to be in the accusative as a second object (mafʿūl thānī), meaning: and thus We appointed the devils of mankind and the jinn as enemies to their peoples. Regarding "shayāṭīna al-insi wa al-jinn" there are three opinions.

The first: they are the rebellious ones (maradah) among mankind and the jinn. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatada. The second: the devils of mankind are those who are with mankind, and the devils of the jinn are those who are with the jinn. This was said by Ikrima and al-Suddi. The third: the devils of mankind and the jinn are their disbelievers. This was said by Mujahid.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿yūḥī﴾ (they inspire). The original meaning of wahy (inspiration) is informing and indicating in a concealed and hidden manner.

Regarding what is meant by it here, there are three opinions.

The first: its meaning is "yaʾmuru" (commands). The second: "yuwaswisu" (whispers). The third: "yushīru" (signals).

As for ﴿zukhruf al-qawl﴾ (ornamented speech), it is what is adorned from it, made attractive, and embellished with falsehood. The root of zukhruf is gold. Abu ʿUbayda said: every thing that you make attractive and adorn while it is false is zukhruf. Al-Zajjaj said: "al-zukhruf" in the language means adornment. So the meaning is that some of them adorn certain evil deeds for others. "Ghurūran" (as deception) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and this verbal noun is understood according to the sense, because the sense of "īḥāʾ al-zukhruf min al-qawl" (inspiring ornamented speech) is the sense of deception, so it is as if he said: they deceive with deception. Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿zukhruf al-qawl ghurūran﴾ means wishful thinking in falsehood. Muqatil said: every Iblis (satan) has among mankind devils who lead them astray.
