So when a devil of mankind meets a devil of the jinn, one of them says to his companion: "I have led my companion astray with such and such, so lead your companion astray with such and such." That is the inspiring of some of them to others. Someone else said: when a believer wearies his devil, he goes to a rebellious one among mankind, who is a devil of mankind, and incites him against the believer so that he may tempt him. Qatada said: among the jinn there are devils, and among mankind there are devils. Malik ibn Dinar said: the devil of mankind is more severe against me than the devil of the jinn, because when I seek refuge from that one it departs from me, whereas this one drags me into sins openly.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had your Lord willed, they would not have done it﴾. Regarding the pronoun (hāʾ al-kināya) in it, there are three opinions.

The first: it refers to the whispering. The second: it refers to disbelief. The third: it refers to the deception and the harm done to the prophets.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So leave them and what they fabricate﴾. Muqatil said: he means the disbelievers of Makkah, and what they fabricate of lies. Others said: leave the polytheists and what they dispute with you by, of what their allies inspire to them, and what they invent of falsehood. This portion of this verse is abrogated (mansūkh) by the verse of the sword (āyat al-sayf).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 113:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline toward it﴾. That is: "and that they may incline." The pronoun (ha') refers to the ornate deception (al-zukhruf) and delusion (al-ghurur). Al-af'idah is the plural of fu'ad (heart), like ghurab (crow) and aghribah (crows). Ibn al-Anbari said: We did that to them so that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter would incline toward falsehood, and that they would be pleased with falsehood. ﴿And that they may commit what they commit﴾: that is, that they may earn (layaktasibu), and that they may know what they are doing (wa liya'lamu ma hum 'amiluna).

(p-110) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Shall I seek a judge other than Allah?﴾ The occasion of its revelation: "The polytheists of Quraysh said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'Appoint between us and you a judge, whether from among the rabbis (aḥbār) of the Jews, if you wish, or from among the rabbis of the Christians, and they will inform us about you from what is in their scripture regarding your affair.' So this verse was revealed." Al-Mawardi mentioned it. As for "al-ḥukm" (judge), it has the meaning of "al-ḥākim" (the one who judges). The meaning is: "Shall I seek a judge other than Allah to rule between me and you?!" And "the Book" is the Qur'an, and "al-mufaṣṣal" (the clearly explained) is the one made clear, in which the truth is distinguished from falsehood, the command from the prohibition, and the lawful from the unlawful.

﴿And those to whom We have given the Book﴾ concerning them there are two opinions.

One: they are the scholars of the two People of the Book; this is the view of the majority. The second: they are the leaders of the companions of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, such as Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthman, ʿAli, and their likes; this is the view of ʿAṭāʾ.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿they know that it is sent down﴾. Ibn ʿĀmir and Ḥafs, on the authority of ʿĀṣim, recited "munazzal" with the doubled letter (tashdīd); the rest recited it with the single letter (takhfīf).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 115:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled⦆. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and Nafi' read "kalimat" (words) in the plural. 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read "kalimah" (word) in the singular. The Arabs have used the singular "kalimah" while intending abundance. They say: "Qass said in his kalimah," meaning in his sermon (khutbah), and "Zuhayr in his kalimah," meaning in his qasidah (ode).

(p-111) Regarding what is meant by these words, there are three opinions.

The first is that they are the Qur'an; this is the view of Qatadah. The second is that they are His decrees and His promises. The third is that they are His promise and His threat, and His reward and His punishment. Regarding His saying, ﴿in truth and justice⦆, there are two opinions.

One is: truthful in what He informs, and just in what He decrees and determines. The second is: truthful in what He promises and threatens, and just in what He commands and forbids. Regarding His saying, ﴿None can alter His words⦆, there are two opinions. One is: the fabricators cannot add to them or subtract from them.

The second is: there is no breaking of His promises, and no changing of His judgment.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 116:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you obey most of those on earth﴾. The occasion of its revelation: the disbelievers said to the Muslims, "Do you eat what you have slaughtered, and not eat what your Lord has slaughtered?" So this verse was revealed. Al-Farra' mentioned it. By ﴿most of those on earth﴾ is meant the disbelievers. Regarding what they would have you obey them in, there are four opinions.

The first: in eating carrion (al-maytah). The second: in eating what they slaughtered for idols (al-asnam). The third: in worshipping idols (al-awthan). The fourth: in following the creeds of the forefathers (milal al-aba'). And ﴿the way of Allah﴾: His religion. Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning of yakhrusun is that they guess and conjecture; and from this the one who estimates (the fruit crop) is called kharis. If it is said: how is it permissible to punish one who is upon an assumption regarding his polytheism, and not upon certainty regarding his disbelief? The answer: when they abandoned the seeking of proof, followed their desires, and confined themselves to conjecture and ignorance, they were punished. Al-Zajjaj mentioned it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 117:

(p-112) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The position of "man" (مَن) is in the nominative by being the subject of a nominal sentence (al-ibtida'), while its wording is that of an interrogative (al-istifham). The meaning is: Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of which of the people strays from His way. Al-Hasan recited "man yudillu" with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the ḍād (i.e., yuḍillu, "He causes to stray"), and this is the transmission of Ibn Abi Shurayh. Abu Sulayman said: The purpose of the verse is: do not turn your attention to the oath of one who swears that he will believe when the signs come; none will believe except those for whom the decree of faith has preceded.

Allah's saying: ﴿So eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned﴾. The occasion of its revelation: when Allah the Exalted prohibited carrion (al-maytah), the polytheists said to the believers: "You claim that you worship Allah. Then what Allah has killed (i.e., carrion) is more deserving that you eat it than what you have killed yourselves." They meant carrion. So this verse was revealed. Narrated by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 119:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not eat [of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned]?﴾ Al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH, a grammarian and Qur'an scholar) said: The meaning is: "And what befalls you in not eating?" The position of *an* (أنْ, "that") is in the accusative, because *fi* (فِي, "in") was dropped, so the meaning reached *an* and it took the accusative case.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And He has already detailed for you﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr and Ibn Amir recited *faṣṣala lakum mā ḥarrama ʿalaykum* (فَصَّلَ لَكم ما حَرَّمَ عَلَيْكُمْ) with both verbs in the nominative (marfūʿatān). Nafi', Hafs on the authority of Asim, Ya'qub, and al-Qazzaz on the authority of Abd al-Warith recited *faṣṣala* (فَصَّلَ) with a fatḥah on the fā', and *mā ḥarrama* (ما حَرَّمَ) with a fatḥah on the ḥā'. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr on the authority of Asim recited *faṣṣala* (فَصَّلَ) with a fatḥah on the fā', and *mā ḥarrama* (ما حَرَّمَ) with a ḍammah on the ḥā'. (These are the qira'at, the canonical recitation variants.)

Al-Zajjaj said: That is, He has detailed for you the lawful from the unlawful, and has permitted for you in cases of necessity what He had forbidden.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: He has detailed for you what He forbade to you, meaning what was explained in [Surat al-Ma'idah] concerning carrion, blood, and so on until the end of the verse.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And indeed, many [people] lead [others] astray by their desires without knowledge﴾. This means the polytheists of the Arabs, who went astray regarding the slaughtering of animals and other matters.

Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr recited *liyaḍillūna* (لَيَضِلُّونَ) with a fatḥah on the yā'... [as written in the source: "لَيَضِلُّونِ"]. In [Yunus: 88], ﴿Our Lord, that they may lead [others] astray﴾ (لِيُضِلُّوا), in [Ibrahim: 30], ﴿rivals [to Allah] in order to lead [others] astray﴾ (لِيُضِلُّوا), in [al-Hajj: 9], ﴿turning his side [in arrogance], to lead [others] astray﴾ (لِيُضِلَّ), in [Luqman: 6], ﴿to lead [others] astray from the way of Allah without knowledge﴾ (لِيُضِلَّ), and in [al-Zumar: 8], ﴿rivals [to Allah] in order to lead [others] astray﴾ (لِيُضِلَّ), with a fatḥah on the yā' in these six places. Asim, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i recited them with a ḍammah.

Nafi' and Ibn Amir recited *liyuḍillūna bi-ahwā'ihim* (لَيُضِلُّونَ بِأهْوائِهِمْ). In [Yunus], *liyaḍillū* (لَيَضِلُّوا) is with a fatḥah, and the remaining four places were recited with a ḍammah.

Whoever recited with a fatḥah intended that they themselves are the ones who went astray. Whoever recited with a ḍammah intended that they led others astray, and this is more emphatic in misguidance, because every one who misleads is astray, but not every one who is astray misleads.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 120:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And leave the outward and the inward of sin﴾. Regarding "sin" (al-ithm) here there are three opinions.

The first: it is fornication (al-zina). This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. On this view, there are two opinions regarding "its outward and its inward." One of them: its outward is openly committing it, and its inward is doing it secretly. This was said by al-Dahhak and al-Suddi. Al-Dahhak said: They used to regard fornication done in secret as permissible. The second: its outward is marrying the forbidden women, such as mothers, daughters, and what fathers have married, and its inward is fornication. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second: it is general, covering every sin. The meaning is: leave sins, both their secret and their public forms. This is the view of Abu al-Aliyah, Mujahid, Qatadah, and al-Zajjaj. Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning is, leave sin from all its aspects.

The third: sin means disobedience, but what is intended here is a specific matter. Ibn Zayd said: its outward here is the removal of their garments, since they used to circumambulate the House naked, and its inward is fornication.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 121:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned﴾. The occasion of its revelation: the disputing of the polytheists with the believers in their saying: "Do you eat what you have killed yourselves, and not eat what Allah has killed?" This is according to what we mentioned regarding the occasion of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned﴾ [al-An'am: 118]. This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas. ʿIkrimah said: Persia wrote to Quraysh: "Muhammad and his companions do not eat what Allah has slaughtered, but they eat what they have slaughtered for themselves." So the polytheists wrote to the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) about this, and something of that occurred in the hearts of some of the Muslims, so this verse was revealed. (p-115) Regarding the meaning of "that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned," there are four opinions.

The first: that it refers to carrion (maytah). This was narrated by Ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that it refers to carrion and the strangled animal, up to His saying: "and what is slaughtered on the stone altars" [al-Ma'idah: 3]. This was reported from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: that it refers to slaughtered animals which the Arabs used to slaughter for their idols. This was said by ʿAta'.

The fourth: that it is general, covering whatever Allah's name was not mentioned over at the time of slaughter. This meaning was adopted by ʿAbd Allah ibn Yazid al-Khatmi and Muhammad ibn Sirin.

Section

If someone deliberately abandons the mention of the name (tasmiyah, the saying of "Bismillah" at slaughter), is it permissible? On this there are two reports from Ahmad. If he abandons it forgetfully, it is permissible. Al-Shafi'i said: it is not forbidden in either case at all. Our shaykh 'Ali ibn 'Ubayd Allah said: If we say that deliberately abandoning the mention prevents permissibility, then the slaughter of the People of the Book has been abrogated (naskh) from this verse by His saying: ﴿And the food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5]. But according to al-Shafi'i's view, the verse is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed it is defiance (fisq)﴾. That is: even if one eats what the name of Allah has not been mentioned over, it is fisq, meaning departure from the truth and the religion. Regarding the meaning of "the devils" (al-shayatin) here, there are two opinions.

The first: that they are the devils of the jinn. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that they are a people from among the Persians, which we have mentioned from 'Ikrimah. According to the first, their inspiration is whispering (waswasah), and according to the second, their inspiration is the message (risalah). By "their allies" (awliya'ihim) is meant the disbelievers who disputed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning abandoning the eating of carrion. Then regarding them there are two opinions. (p-116) The first: that they are the polytheists of Quraysh. The second: the Jews; ﴿And if you obey them﴾ in making carrion lawful ﴿indeed you are polytheists﴾.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 122:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life﴾ — the scholars (mufassirun) differed concerning whom it was revealed, in five opinions.

The first: it was revealed concerning Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib and Abu Jahl. The reason was that "Abu Jahl threw at the Messenger of Allah ﷺ some dung, and Hamzah had not yet become a believer. Hamzah was informed of what Abu Jahl had done, so he came and struck Abu Jahl with his bow and said to him: 'Do you not see what he has brought? He has made foolish our minds and reviled our gods.' Hamzah said: 'And who is more foolish than you, who worship stones instead of Allah? I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is His servant and His Messenger.' Then this verse was revealed." This is the statement of Ibn Abbas.

The second: it was revealed concerning Ammar ibn Yasir and Abu Jahl. Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn Abbas, and Ikrimah said likewise.

The third: it was revealed concerning Umar ibn al-Khattab and Abu Jahl. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam and al-Dahhak.

The fourth: it was revealed concerning the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Jahl. This was said by Muqatil.

The fifth: it is general, encompassing every believer and disbeliever. This was said by al-Hasan and others.

Regarding His saying: ﴿was dead and We gave him life﴾, there are two opinions.

One: he was astray and We guided him. This was said by Mujahid. The second: he was ignorant and We taught him. This was said by al-Mawardi. Nafi' read "maytan" (dead) with a doubled ya (shaddah). Abu Ubaydah said: "al-maytah," unstressed, is from "mitah," and the meaning is the same.

Concerning "al-nur" (the light), there are three opinions:

One: it is guidance. This was said by Ibn Abbas. The second: it is the Qur'an. This was said by al-Hasan. The third: it is knowledge.

Regarding His saying: ﴿walks with it among the people﴾, there are three opinions:

One: he is guided by it among the people. This was said by Muqatil. The second: he walks with it among the people toward Paradise. The third: he spreads his religion by it among the people, so he becomes like one who walks. Al-Mawardi mentioned both of these.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿like one whose likeness is﴾ — "al-mathal" is an added element (silah); the meaning is "like one who is in darkness." It was also said: the meaning is, "like one who, if he were compared to something, his likeness would be one who is in darkness." And it was said: what is meant by "darkness" here is disbelief (kufr).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And thus was made attractive﴾ — that is, just as this one remains in his darkness, unable to escape from it, so likewise was made attractive "to the disbelievers what they used to do" of shirk and sins.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 123:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And thus We placed in every town its greatest criminals﴾, meaning: Just as We made their deeds appear attractive to the disbelievers, so likewise We placed in every town its wicked ones, namely its chieftains (akabir, the great ones). The greatest ones were made the wicked ones of every town because they are closest to disbelief through the leadership and abundance they were given. Ibn Qutaybah said: The sense of the verse is: "And thus We placed in every town its criminals, the greatest of them." "Akabir" is not declined (la yanṣarif, i.e., it takes the diptotic form), and they are the mighty ones.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That they may plot therein﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: al-makr (plotting) means deceit, trickery, treachery, immorality, betrayal, and opposition. Ibn 'Abbas said: "That they may say falsehood therein." Mujahid said: They stationed four men on every road of Makkah, to turn the people away from belief in Muhammad (ﷺ), saying to the people: "This is a poet, and a soothsayer."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they plot only against themselves﴾, meaning: that plotting of theirs returns upon them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 124:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when a sign comes to them﴾. The occasion of its revelation: Abu Jahl said, "The sons of ʿAbd Manaf have competed with us in nobility, until we became like two horses in a race, and they said: 'Among us is a prophet to whom revelation comes.' By God, we will not believe in him or follow him unless revelation comes to us just as it comes to him." So this verse was revealed. This is related by Muqatil. Al-Zajjaj said: the pronoun (the ha' and the mim) refers to the great men (akabir) who were mentioned. Abu Sulayman said: it refers to those who disputed about the prohibition of carrion. Muqatil said: the sign is the splitting of the moon and the smoke. Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿like what was given to the messengers of God﴾, said: "Until revelation comes to us, and Gabriel comes to us and informs us that Muhammad is truthful." Al-Dahhak said: each one of them asked to be singled out for messengerhood and revelation.

His saying, the Exalted: (God knows best where to place His message). Ibn Kathir and Hafs on the authority of ʿAsim read "risalatahu" (His message) in the singular with a fatha on the ta', according to tawhid (the singular form). The meaning: they are not worthy of it. This is because al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said: "By God, if prophethood were true, I would have been more deserving of it than you, for I am older than you and have more wealth than you." So the Exalted's saying was revealed: (God knows best where to place His message). The scholars of meanings (ahl al-maʿani) said: the most eloquent confirmation of the messengers is that they were not obeyed among their people before their mission, because criticism would be directed at them, and it would be said: "They were only leaders, so they were followed." So God knew best where to place the message: in the orphan of Abu Talib, rather than Abu Jahl, al-Walid, and the great men of Mecca.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those who committed crimes will be struck with humiliation﴾. Abu ʿUbayda said: al-saghar (humiliation) is the most severe abasement. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: they, although they were great in this world, humiliation will befall them in the sight of God, that is, a humiliation fixed for them in the sight of God. It is also permissible that the meaning is: humiliation will befall them in the sight of God. Al-Farra' said: its meaning is: humiliation from God, with "min" omitted. Abu Rawq said: humiliation in this world, and severe punishment in the Hereafter,

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 125:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So whomever Allah wills to guide﴾. Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and Abu Jahl.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He will expand his breast﴾. Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-sharh (expansion) means opening. Ibn Qutaybah said: From this one says, "I explained (sharahtu) the matter to you," and "I slit (sharahtu) the meat," meaning when you opened it. Ibn 'Abbas said: (He will expand his breast), that is, He will widen his heart for tawhid (monotheism) and faith. Ibn Mas'ud narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited: ﴿So whomever Allah wills to guide, He will expand his breast for Islam﴾. It was said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, what is this expansion?" He said: "A light that Allah casts into the heart, so the heart opens." They said: "Is there a sign of that?" He said: "Yes." It was asked: "And what is it?" (p-120) He said: "Turning back in repentance to the abode of eternity, withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before it comes."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿constricted (ḍayyiqan)﴾. Most readers recited it with a shadda (doubled letter). Ibn Kathir recited "ḍayyiqan" and, in al-Furqan (25:13), ﴿a constricted place (makanan ḍayyiqan)﴾, with the yā' sukūn and light. Abu 'Ali said: al-ḍayyiq and al-ḍayq are like al-mayyit and al-mayt.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿ḥarajan (tight)﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited (ḥarajan) with a fatḥah on the rā'. Nafi' and Abu Bakr from 'Asim recited it with a kasrah on the rā'. Al-Farra' said: Both are dialects. Yunus ibn Habib the grammarian likewise said: Both are dialects, except that the fatḥah is more common in the speech of the Arabs than the kasrah, and their pattern is like danaf and danif. Al-Zajjaj said: In the language, al-ḥaraj is the utmost of the constricted.

His saying, Exalted is He: ( ka'annama yaṣṣā'adu ) Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited "yaṣ'adu" with a shadda on the ṣād and the 'ayn, with a fatḥah on the ṣād and without an alif. Abu Bakr from 'Asim recited "yaṣṣā'adu" with a shadda on the ṣād and an alif after it. Ibn Kathir recited "yaṣ'adu" with the ṣād and 'ayn lightened, without an alif, the ṣād being sākin. Ibn Mas'ud and Talhah recited "taṣ'adu" with a tā' and without an alif. Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited "yatasa'adu" with an alif and a tā'. Al-Zajjaj said: His saying, "ka'annama yaṣṣā'adu fi al-sama'" and "yaṣ'adu," its origin is "yatasā'adu" or "yatasa''adu," except that the tā' is assimilated into the ṣād because of their closeness, and the meaning is: as if he has been burdened to ascend to the sky when he is invited to Islam, because of the constriction of his breast toward it. It is also possible that the meaning is: as if his heart ascends into the sky, recoiling from Islam and wisdom. Al-Farra' said: The path was closed to him, so he found nothing but to ascend into the sky, and he is not able to do that. Abu 'Ali said: "yaṣ'adu" and "yaṣṣā'adu" come from hardship and the difficulty of a thing, and from it is the saying of 'Umar: "Nothing has burdened me as the marriage proposal has burdened me," meaning nothing was as hard for me as its hardship.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus﴾, that is, like what We have related to you. ﴿Allah places the filth (al-rijs)﴾, and concerning it there are five views.

The first: that it is Satan, narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, meaning that Allah empowers him over them.

The second: that it is the calamity, narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: that it is what has no good in it, said by Mujahid.

The fourth: that it is the punishment, said by 'Ata', Ibn Zayd and Abu 'Ubaydah.

The fifth: that it is the curse in this world and the punishment in the Hereafter, said by al-Zajjaj. This verse cuts off the speech of the Qadariyyah, since it clearly states that guidance and misguidance are connected to the will of Allah, Exalted is He.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 126:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And this is the path of your Lord﴾, has three opinions.

The first: that it is the Qur'an. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud. The second: that it is monotheism (tawhid). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. (p-122) The third: that it is the religion that He is upon. This was said by 'Ata'.

The meaning of its being straight (istiqamah) is that it leads its traveler to success. Makki ibn Abi Talib said: "Mustaqiman" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "sirat." This type of hal is called the emphatic hal (al-hal al-mu'akkidah), because the path of Allah is never anything but straight. It was not brought to distinguish between two states, since the path of Allah never changes from being straight, ever. And this hal is not like the hal in your saying: "This is Zayd riding," because Zayd may at times be free of riding.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 127:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿For them is the abode of peace﴾, meaning Paradise. Regarding its being named so, there are four opinions.

The first: that "al-Salam" (Peace) is Allah, and it is His abode. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and al-Suddi.

The second: that it is the abode of safety that does not end. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The third: that the greeting of its people within it is "peace." This was mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

The fourth: that all its states are associated with peace. At the beginning of their entry: (﴿Enter it in peace﴾) [al-Hijr 15:46], and after their settling: ﴿The angels will enter upon them from every gate﴾ and ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ [al-Ra'd 13:23-24]. And His saying: ﴿except the saying "Peace, peace"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:26]. And at the meeting with Allah: ﴿"Peace," a word from a Lord Most Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:58]. And His saying: ﴿Their greeting on the Day they meet Him will be "Peace"﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:44]. As for the meaning of ﴿with their Lord﴾, i.e., it is guaranteed for them with Him; ﴿and He is their Protector﴾, i.e., the one who brings benefits to them and repels harms from them; ﴿because of what they used to do﴾ of acts of obedience.

(p-123) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the Day We gather them all﴾, meaning the jinn and the humans. Hafs, on the authority of ʿAsim, read "yaḥshuruhum" with the yāʾ. Abu Sulayman said: it means the polytheists and their devils, who used to inspire to them, through disputation, [the claim] that you should [eat] what Allah has forbidden of carrion.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O assembly of the jinn﴾. There is an ellipsis in it, so it is said to them: "O assembly" (maʿshar). The maʿshar (assembly) is the group whose affair is one; its plural is al-maʿāshir.

His saying: ﴿You have taken much of mankind﴾, that is, of their misleading and leading astray. ﴿And their allies from among mankind will say﴾, meaning those whom the jinn misled. ﴿Our Lord, some of us have enjoyed others﴾. There are three opinions concerning this.

The first: the enjoyment of humans from the jinn was that when they traveled, they would halt in a valley and wish to spend the night there, and one of them would say: "I seek refuge in the greatness of this valley from the evil of its inhabitants." The enjoyment of the jinn from humans was that they would boast over their people and say: "We have become lords over humans, until they seek refuge with us." This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas, and it was the view of Muqatil and al-Farra.

The second: the enjoyment of the jinn from humans was their obedience to them in what they incited them to of misguidance, disbelief, and sins. The enjoyment of humans from the jinn was that the jinn adorned for them the matters they desired and made them attractive to them until doing them became easy for them. This meaning was related by ʿAta from Ibn ʿAbbas, and it was the view of Muhammad ibn Kaʿb and al-Zajjaj. (p-124) The third: the enjoyment of the jinn from humans was their misleading them. The enjoyment of humans from the jinn was what they acquired from them of sorcery, soothsaying, and the like. The jinn in this verse means the devils.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have reached our term which You appointed for us﴾. There are two opinions concerning it.

One: death, said by al-Hasan and al-Suddi. The second: the gathering (al-hashr), mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He said: The Fire is your abode﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: al-mathwa is the place of residence. "Khalidin" (abiding) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. The meaning: the Fire is your place of residence, in a state of lasting eternal abiding. ﴿Except what Allah wills﴾ is an exception from the Day of Resurrection. The meaning: ﴿abiding therein﴾ from the time they are raised ﴿except what Allah wills﴾ of the duration of their gathering from their graves and the length of their reckoning. It is also possible that ﴿except what Allah wills﴾ refers to Allah increasing them in punishment. Some of them said: except what Allah wills of their being in the world without punishment. Other views have been stated on this, and you will find them explained in (Hud), if Allah wills.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 129:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And thus do We make some of the wrongdoers allies of others﴾. Concerning its meaning there are four opinions.

The first: We make some of them allies of others. Narrated by Sa'id from Qatadah.

The second: We cause some of them to follow others into the Fire according to their deeds, from al-muwalah (allegiance), which is al-mutaba'ah (following). Narrated by Ma'mar from Qatadah.

The third: We empower some of them over others. Said by Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: We leave some of them to others and do not help them. Mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿because of what they used to earn﴾, that is, because of the sins.

(p-125) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ Al-Hasan and Qatada read "تَأْتِكُمْ" (ta'tikum) with a *ta'* (feminine form of the verb). The scholars differed concerning whether messengers were sent to the jinn, and they held four opinions.

The first: The messengers were only sent to humankind, and God, exalted is He, sent Muhammad (ﷺ) to both humankind and the jinn. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

The second: The messengers of the jinn are those who heard the Qur'an and then returned to their people as warners. This was also narrated from Ibn Abbas. Mujahid said: "The messengers are from humankind, and the warners are from the jinn, and they are a people who hear the speech of the messengers and then convey to the jinn what they heard."

The third: God, exalted is He, sent messengers to them from among themselves, just as He sent messengers to humankind from among them. This was said by al-Dahhak, Muqatil, and Abu Sulayman, and it is the apparent meaning of the speech.

The fourth: God, exalted is He, did not send messengers to them from among themselves, but rather the messengers of humankind came to them. This was said by Ibn Jurayj, al-Farra', and al-Zajjaj. They said: "The plural in His saying, ﴿did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ does not prevent the messengers from being from one of the two groups, like His saying: ﴿from both of them come forth pearls and coral﴾ [al-Rahman: 22], whereas it comes forth only from the salt water."

Concerning the entry of the jinn into Paradise when they believe, there are two opinions.

One: They enter it and they eat and drink. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The second: Their reward is that they are protected from the Fire and they become dust. This was narrated by Sufyan from Layth.

(p-126) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿they recount to you My verses﴾, meaning: they recite My Book to you. ﴿And warn you﴾, meaning: they frighten you with the Day of Resurrection. Concerning His saying: ﴿We bear witness against ourselves﴾, there are two opinions.

One: We acknowledge against ourselves that the messengers warned us.

The second: Some of us bear witness against others that the messengers warned them. Then God, exalted is He, informed us of their condition, saying: ﴿and the life of this world deceived them﴾, meaning: by its adornment and by the respite granted to them in it. ﴿And they bear witness against themselves﴾, meaning: they confessed that they had been disbelievers in the world. Muqatil said: "That is when their limbs bore witness against them to polytheism and disbelief."

The words of the Most High: ﴿That is because your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people were unaware﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "That" refers to what We have related to you about the affair of the messengers and the punishment of those who denied. "Because your Lord would not destroy the towns unjustly" means: He would not destroy you until He sent a messenger to them. Ibn Abbas said: "Unjustly" means with polytheism. ﴿And its people were unaware﴾ means no messenger had come to them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 132:

Allah's words: ﴿And for each there are degrees according to what they have done﴾. That is: for every doer, whether in obedience to Allah or in disobedience to Him, there are degrees, i.e., stations that he reaches by his deed. If it is good, then it is good; and if it is evil, then it is evil. The reason they are called "darajat" (degrees) is the difference between them in elevation and descent, like the difference between the steps of a staircase (daraj).

Allah's words: ﴿and your Lord is not unaware of what they do﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read it with the yā' (ya), while Ibn 'Amir read it with the tā' (ta), as an address (al-khitab).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verses 133–134:

﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, the Possessor of mercy. If He wills, He can remove you and grant succession after you to whom He wills, just as He produced you from the descendants of another people.﴾ ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is coming, and you cannot escape.﴾ (p-127) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient﴾ means: Self-Sufficient above His creation. ﴿Possessor of mercy﴾ — Ibn ʿAbbas said: toward His allies and the people of His obedience. Others said: toward everyone. And among His mercy is the delay of retribution against those who oppose Him. ﴿If He wills, He can remove you﴾ by destruction. It was also said: this threat is directed at the people of Makkah. ﴿And grant succession after you to whom He wills, just as He produced you﴾, that is, originated you ﴿from the descendants of another people﴾, meaning: their past forefathers. ﴿Indeed, what you are promised﴾ of the coming of the Hour and the Gathering ﴿is coming, and you cannot escape﴾, that is: you cannot outrun it. Abu ʿUbayda said: it is said, "a‘jazani kadha" (he has made me unable), meaning: it escaped me and outran me.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verses 133–134:

﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, the Possessor of mercy. If He wills, He can remove you and grant succession after you to whom He wills, just as He produced you from the descendants of another people.﴾ ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is coming, and you cannot escape.﴾ (p-127) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient﴾ means: Self-Sufficient above His creation. ﴿Possessor of mercy﴾ — Ibn ʿAbbas said: toward His allies and the people of His obedience. Others said: toward everyone. And among His mercy is the delay of retribution against those who oppose Him. ﴿If He wills, He can remove you﴾ by destruction. It was also said: this threat is directed at the people of Makkah. ﴿And grant succession after you to whom He wills, just as He produced you﴾, that is, originated you ﴿from the descendants of another people﴾, meaning: their past forefathers. ﴿Indeed, what you are promised﴾ of the coming of the Hour and the Gathering ﴿is coming, and you cannot escape﴾, that is: you cannot outrun it. Abu ʿUbayda said: it is said, "a‘jazani kadha" (he has made me unable), meaning: it escaped me and outran me.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 135:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Upon your station﴾. Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read "makanatikum" (your stations) in the plural. Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, upon your place. It is said makan (place) and makana (station), and manzil (abode) and manzila. Al-Zajjaj said: "Act according to your established condition (tamakkun)." He said: The meaning may also be: act upon what you are upon. You say to a man when you order him to remain in a state: "Be upon your station (kun ʿala makanatika)."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed I am acting﴾, that is: acting in accordance with what my Lord has commanded me, ﴿so you will come to know who will have the good outcome of the abode.﴾ Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿAmir, and ʿAsim read "takunu" (will be) with a ta'. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a ya'. Their difference in [al-Qasas 37] is similar. The reasoning for the feminine form is the wording, and the reasoning for the masculine form is that it is not a true feminine. The "good outcome of the abode" is Paradise. The wrongdoers here are the polytheists.

If it is said: the apparent meaning of this verse is an order for them to persist in what they are upon, and that is not permissible. The answer: the meaning of this command is an emphasis on the threat; it is as if He said: "Persist in what you are upon, if you are content with the punishment." This was said by al-Zajjaj. (p-128)

Section

There are two opinions regarding this verse.

The first: that it is intended as a threat; according to this, it is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated).

The second: that it is intended as leaving off fighting; according to this, it is mansukh (abrogated) by the verse of the sword.

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 6, verse 136:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they assigned to God a share of what He created of the tilth and the cattle.﴾ Ibn Qutaybah said: *dhara'a* means "created." ﴿Of the tilth﴾ is the crops. ﴿And the cattle﴾: camels, cows, and sheep.

When they sowed, they drew a line and said, "This is for God, and this is for our gods." When they harvested what they had assigned to God, and some of it fell into what they had assigned to their gods, they left it and said, "It is in need of it [i.e., the gods]." And when they harvested what they had assigned to their gods, and some of it fell into God's share, they returned it to its place. They also designated some of the cattle for God. When the females among them gave birth to a stillborn, they ate it; but when the cattle of their gods gave birth to a stillborn, they venerated it and did not eat it.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the verse is: "They assigned to God a share of what He created of the tilth and the cattle, and they assigned to their partners a share." This is indicated by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They say, "This is for God, by their claim, and this is for our partners."﴾ Thus by the pointing to the two shares, it indicates the share of the partners. When what was for God grew, but what was for their partners did not grow, they returned the grown produce to their idols and said, "These need it more, and God is self-sufficient." And when what was for the idols grew, but what was for God did not, they left it as it was.

The exegetes said: They used to spend what they had assigned to God on guests and the needy. So the meaning of His saying, ﴿it does not reach God﴾ is: it does not reach these people. And they would spend the share of their gods in the crops on the upkeep of their attendants. As for the share of their gods in the cattle, there are three opinions concerning it:

The first: that it was also for the upkeep of the gods. The second: that they drew near to God by it, slaughtering it for them. The third: that it refers to the *baḥīrah* (a she-camel whose ear was slit), the *sā'ibah* (a freed animal), the *waṣīlah* (a ewe that bore twins in succession), and the *ḥām* (a stallion camel freed after a number of offspring).

Al-Hasan said: When what belonged to their idols was lost, they compensated for it, but when what belonged to God was lost, they did not compensate for it. Ibn Zayd said: They would not eat what they had assigned to God until they mentioned over it the names of their idols, and they did not mention God over what they had assigned to the idols.

As for His saying "*bi-za'mihim*" (by their claim): the majority [of readers] recited it with a fatḥah on the *zāy* (*bi-za'mihim*), while al-Kisa'i and al-A'mash recited it with a ḍammah on it (*bi-zu'mihim*). In *al-za'm* (the word for "claim") there are three dialectal forms: with a ḍammah on the *zāy*, with a fatḥah, and with a kasrah. Similar to it are *al-saqt*, *al-saqt* and *al-siqt* (a fall/a mistake), *al-fatk*, *al-fitk*, and *al-futk* (treachery); and *al-za'm*, *al-zi'm*, and *al-zu'm* (claim). Al-Farra' said: the fatḥah on the *zāy* in *al-za'm* belongs to the people of the Ḥijāz; its ḍammah belongs to the tribe of Asad; and its kasrah belongs to some of Qays, as al-Kisa'i reports.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 137:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And thus has been made attractive﴾, meaning: and in the same manner as that evil act, in what they divided, was made attractive through ignorance. Ibn al-Anbari said: It is permissible that "wa-kadhalika" (and thus) be a new (independent) clause, not referring back to what precedes it; so the meaning would be: "and likewise was it made attractive." The majority read it "zayyana" with a fatha on the zay and the ya, the lam of "qatl" in the accusative, and the dal of "awladihim" in the genitive (kasra), with "al-shuraka'" in the nominative. The reasoning behind this reading is clear. Ibn 'Amir read it with a damma on the zay of "zuyyina" (p-130), the lam of "qatl" [in "qatl"] in the nominative, the dal of "awladihim" in the accusative, and "al-shuraka'" in the genitive. Abu 'Ali said: its meaning is: the killing by their partners of their children; so he separated between the genitive construct and what it is attached to with the direct object, and this is ugly and rare in usage. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and al-Hasan read "zuyyina" with a damma, "qatlu" with a damma as well, "awladihim" in the genitive, and "shuraka'uhum" in the nominative. Al-Farra' said: he made "qatl" nominative because its agent was not named; and he made "al-shuraka'" nominative by a verb that is implied, as if he said: "zayyanahu lahum shuraka'uhum" (their partners made it attractive to them). Sibawayh likewise said regarding this reading: it is as if it was said: "Who made it attractive?" and it was answered: "Their partners." Makki ibn Abi Talib said: It has also been narrated from Ibn 'Amir that he read with a damma on the zay, a raf' on the lam, and a genitive on "al-awlad" and "al-shuraka'"; so "al-shuraka'" becomes a term for the children, because they share with the fathers in lineage, inheritance and religion.

The exegetes have four opinions concerning who is meant by "their partners."

One: they are the devils; this was said by al-Hasan, Mujahid, and al-Suddi. The second: their partners in polytheism; this was said by Qatadah. The third: people who used to serve the idols; this was said by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. The fourth: they are the misguided among the people; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi. The "partners" are attributed to them because they are the ones who invented that and claimed it.

Concerning what they made attractive to them of killing their children, there are two opinions.

One: it is the burying of daughters alive out of fear of poverty; this was said by Mujahid.

The second: one of them would swear that if so-and-so many boys were born to him, he would sacrifice one of them, as 'Abd al-Muttalib swore concerning the sacrifice of 'Abd Allah; this was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿that they may ruin them﴾, meaning: that they may destroy them. Concerning this lam there are two opinions.

One: it is the lam of purpose (kay). The second: it is the lam of consequence (al-'aqibah), like His saying: ﴿that it may become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8], meaning: their affair ended in ruin, not that they intended that.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and that they may confuse them regarding their religion﴾, meaning: that they may mix it up. Ibn 'Abbas said: that they may introduce doubt into their religion; and they were upon the religion of Isma'il, but they turned away from it through the adornment of the devils.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So leave them and what they fabricate﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: When the people of the Jahiliyyah buried their daughters, they would say: "Allah has commanded us to do this." So He said: ﴿So leave them and what they fabricate﴾, meaning: what they lie about. This is a threat and warning, and so it is muhkam (definitive). But some people said: its intent is to leave off fighting them, so it is mansukh (abrogated) by the verse of the sword.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 6, verse 138:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they say, "These are livestock and tilth set apart (ḥijr)."﴾ *Al-ḥarth* means cultivated crops, and *ḥijr* means forbidden. The meaning is that they declared forbidden certain livestock and crops which they had dedicated to their idols.

Ibn Qutayba said: *Ḥijr* was applied to the forbidden because it places a barrier (*ḥajara*) on people, preventing them from touching it.

Al-Ḥasan and Qatada read *ḥujr* with a *ḍamma* on the *ḥā'*. Al-Farra' said: It is said *ḥijr* and *ḥujr*, with a *kasra* and with a *ḍamma* on the *ḥā'*. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is *ḥaraj* (حَرَجٌ), which is like *jadhaba* (جَذَبَ) and *jabadha* (جَبَذَ).

Regarding these livestock which they dedicated to the idols, there are two opinions:

One: They are the *baḥīra* (a she-camel whose ear was slit and released), the *sā'iba* (a animal released freely), the *waṣīla* (a ewe that gave birth to twins of alternating sex), and the *ḥām* (a stallion camel released after a certain number of covers).

The second: They are the sacrificial animals offered to the idols, and the two have already been mentioned.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿None may eat of them except whom We will.﴾ This is like your saying: "None may taste it except whom we wish." Concerning those to whom they permitted eating them, there are two opinions:

One: They forbade them to women and made them for men. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The second is the reverse of this, said by Ibn Zayd. Al-Zajjaj said: Allah the Exalted informed that this prohibition is a claim made by them, with no proof or evidence for it.

Concerning His saying: ﴿And livestock whose backs have been forbidden﴾ there are three opinions:

One: They are the *ḥām*, said by Ibn Abbas.
The second: They are the *baḥīra*; they would not ride upon them, said by Abu Wa'il.
The third: They are the *baḥīra*, the *sā'iba* and the *ḥām*, said by al-Suddi.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And livestock over which they do not mention the name of Allah﴾ These are the offerings of their gods; they mention over them only the names of the idols. Abu Wa'il said: They are those upon which they would not ride. We have already mentioned this from him in His saying: ﴿whose backs have been forbidden﴾, so according to his view the two descriptions apply to one single category. Mujahid said: Among their camels there was a group over which they never mentioned the name of Allah in anything: not when they rode them, not when they carried loads upon them, not when they gave them to drink, nor when they gave birth.

Concerning His saying: ﴿as a fabrication against Allah﴾ there are two opinions:

One: That mentioning the names of their idols and leaving out the mention of Allah is the fabrication.

The second: That their attributing this to Allah the Exalted is the fabrication, because they used to say: "He forbade this."

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 139:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they say, "What is in the wombs of these livestock"﴾. By "livestock" he means the animals they considered forbidden: the *bahira* (a she-camel whose ears were slit and which was released), the *sa'iba* (a beast released freely for its gods), and the *wasila* (a ewe that bore twins in succession, with a male among them). Regarding what is meant by "what is in their wombs," the exegetes give three opinions.

The first is that it is the milk. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada. The second is that it is the fetuses. This was said by Mujahid. The third is that it is the offspring and the milk. This was said by al-Suddi and Muqatil.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿exclusively for our males﴾. The majority read *khalisatan* in the feminine form. There are four explanations for this.

The first is that it is feminine because *al-an'am* (livestock) is feminine, and what is in their wombs is similar to them. This was said by al-Farra'.

The second is that the meaning of *ma* (what) is feminine, because it carries the sense of a group. It is as if he said: the group of what is in the wombs of these livestock is exclusive. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The third is that the *ha'* (ة) entered for emphasis in the description, as they say *'allama* (very knowledgeable) and *nassaba* (a great genealogist).

The fourth is that it was treated like the verbal nouns (masadir) that take a feminine form while referring to masculine nouns, as in your saying: "your giving is well-being (*'afiyah*)," and "cheapness is a blessing (*ni'mah*)." Ibn al-Anbari mentioned both examples.

Ibn Mas'ud, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Dahhak, al-A'mash, and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read *khalisun* in the nominative, without the *ha'*. Al-Farra' said: it is masculine because *ma* is masculine in meaning.

Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Razin, Ikrima, and Ibn Ya'mur read *khalisahu*, with *sad* and *ha'* in the nominative, as a masculine pronoun. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "what came out alive."

Qatada read *khalisatan* in the accusative.

As for *al-dhukur* (the males), they are the men, and the husbands and the women.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if it is stillborn﴾. Most readers read *yakun* with the *ya'*, and *maytatan* in the accusative. This refers back to the wording of *ma* (what). The meaning is: "And if what is in the wombs of these livestock is stillborn."

Ibn Kathir read *yakun* with the *ya'* and *maytatun* in the nominative. Ibn 'Amir agreed with him on the nominative of *maytatun*, except that he read *takun* with the *ta'*. The meaning is: "And if it comes to be and occurs," so he made *kana* a complete verb that does not need a predicate.

Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read *takun* with the *ta'* and *maytatan* in the accusative. The meaning is: "And if the livestock that are in the wombs are stillborn."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿then they are partners in it﴾. This means the men and the women. ﴿He will repay them for their description﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: he intended the repayment for their description, which is a lie.

(p-134) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who have killed their children foolishly, without knowledge, have certainly lost﴾. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read "qattalū" with the doubled (shadda) form. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning Rabi'ah and Mudar, and those among the Arabs who used to bury their daughters alive in the Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance before Islam). Qatadah said: the people of the Jahiliyyah would kill one of their daughters for fear of her being taken captive and of poverty, while they fed their dog. Al-Zajjaj said: His saying "safahan" (foolishly) is in the accusative on the sense of the lam (of purpose), its implied meaning being "for folly" (lil-safah); you say, "I did that out of fear of evil" (hadhar al-sharr). Ibn al-Sumayfa', al-Jahdari and Mu'adh al-Qari read "sufahā'" with a damma on the sin, a fatha on the fa' and the ha', with a long vowel (madd) and a hamza, in the accusative.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿without knowledge﴾, meaning: they did that out of folly without any knowledge having come to them concerning it. They forbade what Allah had provided them of livestock and tilth, and they claimed that Allah had commanded them to do so.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 141:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿It is He who produces gardens, trellised and untrellised﴾. Concerning this there are four opinions.

The first: the trellised (ma'rushat) are those that spread over the surface of the earth, so that they spread out from what is supported on trellises, such as the vine, the gourd and the watermelon; and the untrellised (ghayr ma'rushat) are those that stand upon a stalk, such as the date palm, the crops and all other trees.

The second: the trellised are what people have planted, and the untrellised are the fruits that grow in the wilderness and the mountains. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas.

(p-135) The third: the trellised and the untrellised are both the vine; some of it is trellised and some of it is not trellised. This is the saying of al-Dahhak.

The fourth: the trellised are the vineyards whose grapes have been trellised, and the untrellised are all the trees that are not trellised. This is the saying of Abu 'Ubayda. "Eating" (al-akl) refers to the fruit. ﴿And the olive and the pomegranate, similar and dissimilar﴾ — its explanation has already passed.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Eat of its fruit when it bears fruit﴾. This is a command of permission. It was said: he mentioned eating first so as to forbid the practice of the people of the Jahiliyya in their crops, of prohibiting some of them.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And give its due on the day of its harvest﴾. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Abu 'Amr read it with a fatha on the ha' (ḥaṣādihi, ḥaṣādihi with fatha: "ḥaṣādihi" as read with fatha), and this is the dialect of the people of Najd and Tamim. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a kasra, and this is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz; al-Farra' mentioned it.

Concerning the intended meaning of this due (haqq) there are two opinions.

The first: it is the zakat. This is related from Anas ibn Malik, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, al-Hasan, Tawus, Jabir ibn Zayd, Ibn al-Hanafiyya, Qatada and others. On this view, the verse is muhkam (not abrogated).

The second: it is a due other than zakat, which was prescribed on the day of harvest, namely feeding those present and leaving what falls from the crop and the fruit. This is the saying of 'Ata' and Mujahid. Was it abrogated or not? If we say it is an obligatory command, then it is abrogated by zakat; and if we say it is a recommended command, then its ruling remains.

If it is asked: is it obligatory to give the due on the day of harvest? The answer: if we say it is feeding the poor who are present, then that occurs on the day of harvest; and if we say it is zakat, then three answers have been reported concerning it.

(p-136) The first: the command to give is understood as applying to the date palms, because their charity becomes due on the day of harvest. As for the crops, the command to give from them is understood as the obligation to pay, except that this cannot be done at the time of harvest, so it is postponed until the time of cleaning. This was mentioned by some of the early scholars.

The second: the day is a time-frame for the due, not for the giving; so it is as if He said: "And give the due that became obligatory on the day of its harvest, after cleaning."

The third: the purpose of mentioning the harvest is that the due is not obligatory by the mere emergence and maturing of the produce; rather it becomes obligatory on the day it comes into the hand of its owner. It might have been assumed that the due is binding by the mere growing of the crop before it is cut, so the verse clarifies that the obligation applies to what comes into the hand, not to what is destroyed. This is the mention of the two answers by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la.

His saying: ﴿And do not be wasteful﴾. Concerning this there are six opinions.

The first: that it exceeds what is prescribed in zakat to a degree that harms the giver. This is the saying of Abu al-'Aliya and Ibn Jurayj. Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas that Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas cut five hundred date palms, then distributed them in a single day, so that by evening he had left nothing for his family; so Allah the Exalted disliked that for him, and the verse was revealed: ﴿And do not be wasteful; indeed, He does not love the wasteful﴾.

The second: that wastefulness (al-israf) is withholding the obligatory charity. This is the saying of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib.

The third: that it is spending in disobedience. This is the saying of Mujahid and al-Zuhri.

The fourth: that it is associating other deities with Allah in the tilth and the livestock. This is the saying of 'Atiyya al-'Awfi and Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The fifth: that it is an address to the ruler, lest he take more than the obligatory amount of charity. This is the saying of Ibn Zayd.

The sixth: that it is excess in eating before paying zakat. This is the saying of Ibn Bahr.

(p-137) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And of the cattle, some for burden and some for [slaughter for] meat﴾. This is a continuation of what precedes it; the meaning is: He produced gardens, and He produced burden-animals and [animals for] meat. On this there are five opinions.

The first: the burden-animals are those that carry loads of camels, and the "meat" animals are their young. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, Mujahid, and Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: the burden-animals are those whose backs are used for benefit, and the "meat" animals are the grazing ones. It was transmitted by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: the burden-animals are camels, horses, mules, donkeys, and everything upon which loads are carried; and the "meat" animals are sheep. It was transmitted by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: the burden-animals are from among the camels, and the "meat" animals are from among the sheep. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The fifth: the burden-animals are camels and cattle, and the "meat" animals are sheep, and camels that are not used for carrying loads. This was said by Qatadah. 'Ikrimah, Abu al-Mutawakkil, and Abu al-Jawza' read ḥumūlatan with a ḍammah on the ḥā'.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Eat of what Allah has provided for you﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: do not forbid what you have forbidden of what has been mentioned, ﴿and do not follow the steps of Satan﴾, i.e., his paths. He said: His saying ﴿eight pairs﴾ is a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿burden-animals and [animals for] meat﴾. And the zawj (pair), in the language, is the single one that has another with it. The author [Ibn al-Jawzi] said: This statement needs completion, namely that it be said: the zawj is that which has another of its kind with it, and then each one of the two is called a zawj.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 143–144:

(p-138) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿of the sheep, two (males and females)﴾. Ad-Da'n (sheep): the females of the flock that have wool; al-Ma'iz (goats): the females of it that have hair. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir recited "al-Ma'iz" with a fatha on the ayn. Nafi', Hamzah, 'Asim and al-Kisa'i recited it with the ayn sukun. What is meant by "two females" is the male and the female. ﴿Say: Has He forbidden the two males or the two females?﴾ of the sheep and the goats. ﴿Or what the wombs of the two females contain?﴾ The meaning: if what He forbade is the two males, then every male is forbidden; if He forbade the two females, then every female is forbidden; and if He forbade what the wombs of the two females contain, then they contain males, contain females, and contain both males and females, so every fetus would be forbidden. Ibn al-Anbari said: The meaning of the verse is: Did the prohibition come to you from the direction of the two males, or from the direction of the two females? If they say, from the direction of the two males, then every male is forbidden to them; if they say, from the direction of the two females, then every female is forbidden to them; and if they say, from the direction of the womb, then the male and the female are forbidden to them. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: If they say, "He forbade the two males," they have made obligatory the prohibition of every male of the sheep and the goats, while they enjoy the flesh and backs of some of the males of them, and in that is the corruption of their claim. And if they say, "He forbade the two females," they have made obligatory the prohibition of the flesh of every female of the young of the sheep and the goats, while they enjoy the flesh and backs of some of that (p-139) as well. And if they say, "what the wombs of the two females contain," then they have been enjoying some of their males and females. The exegetes said: Allah, exalted is He, argued against them with this verse and the one after it, because they used to forbid kinds of livestock, some of which were forbidden to both men and women, and some of which were forbidden to women but not to men.

In His saying, ﴿Has He forbidden the two males or the two females?﴾ there is a refutation of what they had forbidden of the baḥīrah, the sā'ibah, the waṣīlah and the ḥām.

In His saying, ﴿Or what the wombs of the two females contain?﴾ there is a refutation of their saying: ﴿What is in the bellies of these cattle is exclusively for our males and forbidden to our wives.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Inform me with knowledge﴾. Az-Zajjaj said: The meaning: explain what you have forbidden with knowledge, i.e., you have no knowledge, because you do not believe in a Book. ﴿Or were you witnesses?﴾ i.e., did you witness that Allah had forbidden this, since you do not believe in a Messenger?

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah to mislead the people without knowledge?﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: He means 'Amr ibn Luhayy and whoever came after him. The wrongdoers here are the polytheists.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 143–144:

(p-138) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿of the sheep, two (males and females)﴾. Ad-Da'n (sheep): the females of the flock that have wool; al-Ma'iz (goats): the females of it that have hair. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir recited "al-Ma'iz" with a fatha on the ayn. Nafi', Hamzah, 'Asim and al-Kisa'i recited it with the ayn sukun.
