And if they say, "He forbade the two females," they have made obligatory the prohibition of the flesh of every female of the young of the sheep and the goats, while they enjoy the flesh and backs of some of that (p-139) as well. And if they say, "what the wombs of the two females contain," then they have been enjoying some of their males and females. The exegetes said: Allah, exalted is He, argued against them with this verse and the one after it, because they used to forbid kinds of livestock, some of which were forbidden to both men and women, and some of which were forbidden to women but not to men.

In His saying, ﴿Has He forbidden the two males or the two females?﴾ there is a refutation of what they had forbidden of the baḥīrah, the sā'ibah, the waṣīlah and the ḥām.

In His saying, ﴿Or what the wombs of the two females contain?﴾ there is a refutation of their saying: ﴿What is in the bellies of these cattle is exclusively for our males and forbidden to our wives.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Inform me with knowledge﴾. Az-Zajjaj said: The meaning: explain what you have forbidden with knowledge, i.e., you have no knowledge, because you do not believe in a Book. ﴿Or were you witnesses?﴾ i.e., did you witness that Allah had forbidden this, since you do not believe in a Messenger?

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah to mislead the people without knowledge?﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: He means 'Amr ibn Luhayy and whoever came after him. The wrongdoers here are the polytheists.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 145:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who would eat it⦆. By this he alerts them that prohibition and permission are established only by revelation. Tawus and Mujahid said: the meaning of the verse is: I do not find anything forbidden among what you used to consider lawful in the Jahiliyyah except this. What is meant by "eater" (ṭāʾim) is the one who eats. ﴿Unless it be carrion⦆, i.e., unless what is eaten is carrion. Ibn Kathir and Hamzah read "Illā an yakūna" with the yāʾ, and "maytatan" in the accusative. Ibn ʿAmir read "Illā an takūna" with the tāʾ, and "maytatun" in the nominative, meaning: unless carrion occurs or comes to be. ﴿Or blood poured forth⦆. Qatadah said: only flowing blood is prohibited; as for meat mixed with blood, there is no harm in it. al-Zajjaj said: al-masfūḥ means the poured out. They used to eat the blood along with the meat when they slaughtered. Al-rijs is a name for what is loathed, and for punishment; or fisqan, the meaning being: or that what is eaten be fisq. ﴿Or what has been dedicated to other than God⦆, i.e., the voice is raised over its slaughter in the name of other than God; so whatever is mentioned over it other than the name of God is called fisq. Fisq is departure from the religion.

Section

The scholars of abrogation (al-nāsikh wa-al-mansūkh) differed regarding this verse into two opinions.

One of them: that it is muḥkam (not abrogated). Those who hold this view have three statements regarding the reason for its being muḥkam. The first: that it is a report (khabar), and a report is not subject to abrogation. The second: that it came as an answer to a question they asked; so the answer was according to the extent of the question, and then He prohibited what He prohibited after that. The third: that there is no prohibited animal except what is mentioned in it.

The second opinion: that it is mansūkh, abrogated by what is mentioned in [al-Ma'idah] regarding the strangled, the beaten to death, and in the Sunnah regarding the prohibition of domestic donkeys and every animal with fangs among the predators and every bird with talons. It was also said: the verse of [al-Ma'idah] is included within this verse, because all those things are carrion.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 146:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And to those who were Jews We prohibited every animal with claws﴾. Al-Hasan and Al-A'mash read "ẓufrin" (ظُفُرٍ) with a sukun on the fa'. This prohibition was a prohibition of trial and punishment.

Regarding "dhi al-ẓufr" (the one with claws) there are three opinions.

The first: it is that which does not have separated toes, such as camels, ostriches, geese, and ducks. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Qatadah, and al-Suddi.

The second: only camels. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: every animal with a hoof among the beasts, and every bird with a talon. This was said by Ibn Qutaybah. He said: the hoof was called "ẓufr" by way of metaphor (isti'arah), and the Arabs use "hoof" and "cloven hoof" to mean the foot, as a metaphor. And they recited:

"I will restrain her, or I will leave her matter to a king whose hooves have not been split."

He meant his feet; cloven hooves belong only to sheep and cattle. Ibn al-Anbari said: "ẓufr" here functions as "ẓufr" does for a human being. It has three dialectal forms (lughat). The highest of them is "ẓufur" (ظُفُرٌ); it is also said "ẓufr" (ظُفْرٌ) and "uẓfur" (أُظْفُورٌ). A poet said:

"Did you not see that death overtook those who passed away, so that none of them remains, one with a wing or one with a claw?"

And another said:

"You were indeed one with fang and claw against the enemies, but now you have become one whom they do not fear for my fang or my claw."

And another said:

"Between his first morsel, when it goes down, and another that follows it, there is the space of a claw-tip."

Regarding the fat of cattle and sheep there are three opinions.

The first: He prohibited from them only the fat of the kidneys (thurub) specifically. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: the fat of the thurub and the kidneys. This was said by al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd.

The third: every fat that is not mixed with bone, nor upon bone. This was said by Ibn Jurayj. Regarding His saying: ﴿except what their backs have carried﴾ there are three opinions.

The first: it is what clung to the back of fat. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: the rump (al-ilyah), said by Abu Salih and al-Suddi. The third: what clung to the back and the flank from the inside of their bellies, said by Qatadah. As for the "hawaya" (intestines), the commentators have opinions whose meanings are close. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi, and Ibn Qutaybah said: they are the "mabi'ir" (the intestinal coils). Ibn Zayd said: they are "banat al-laban" (the daughters of milk), which are the enclosures in which the intestines lie. al-Farra' said: the hawaya are the mabi'ir and banat al-laban. al-Asma'i said: they are banat al-laban, and their singular is "hawa'" (حاوِياءُ), "hawiyah" (حاوِيَةٌ), and "hawiyyah" (حَوِيَّةٌ).

A poet said:

"I kill them, and I do not see Mu'awiyah, the large-eyed, great of the hawiyah."

Another said:

"As if the croaking of love in its hawi'ah were the hissing of vipers or the chirping of scorpions."

Abu 'Ubaydah said: the hawaya are what encloses of the belly, that is, what curves around of it. al-Zajjaj said: hawaya is a name for everything that encloses of the belly, gathered and curved; they are banat al-laban, they are the mabi'ir, and they are called the marabid (resting places), and within them are the intestines.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿or what is mixed with bone﴾ has two opinions.

One: it is the fat of the belly and the rump, because they are upon bone, said by al-Suddi. The second: every fat on the legs, the flank, the head, the two eyes, and the two ears, is what is mixed with bone, said by Ibn Jurayj. They agreed that what their backs carried is lawful, by way of exception from the prohibition. As for what the hawaya carried, or what is mixed with bone, there are two opinions.

One: it falls within the exception, so it is permitted; the meaning being: there was made lawful for them what the hawaya carried of fat and what was mixed with bone. This is the view of most scholars.

The second: it is coordinated with what was prohibited, not with the exception; the meaning being: We prohibited to them their fats, or the hawaya, or what is mixed with bone, except what the backs carried, for that is not prohibited. This was said by al-Zajjaj. As for the "aw" (or) mentioned here, it is in the sense of "wa" (and), like His saying: ﴿sinful or ungrateful﴾ [al-Insan 76:24].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That We repaid them﴾, i.e., that prohibition was a punishment for them because of their transgression.

Regarding their transgression there are two opinions.

One: it is their killing of the prophets and their consuming of usury. The second: it is the prohibition of what had been made lawful for them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 147:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if they deny you﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to the polytheists, 'This is what has been revealed to me: that it is forbidden to the Muslims and to the Jews,' they said: 'Indeed you have not been correct,' and this verse was revealed." Regarding who the deniers are, there are two opinions.

One: they are the polytheists. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: they are the Jews, as said by Mujahid. The purpose of mentioning "the all-encompassing mercy" is that He does not hasten the punishment, and "al-baʾs" (the severity) means the punishment.

Regarding the intended meaning of "the criminals" (al-mujrimin), there are two opinions.

One: they are the polytheists. The second: they are the deniers.

(p-145) His words, may He be exalted: ﴿The ones who associated partners [with Allah] will say﴾, that is, when the proof has become binding upon them and they have become certain of the falsity of their polytheism and of their prohibition of what Allah has not prohibited: ﴿Had Allah willed, we would not have associated [anything with Him]﴾. They took this as a proof for themselves in their maintaining of falsehood. It is as though they said: if He were not pleased with what we are upon, He would have prevented between us and it. They only said this mockingly and as a way of repelling the argument against them. It is said to them: Why do you call your opponents misguided, when they too are under [Allah's] will? Then they have no proof, because they clung to the will and abandoned the command. Allah's will encompasses all existing things, whereas His command does not encompass all that He wills. So it is incumbent upon the servant to follow the command, and he has no right to make excuses by the will after the command has come.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Thus did those before them deny﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: That is, they said to their messengers the same as what these people have said to you. ﴿Until they tasted Our might﴾, that is, Our punishment. ﴿Say: Do you have any knowledge [to show us]?﴾, that is, a Book sent down from Allah concerning the prohibition of what you have prohibited. ﴿If you follow only conjecture﴾, not certainty; "in" here carries the meaning of "má" (only). And "takhrusūn" means: you lie.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: "Then to Allah belongs the conclusive argument."﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: His conclusive argument is His making clear that He is the One, and His sending of the prophets with miraculous proofs. Al-Suddi said: ﴿Then if He had willed, He would have guided you all.﴾ (refers to) the Day of the taking of the covenant.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 150:

(p-146) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Bring forward your witnesses﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: Sibawayh held that "halumma" is a hā' (interjection) to which "lamma" was joined, and the two were made to function as a single word. Most dialects say "halumma" for the singular, the dual, and the plural alike, and the Qur'an came in this form. Some of the Arabs inflect it for the dual, the plural and the feminine: for the masculine they say "halumma," for the woman "halummī," for two males "halummā," for two females "halummā," for a group "halummū," and for women "halummna." Ibn Qutayba said: "halumma" means "ta'āla" (come here). The people of the Hijaz do not inflect it or make it plural, while the people of Najd treat it as derived from "halmamtu," so they inflect it for the dual, the plural and the feminine, and it is connected with the lām, so they say "halumma laka" and "halumma lakumā." He said: Al-Khalil said: its origin is "lamma," and the hā' was added at its beginning. Al-Farra' disagreed with him, saying: its origin is "hal," to which "am" was joined; the vowel of the hamza in "am" was transferred to the lām when the hamza was dropped and moved onto what precedes it. Similarly, for "allahumma," he holds its origin to be "yā Allāhu ummanā bi-khayr" (O Allah, aim us toward good), which was used so often in speech that it blended together and the hamza was dropped. Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning of "halumma" is "aqbil" (come forward). Its origin is "um yā rajul" (i.e., "aqṣid," make for it), so they joined "hal" to "um" and made them a single particle, removed "um" from inflection, transferred the vowel of the hamza of "um" to the lām, dropped the hamza, and so the mīm was attached to the lām. If a man says to another "halumma" and he wishes to say "I will not do it," he says: "lā ahallumu" and "wa lā uhallimu." Mujahid said: this verse is the answer to their saying that Allah prohibited the baḥīra and the sā'iba. Muqatil said: those who testify that Allah prohibited this tilth and livestock, so if they bear witness that Allah prohibited it, ﴿then do not testify with them﴾, that is: do not confirm their statement.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 151:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden you: that you associate nothing with Him⦆. "Mā" here means "alladhī" (that which). Regarding "lā" there are two opinions.

One of them: it is superfluous (zāʾidah), as in His saying: "that you do not prostrate" [al-Aʿraf: 12].

The second: it is not superfluous, but is a negation. According to this view, there are three opinions concerning the construction of the sentence.

The first: that His saying "an lā tushrikū" (that you do not associate) is understood according to meaning, so its estimate is: "Recite to you that you do not associate," i.e., recite the prohibition of shirk.

The second: that the meaning is: "I enjoin upon you that you do not associate," because His saying ﴿and to parents, goodness﴾ [al-Isra: 23] is understood as meaning: "I enjoin upon you goodness to parents." This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

The third: that the speech is complete at His saying ﴿your Lord has forbidden﴾. Then, regarding His saying "ʿalaykum" (upon you), there are two opinions.

One of them: it is an incitement (ighrāʾ), as in His saying ﴿upon you is yourselves﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 105]. So the estimate is: "Upon you that you do not associate." This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

The second: that it means "it is obligatory upon you" and "it is required of you that you do not associate." Regarding this shirk there are two opinions.

One of them: that it is claiming a partner with Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The second: that it is obeying others in disobedience to Him.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not kill your children﴾ refers to burying daughters alive. ﴿Out of poverty﴾ means: out of fear of poverty.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not approach the indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is hidden﴾. Concerning this there are five opinions.

The first: that the indecencies (al-fawahish) are fornication (al-zina), what is apparent of them is publicizing it, and what is hidden is concealing it. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, and al-Suddi.

The second: that what is apparent is wine-drinking and marrying forbidden women, and what is hidden is fornication. This was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr and Mujahid.

The third: that what is apparent is wine-drinking, and what is hidden is fornication. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The fourth: that it is general regarding indecencies; its apparent part is their openness and its hidden part is their secrecy. This was said by Qatadah.

The fifth: that what is apparent is the actions of the limbs, and what is hidden is the beliefs of the hearts. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi in his tafsir of this place and in his tafsir of His saying ﴿Leave the outward and inward of sin﴾ [al-Anʿam: 120].

"The soul which Allah has forbidden" is the soul of a Muslim or of a covenanted non-Muslim. "The truth" means the permission of the Sharia.

In his statement ﴿except with that which is best﴾ there are four opinions.

The first is that it means the guardian who is reforming the property should eat from it in a reasonable manner when he is in need. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd.

The second is that it means trading with it. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi.

The third is that it means he keeps it for him until the time he hands it over to him. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The fourth is that it means guarding it for him and making it grow for him. This was said by al-Zajjaj, who said: "'Hatta' (until) is to be understood in terms of meaning. The meaning is: guard it for him until he reaches his ashudd (full maturity), and when he reaches his ashudd, hand it over to him." As for al-ashudd (full maturity), it is the consolidation of the strength of youth and age. Ibn Qutayba said: "The meaning of the verse is: until he grows in his development to the limit of men. It is said: 'He reached his ashudd' when he has arrived at its endpoint before he begins to decline." Abu 'Ubayda said: "al-Ashudd has no singular form from its own root. If they are compelled to give it one, they say shadd, on the pattern of dabb, and its plural is adubb." Ibn al-Anbari said: "A group of the Basran grammarians said: the singular of al-ashudd is shudd, with a dammah on the shin. Some of the Basran grammarians said: the singular of al-ashudd is shiddah, as in their saying ni'mah and an'um." Some of the lexicographers said: "al-Ashudd is a noun that has no singular." The commentators have eight opinions regarding al-ashudd.

The first is that it is thirty-three years. This was narrated by Ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second is what lies between eighteen and thirty years. This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third is forty years. This was narrated from 'A'isha, may peace be upon her.

The fourth is eighteen years. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Muqatil.

The fifth is twenty-five years. This was said by 'Ikrimah.

The sixth is thirty-four years. This was said by Sufyan al-Thawri.

The seventh is thirty years. This was said by al-Suddi, who said: "Then after this verse there came ﴿until, when they reach marriageable age﴾ [al-Nisa': 6], so it seems he is alluding to abrogation (naskh)."

The eighth is reaching the age of puberty (bulugh al-hulum). This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam, al-Sha'bi, Yahya ibn Ya'mur, Rabi'ah and Malik ibn Anas, and it is the correct view. I do not think that those whose opinions we have cited before them interpreted this verse in the manner attributed to them. Rather, I think that those who compiled the tafsir works transferred these opinions from the interpretation of the words of God Most High ﴿and when he reaches his full strength﴾ [Yusuf: 22; al-Qasas: 14] to this place, because that is the end of al-ashudd, whereas this is the beginning of its completion, and the two are not alike.

Ibn Jarir said: "There is an omitted element in the speech, which was left out relying on what is evident from what was omitted, because the meaning is: until he reaches his ashudd; then, when he reaches his ashudd, if you perceive in him right judgement (rushd), then hand over to him his property."

The author said: "If by what is evident he means what is evident in this verse, then it is not correct. Rather, the perception of right judgement and maturity is derived from another verse. What is absolute in this verse has been restricted in other verses, so the absolute is understood in light of the restricted."

God Most High says: ﴿And give full measure﴾, that is, complete it and do not diminish from it. ﴿And the balance﴾, that is, weigh with the balance. ﴿And justice﴾ means equity. ﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾, that is, what it can bear, and it does not fall short of it. Qadi Abu Ya'la said: "Since measuring and weighing make precise limitation to the smallest amount difficult, He obligated us to exert ourselves in striving for accuracy, rather than requiring the exact realisation of measure and weight."

God Most High says: ﴿And when you speak, be just﴾, that is, when you speak or give testimony, say what is true, even if the one for whom or against whom the testimony is given is a relative. ﴿The covenant of God﴾ includes what He has enjoined upon creation and what He has charged them with, and what a person has made obligatory upon himself, such as a vow and other things. ﴿This He has enjoined upon you, that perhaps you may remember﴾, that is, that you may remember it and act upon it.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited ﴿tadhakkarūn﴾ [al-An'am: 153], ﴿yadhkurūn﴾ [al-An'am: 126], ﴿yadhkuru al-insān﴾ [Maryam: 67], ﴿an yadhkura﴾ [al-Furqan: 62], and ﴿liyadhdhakarū﴾ [al-Isra': 41], all with the letter dhal doubled (shaddah). Nafi', Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir recited all of these with doubling, except ﴿awa-la yadhkuru al-insān﴾ [Maryam: 67], which they read without doubling. Aban and Hafs narrated from 'Asim: "yadhkurūn" with a light dhal throughout the Qur'an. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited "yudhakkirūn" with doubling when it is with the letter ya' (yā'), and without doubling when it is with the letter ta' (tā').

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 153:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that this is My path, straight﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim and Abu 'Amr recited "wa-anna" with the alif vowelled (fath) and the nun doubled (tashdid). Al-Farra' said: If you wish, make "anna" vowelled with fath, by the governing of "utlu" (recite) over it; and if you wish, make it in the genitive (khafd), meaning: "That which He has enjoined upon you, and [that] this is My path, straight." Ibn 'Amir also recited with the alif vowelled (fath), except that he lightened the nun, making it the lightened form of the heavy (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah); and its grammatical case-ending follows the same rule as those. Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited with the nun doubled and the alif kasra. Al-Farra' said: The kasra of the alif is by way of resumption (isti'naf). Regarding "al-sirat" there are two opinions:

One of them: that it is the Qur'an. The second: that it is Islam. We have also explained the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of His saying "mustaqiman" (straight). As for "al-subul" (the ways), Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the misguidances (al-dalalat). Mujahid said: (p-152) the innovations (bida') and doubtful matters (shubuhat). Muqatil said: He meant what they had forbidden to themselves of the livestock and the tilth. ﴿So that He scatters you from His way﴾, that is: so that they lead you astray from His religion.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 154:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We gave Moses the Book﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "Thumma" (then) here is for conjunction with the sense of recitation; so the meaning is: Recite what your Lord has forbidden, then recite to you what Allah gave Moses.

Ibn al-Anbari said: What comes after "thumma" is prior to what comes before it in intention; the implied meaning is: Then, indeed We had given Moses the Book before Our sending down the Qur'an upon Muhammad (ﷺ).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Complete [favour] upon him who did good﴾. Regarding His saying "tamaman" (completely) there are two views.

One of them: it is a word connected to what follows it. You say: "I gave you such-and-such, tamaman upon such-and-such, and tamaman for such-and-such." This is the view of the majority.

The second: that His saying "tamaman" is a word standing on its own, not connected to what follows it. The implied meaning is: We gave Moses the Book tamaman, that is, in one single instalment, We did not divide its sending down as the Qur'an was divided. This was mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Regarding the referent of "ahsana" (the one who did good) there are four views.

The first: it is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Then, regarding the meaning of the statement, there are two views. One: complete [favour] upon Allah's goodness to His prophets; this was said by Ibn Zayd. The second: complete [favour] upon Allah's goodness to Moses; and according to these two views, "alladhi" (who) carries the meaning of "ma" (what).

The second view: it is Abraham, the Friend (al-Khalil), upon him be peace; so the meaning is: completion of the blessing upon Abraham, who did good in obeying Allah, and Moses's prophethood was a blessing upon Abraham, since he was from his descendants. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

The third view: it is every doer of good among the prophets and others. Mujahid said: "tamaman 'ala al-muhsinin" (completion upon the good-doers), that is, completion for every good-doer. According to this view, "alladhi" carries the meaning of "min" (among), and "ʿala" carries the meaning of the preposition "li" (for). From this is the Arabs' saying: "atamma 'alayhi" and "atamma lahu" (he completed it for him). The poet al-Ra'i said:

"She grazed upon it for months, and [the wild animals] roamed over it"

meaning: for it.

Ibn Qutayba said: Similar to this is your saying: "I bequeath my wealth to al-ladhi ghazā wa ḥajja" (the one who raided and performed Hajj); you mean: to those who raid and those who perform Hajj.

The fourth view: it is Moses. Then, regarding the meaning of "ahsana," there are two views.

One: he did good in the world by obeying Allah, Mighty and Majestic. al-Hasan and Qatada said: completion for his honour in Paradise in addition to his goodness in the world. al-Rabi' said: it is Moses's goodness through his obedience. Ibn Jarir said: completion of Our blessings upon him in return for his goodness in carrying out Our command and prohibition.

The second: he excelled in knowledge and the ancient Books of Allah; as if it was added to what he had excelled in of the Torah; and "tamam" (completion) would carry the meaning of increase. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari. According to these two views, "alladhi" carries the meaning of "ma" (what).

Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Abu Razin, al-Hasan, and Ibn Yu'mar read: "ʿala alladhi aḥsana" with the "alladhi" in the nominative (ʿalā al-ladhī aḥsanu). Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: upon that which is the best of things. ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, Abu al-Mutawakkil, and Abu al-ʿAliya read: "ʿala alladhi aḥsana" with the hamza raised, the sin kasra, and the nun fatha (ʾaḥsana becoming ʾuḥsina-type reading, i.e., "uḥsina" in the passive sense); and it may bear the meaning of goodness (ihsan) and may bear the meaning of knowledge (ʿilm).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And a detailed explanation of all things﴾. That is: a clarification of all things from the matter of their law that they need to know, so that they may believe in the Resurrection and the recompense.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 155:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed﴾, meaning the Qur'an. ﴿So follow it and fear Allah﴾, that you oppose it, ﴿that you may be shown mercy﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "So that you may be hopeful of mercy."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 156:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Lest you should say﴾. The occasion of its revelation: the disbelievers of Makkah said, "May Allah fight the Jews and the Christians! How they denied their prophets! By Allah, if a warner and a Book had come to us, we would have been more guided than them." So this verse was revealed. This is related by Muqatil. Al-Farra' said: "An" (أنْ) is in a position of nasb in two places. One: "We sent it down lest you should say." The other: from His saying, "and fear Allah that you may be shown mercy" (واتَّقَوْا أنْ تَقُولُوا), meaning "lest you should say." Al-Zajjaj mentioned from the Basrans that its meaning is: "We sent it down out of aversion that you should say"; and they do not permit the implied "la" (لا). As for the address in this verse, it is to the people of Makkah, and the intent is to establish the proof against them by the sending down of the Qur'an, so that they would not say on the Day of Resurrection: "The Torah and the Gospel were sent down to the Jews and the Christians, and we were heedless of what is in them." "Wa-dirasatuhum" (وَدِراسَتُهُمْ): their recitation of the Books. Al-Kisa'i said: ﴿And indeed we were heedless of their study﴾ (وَإنْ كُنّا عَنْ دِراسَتِهِمْ لَغافِلِينَ), meaning we did not know what they were, because their books were not in our language. So Allah sent down a Book in their language so that their proof would be cut off.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 157:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Surely we would have been better guided than they are﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: They only said this because they were boastful of their minds and understanding, since they memorized their poetry and their narratives, while they were unlettered and did not write. ﴿There has indeed come to you clear evidence﴾, meaning: that which contains clarification and cuts off doubts. Ibn Abbas said: ﴿There has indeed come to you clear evidence﴾, meaning: a proof, namely the Prophet, the Qur'an, the guidance, the clarification, the mercy, and the blessing. ﴿Who then does greater wrong﴾, meaning: who is more disbelieving, ﴿than one who denies the signs of Allah﴾, meaning Muhammad and the Qur'an, ﴿and turns away from them﴾: he turned away and did not believe in them. And "evil punishment" (su' al-adhab): its severity.

(p-156) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do they await﴾, i.e., do they wait ﴿except that the angels should come to them﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "ta'tiyahum" with a ta' (feminine prefix). Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "ya'tiyahum" with a ya'. This coming is for the seizing of their souls. Muqatil said: by "the angels" is meant the Angel of Death alone.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or your Lord should come﴾. al-Hasan said: or the command of your Lord should come. al-Zajjaj said: or His destruction and retribution should come, either by a hastening punishment or by the Resurrection.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or some of the signs of your Lord should come﴾. 'Abd al-Warith, other than al-Qazzaz, transmitted it with the ya' of "ya'ti" pronounced with sukun, while the rest read it with a fatha. Regarding this verse there are four opinions.

The first: it is the rising of the sun from its west. This was narrated by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri from the Prophet (ﷺ), and Ibn Mas'ud said likewise. It is also reported through Zurarah ibn Awfa from him, and from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Suddi. al-Bukhari and Muslim in their two Sahihs narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The Hour will not be established until the sun rises from its west. When it rises and people see it, whoever is on the earth will believe, but that is the time when faith will not benefit a soul that did not believe before, or that earned no good through its faith." 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Repentance will continue to be accepted until the sun rises from its west. When it rises, a seal is placed upon every heart according to what is in it, and deeds suffice people."

The second: it is the rising of the sun and the moon from their west. Masruq narrated it from Ibn Mas'ud.

The third: it is one of the signs, the three being the rising of the sun from its west, the beast, and the opening of Gog and Magog. al-Qasim narrated this meaning from Ibn Mas'ud.

The fourth: it is the rising of the sun from its west, the Dajjal, and the beast of the earth. This was said by Abu Hurayrah. The first is the most sound. The "good" here means righteous deeds; faith did not benefit at that time because of the manifestation of the sign that compels them to believe, and righteous deeds at that time likewise do not benefit. al-Dahhak said: whoever some of the signs reach while he is upon righteous deeds together with his faith, it is accepted from him, just as it is accepted from him before the sign. It was also said that the wisdom in the sun's rising from its west is that the atheists and astrologers claimed that this would not happen, so Allah shows them His power and brings it up from the west as He brings it up from the east, and to confirm the helplessness of Nimrod when Abraham said to him: ﴿So bring it from the west,﴾ and he was confounded [al-Baqarah 2:258].

(p-158) Section

Regarding His saying: ﴿Say: Wait, indeed we are waiting﴾ there are two opinions.

The first: that it is meant as a threat, and so it is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated).

The second: that it is a command to refrain from fighting, and so it is mansukh (abrogated) by the verse of the sword.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 159:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who divided their religion﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Abu 'Amr read "faraqu" (farraqu) with the doubled letter (tashdid). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "faraqu" (fāraqu) with an alif. They also read it this way in [al-Rum:32]. Whoever reads "farraqu" means: they believed in some and disbelieved in others. Whoever reads "faraqu" means: they separated themselves (bayanu). Regarding those referred to, there are four opinions.

The first: they are the people of misguidance from this community. This is the view of Abu Hurayrah.

The second: they are the Jews and the Christians. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, and al-Suddi.

The third: they are the Jews. This is the view of Mujahid.

The fourth: all the polytheists. This is the view of al-Hasan. According to this view, "their religion" is the disbelief which they hold as a religion; and according to the view before it, "their religion" is that which Allah commanded them. And "shiya'" means factions and groups. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of "shayya'tu" in the language is: I followed. The Arabs say: "shā'akumu al-salām" and "ash'aka-kum," meaning: he followed you. The poet said:

Ala ya nakhlatan min dhāti 'irqin burūdi al-zill, shā'akumu al-salām
(Oh palm tree of the place of Irq, cool of shade, may peace follow you.)

And one says:

"I came to you tomorrow, or in a group (shi'atan)," meaning: or the day that follows it. So the meaning of "shi'ah" is those who follow one another, and not all of them are in agreement.

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You are not of them in anything﴾, there are two opinions.

One: You are not of their fighting in anything; then it was abrogated by the verse of the sword. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The second: You are not of them, meaning you are free of them, and they are free of you; their affair is with Allah regarding their recompense. Thus the verse is muhkam (not abrogated).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 160:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like﴾. Ya'qub (Ya'qub al-Hadrami) and al-Qazzaz, from ʿAbd al-Warith, read "ʿashru" (ten) with tanwin and "amthaluha" (its likes) in the nominative case. Ibn ʿAbbas said: he means: from its work, ten good deeds are recorded for him. ﴿And whoever brings an evil deed will not be recompensed except with the like of it﴾. Regarding the good deed and the evil deed here, there are two opinions.

The first: the good deed is the statement "There is no god but Allah," and the evil deed is shirk (associating partners with Allah). This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid, and al-Nakha'i.

The second: it is general for every good deed and every evil deed. Muslim related in his Sahih, from the hadith of Abu Dharr, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like, or I will increase it, and whoever brings an evil deed will be recompensed with its like, or I will forgive." If it is said: (p-160) If the good deed is the word of monotheism, then what is its like, such that the reward of its speaker is ten times its likes? The answer: the reward of a good deed is of known measure with Allah, so He recompenses its doer with ten times its like, and likewise the evil deed. We have already pointed to this in "al-Ma'idah," at His saying: ﴿it is as if he had slain mankind entirely﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 32]. If it is said: the word "mathal" (like) is masculine, so why did He say "ʿashru amthaliha" (ten of its likes) when the feminine ta' (ha') is dropped only in the numeral for feminine nouns? The answer: the "amthal" are created as good deeds, feminine; and the summary of the meaning is: then for him are ten good deeds of its likes. So the ha' is dropped from "ʿashr" because it is a feminine numeral, just as it is dropped in your saying: "ʿashru niʿal" (ten sandals) and "ʿashru jibab" (ten robes).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 161:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Indeed, my Lord has guided me to a straight path"﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, "Guide me to the religion which is the religion of truth." Then he explained that by His saying: ﴿a correct religion﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Abu 'Amr read "qayyiman" with a fatha on the qaf and a shadda on the ya'. Al-qiyam (a term meaning "upright, straight"): the straight. ʿasim, Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read "qiyaman" with a kasra on the qaf and a lightened ya' (without shadda). Al-Zajjaj said: it is a maṣdar (verbal noun), like al-ṣighar and al-kibar (smallness and greatness). Makki said: whoever reads it lightened has formed it on the pattern "fi'al," and its original form would have come with a waw, saying "qawman kamman," as they said: "iwaḍ" and "ḥiwal," but it deviated from the analogical rule. Al-Zajjaj said: the accusative of His saying ﴿a correct religion﴾ is governed by the sense, because when He said "hadani" (guided me), it indicated "ʿarafani" (made me know) a religion. It is also permissible that it be in apposition (badal) to His saying ﴿to a straight path﴾, so the meaning is: "He guided me to a straight path, a correct religion." And "ḥanifan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥal) of Ibrahim, and the meaning is: "He guided me to the creed of Ibrahim in the state of his ḥanifiyya (pure monotheism)."

(p-161) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say, indeed my prayer﴾ means: the prescribed prayer. And "nusuk" is the plural of "nasikah." Regarding nusuk here there are four opinions.

The first: that it means sacrifices. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and Ibn Qutaybah. The second: religion. This was said by al-Hasan. The third: worship.

Al-Zajjaj said: nusuk is everything by which one draws near to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, though what predominates in it is the matter of slaughter.

The fourth: that it is religion, the Hajj, and sacrifices. This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and my life and my death﴾. The majority recite with a vowel on the ya' of "mahyaya" and a sukun on the ya' of "mamati." Nafi' recited with a sukun on the ya' of "mahyaya" and a fatha on the ya' of "mamatiya." Then the exegetes have two opinions regarding its meaning.

The first: its meaning is: no one owns my life and my death except Allah.

The second: my life is for Allah in obeying Him, and my death is for Allah in my return to His recompense. The purpose of the verse is that He informed them that my actions and my states are for Allah alone, not for anyone else, as you associate others with Him.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and I am the first of the Muslims﴾. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: the first of the Muslims of this Ummah.

(p-161) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say, indeed my prayer﴾ means: the prescribed prayer. And "nusuk" is the plural of "nasikah." Regarding nusuk here there are four opinions.

The first: that it means sacrifices. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and Ibn Qutaybah. The second: religion. This was said by al-Hasan. The third: worship.

Al-Zajjaj said: nusuk is everything by which one draws near to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, though what predominates in it is the matter of slaughter.

The fourth: that it is religion, the Hajj, and sacrifices. This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and my life and my death﴾. The majority recite with a vowel on the ya' of "mahyaya" and a sukun on the ya' of "mamati." Nafi' recited with a sukun on the ya' of "mahyaya" and a fatha on the ya' of "mamatiya." Then the exegetes have two opinions regarding its meaning.

The first: its meaning is: no one owns my life and my death except Allah.

The second: my life is for Allah in obeying Him, and my death is for Allah in my return to His recompense. The purpose of the verse is that He informed them that my actions and my states are for Allah alone, not for anyone else, as you associate others with Him.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and I am the first of the Muslims﴾. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: the first of the Muslims of this Ummah.

(p-162) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Shall I seek a Lord other than Allah?﴾ The occasion of its revelation: "The disbelievers of Quraysh said to the Prophet ﷺ: Turn back from this matter, and we will be your guarantors for whatever harm befalls you from consequences, so this verse was revealed." Related by Muqatil.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And every soul earns not but against itself﴾, meaning: no one is seized for the deeds of another. It was also said: the meaning is that against it is the punishment for its disobedience, and for it is the reward of its obedience.

﴿And no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: no sinful soul is seized for the sin of another. The meaning is: no one is taken to account for the sin of someone else. Abu Sulayman said: When every sect of the Jews, the Christians and the polytheists claimed that they were closer to Allah than others, He informed them that He is the Judge between them with His saying: ﴿Then He will inform you of that about which you used to differ﴾, and its parallel is ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Hajj: 17].

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 6, verse 165:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And it is He who made you successors (khala'if) of the earth﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: "al-Khala'if" is the plural of "khalifa" (successor).

al-Shammakh said:
"They are struck by death while it misses me, and I succeed (akhlufu) in dwellings after dwellings."

Regarding those whom they succeeded, the exegetes have three opinions.

The first: that they succeeded the jinn, who were the inhabitants of the earth. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that some of them succeed others. This was said by Ibn Qutayba.

The third: that the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) succeeded all the other nations. This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He raised some of you above others in degrees﴾, that is, in provision, knowledge, nobility, strength, and other things, ﴿that He may test you﴾, that is, that He may try you, so that there becomes apparent from you what reward and punishment are due.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is swift in punishment﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions.

The first: that He called it swift because it is coming, and everything that is coming is near.

The second: that when He wills punishment, He hastens its punishment.
